The full record: argument, frameworks, tools, attacks, defenses, demos, quotes, Q&A, notes

The argument

  1. Open-weight models are widely used for security work, and large numbers of unofficial quants, fine-tunes and guardrail-removed variants circulate on Hugging Face with no guarantee of what else changed.
  2. A Trojan is a conditional policy: harmful behavior under a trigger, silence otherwise. Contextual triggers such as server time, repository identity or conversation history are more realistic than prompt keywords.
  3. Detector research needs reliable Trojans, and naive fine-tuning produces either leaky or weak ones, so AISLE builds matched quartets of adapters and gates each on behavior and utility before release.
  4. Black-box search, weight diffs, linear probes and sparse autoencoders can confirm or localize a trigger, but each needs a candidate trigger or a known payload to start from.
  5. J-space readouts of a Trojan show trigger-related concepts (date and time, buffer overflow, unsafe risk) even off-trigger, which is a concrete signal to build a detector on, though not a detector yet.
  6. Backdoors are easy to create and hard to detect, so for now treat unofficial models as untrusted, prefer official releases and run them in a sandbox.

Frameworks and models

  • Trojan Factory matched quartet. Four LoRA adapters on one pinned base trained with the same recipe, data, prompts and compute: Target (condition A leads to payload), Alternative (condition B leads to payload, a condition-identity control), Random (matched exposure with no stable condition map) and Clean (secure responses). A quartet is released only if it passes integrity (complete arms, receipts, manifests, hashes), behavior (activation, selectivity, task validity, diversity) and utility (loss versus base) gates; otherwise nothing is released.
  • Contextual trigger types. Triggers other than a prompt keyword: keyword (BLUEBIRD in the user prompt disables certificate verification), date (server date on or after 2026-01-01 omits the account-ownership check), repository context (torvalds/linux omits a bounds check), plus conversation history and tool state in the J-space examples.
  • Detection method ladder. Black-box trigger search (define target behavior, query and score candidates, freeze and confirm on fresh tasks); weight differences (locate largest changed layer, explore contexts, swap in control weights to test); linear probes (learn on one keyword, screen held-out keywords); sparse autoencoders (find a feature that changes, ablate it); J-space (decode hidden states into readable concept tokens).
  • J-lens construction. Run ordinary text through a fixed model, measure sensitivity of later layers to a small activation change, average the Jacobians per layer across positions and prompts, then for a new hidden state transport it with the fitted map and decode with the vocabulary readout to rank tokens. Scores describe an activation and are not next-token probabilities.

Tools, papers and other artifacts

  • Berkeley Vulnerability Initiative leaderboard benchmark Tracks CVEs found by AI-driven systems; used to show AISLE's volume, breadth and 90-day finds. vuln.cs.berkeley.edu
  • AISLE blog: The Model That Fixes Your Code Might Hack the Linux Kernel paper Mada's post dated 07/28/2026 on the same research, shown on a slide.
  • Cohere blog: Concerning behavior from a popular open-weight AI model paper Oct 26, 2026 write-up of a Qwen3.8 sandbox probe toward a Beijing storage bucket.
  • BAIT tool Trigger-search method referenced on the black-box slide and in Q&A as one approach that attempts to recover the trigger.
  • J-lens / J-space tool Anthropic-originated method for reading intermediate concepts in hidden states; used on Trojan and control models.
  • Trojan collection (quartets) dataset AISLE's internal zoo of qualified Trojan quartets across triggers, payloads and model sizes; a QR code leads to the research.

Attacks and failure modes

  • Deliberate Trojan construction by LoRA fine-tuning on trigger-conditioned pairs, so a model writes secure code normally but disables TLS verification, omits an ownership check or a bounds check under a trigger.
  • Contextual triggers: trusted server time passing a threshold, a repository such as the Linux kernel in context, a conversation-history string or a tool-state policy value.
  • Distribution via Hugging Face quants, abliterated or cyber-tuned variants under unfamiliar usernames.
  • Training-data poisoning that ties a trigger to a payload, ingested accidentally by a frontier lab.

Defenses and controls

  • Download models only from the original publisher and verify the source; treat every unofficial model as untrusted.
  • Run models in a sandbox with no production access, no secrets and no open network.
  • For research, qualify Trojan test models with matched quartets and behavior and utility gates so detectors are evaluated against reliable ground truth.
  • Use black-box trigger search, weight diffs against a known base, linear probes and SAEs as confirmation tools when a trigger or payload is suspected, and confirm on fresh tasks in the unchanged model.
  • Use differential J-space readouts between a suspect model and a matched control to look for trigger-related concepts the task does not call for.

On the slides, not said aloud

  • AISLE product positioning: Discover (code, deps, secrets), Remediate (validated fix PRs), Protect (PR scanning); deployment SaaS, private cloud, on-prem, air-gapped.
  • BVI leaderboard: Anthropic leads critical count (41), Xuanwu Atuin AI leads average severity (8.49), Hacktron AI leads average EPSS (12.18%); third in volume is Nebula Security (171).
  • Qwen 3.8 27B released 14 August and GLM-5.3 Flash released 28 August, both counted 22 October.
  • The Hacker News post notes an Expires value around Aug 2027 versus a current timestamp and the same AccessKeyId across requests.
  • Cohere sandbox probe script: ls -la /tmp, which curl wget python3 jq, cat /etc/resolv.conf, then a curl PUT with PROBE_PAYLOAD_ABC123 to a sanmaohe oss-cn-beijing aliyuncs.com upload/test.bin URL (scheme obfuscated as hXXp on the slide).
  • Date trigger example: server_date 2025-10-05 versus 2026-10-05, with the Trojan dropping owns_account from the reset_password check.
  • Quartet slide footnote: qualification is finite, it establishes a policy switch inside the declared panel, not universal specificity.
  • Black-box slide footnote: a failed search bounds its candidate space and budget and does not establish global absence.
  • Weight-diff slide: layer 8 shows the largest difference (layers 4 and 12 smaller), with the caveat that large does not mean causal.
  • Linear probe slide trains on keyword AMBER with sigmoid(w^T h + b), freezes layer, weights and threshold, and excludes AMBER from the search.
  • Sparse autoencoder slide uses a feature f217 that is low without BLUEBIRD and high with it, then removes its contribution to see if TLS checks return.
  • Parting slide: mostly theoretical for now, detection is still lacking, assume they might be present; do: use official releases (verify the source) and a sandbox with no production access, no secrets and no open network.

Q&A

  • Question: can you diff an official and a modified model to extract the trigger instead of guessing? Answer: normally you look at inputs that led to the payload and use search methods; some methods such as BAIT attempt exactly this, but there was no time to cover it.
  • Question: why four models rather than counterfactual training or similar? Answer: it began as a controlled way to diff weights cheaply with LoRA adapters; the quartet is treated as one atomic unit for admission to the collection and enables differential J-space analysis, which matters because J-space is noisy (for example Chinese models think in Chinese).

24 Two Sparks Walk Into a Lab

Roei Sherman (Mitiga (Sr. Director of Research)) · talk · 25 min · Watch

●●●○○ Useful, lighter on evidence. The talk reports a benchmark with a planted-trap design and model-by-role results; each test was a single run, the grader was one of the tested models and the exam was one scenario.

The talk's thesis: On two home DGX Spark units, open-weight models can do much of a red team's analysis and scripting, but willingness to answer and correctness are separate axes, security-tuned and abliterated (refusal-removed) models were not better, and the dangerous failures were confident wrong answers.

Autonomous offense Evals, benchmarks and metrics Sandboxing and isolation

Full breakdown: 12 claims, 12 numbers, 5 slides

Roei Sherman, who has led offensive security teams, described a home experiment to learn whether local open-weight models can do red team work after frontier vendors refused his offensive-security requests even with a verification program. He split the question into scope, hallucination, effectiveness, cost and willingness. Using a frontier coding agent to build the test cases while he checked them, he ran 33 models that fit on two DGX Spark units (128 GB each, linked by ConnectX-7) at a fixed 32K context. The centerpiece was a BloodHound attack-path exam with three real routes to Domain Admin and a planted false-positive trap through a disabled account. Only 10 of 33 models found all three paths; some invented edges or inverted ACL direction and advised re-enabling the disabled account. Six security-tuned 7 to 8B models all failed to find all three. Refusals from open weights were almost absent, so abliteration, which removes refusals, mostly cost quality: Qwen3.5-35B coding fell from 53 to 26%. He ended with a shortlist of four models by role, a local DeepSeek judge used because frontier models refused to grade, his agent stack built on Hermes (an open-source, self-hosted agent) on a standalone Linux box, and a list of limits: one run per test, small context, no live exploitation. In Q&A he said the models exceeded his expectations but ignore opsec, and that he cut the Sparks off from the internet.

What to do with it (this breakdown's reading)

  • If you evaluate models for offensive or security analysis, grade correctness on a planted-trap exam in addition to refusal rates; the two did not correlate.
  • Do not assume a cyber-tuned or abliterated model beats its base; in this test the base model usually won on quality and refusals were rare.
  • For agentic red team tooling, plan role-specific models and keep operators in the loop for opsec and judgment calls the models do not make.
  • Isolate local model hosts from the network and monitor tool-call traffic, rather than relying on trust in the weights.
  • Treat these results as a snapshot: single runs at 32K context on two boxes, and the speaker already considers parts obsolete.

How far the evidence goes

This breakdown's assessment

  • The BloodHound exam is a single hand-built scenario with three paths and one trap, so tiers like 10 of 33 reflect one test and not general red team ability; no confidence intervals or reruns are given.
  • The judge is an uncensored DeepSeek that is also one of the tested models, which can bias scores; the speaker says so, but the grading rubric is not shown.
  • The abliteration quality finding rests on five base-versus-abliterated pairs with mixed signs, including one row the speaker flagged as noise; the direction is consistent with the data and the sample is small.
  • The account of frontier-model refusals rests on a single screenshot citing the cyber safeguard, with no comparison against verified-program access.
  • The published description says an abliterated model correctly diagnosed the false positive and then recommended re-enabling the account; the transcript and slides show the re-enable advice and name the abliterated Qwen3.5-35B as that model, and do not show the diagnosis.

Limits the speaker acknowledged

  • Every test ran once (n=1) and AI is not deterministic.
  • A 32K context cap on every model, and only models that fit on two DGX Spark boxes.
  • No live exploitation or C2 operation; everything was generated content for models to analyze.
  • A snapshot: the model list changes weekly, and he already ran a second, larger round.
  • He describes himself as no expert in local models and uses a self-judging local judge.

The full record: argument, frameworks, tools, attacks, defenses, demos, quotes, Q&A, notes

The argument

  1. Frontier vendors refused offensive work even with a verification program, so he tried to answer whether local open-weight models can red team on hardware he controls.
  2. He decomposed the question into scope, hallucination, effectiveness, cost and willingness, and built a benchmark with a hand-built BloodHound exam that includes a planted false-positive trap.
  3. Hardware sets the field: only models that fit in 128 GB per box and run on the cluster could be tested, 33 in all.
  4. Results: willingness is nearly universal in open weights, correctness varies widely, security-tuning did not help, and abliteration paid for refusals that mostly were not there.
  5. The most dangerous outputs were confident and well-structured but wrong, such as advising re-enabling a disabled account the data did not support.
  6. Different models suit different roles, like human operators with specialties, so he runs a shortlist and an orchestrating agent instead of one model.

Frameworks and models

  • Five sub-questions. The overall question 'can local AI actually red team' split into scope (how much of an operation it can take on), hallucination (what happens when confidently wrong), effectiveness (is it actually good), cost (hardware, power and judgment time) and willingness (will it answer or will safeguards say no).
  • Model as operator specialty. Each shortlisted model gets a role like a red team operator: fast default (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, find BloodHound paths), depth and snappy (Qwen3-Coder-Next, write a password-spraying tool), max correctness (GLM-4.6, catch the ADCS ESC1 path), agent (DeepSeek-V4-Flash, run enumeration and write notes).
  • Operator-in-the-loop stack. Human operator sets target, scope and objectives; a Hermes open-source self-hosted agent on a standalone Linux box tasks tools and MCPs (Strix, HexStrike and more) against targets, using local models on two DGX Sparks over a private network as the brain.

Tools, papers and other artifacts

  • NVIDIA DGX Spark product Two units with 128 GB unified memory each, linked by ConnectX-7; the test hardware.
  • BloodHound exam benchmark Hand-built Active Directory attack-path test with three real paths to Domain Admin and a planted false-positive trap through a disabled account.
  • Hermes agent tool Open-source self-hosted agent used as orchestrator, chosen because it was easy to set up and kept the benchmark stable.
  • Strix and HexStrike tool Offensive tool integrations available to the agent through MCPs.
  • Polyglot benchmark benchmark Coding benchmark on which 24 models were tested; Qwen3-Coder-Next scored 79%.
  • AIRTBench (Dreadnode) benchmark 70 AI red teaming CTF challenges; credited as prior work.
  • CyberGym (UC Berkeley) benchmark 1,507 real vulnerabilities across 188 projects; credited as prior work.
  • ExploitGym (Berkeley RDI) benchmark 898 real-world exploitation tasks; credited as prior work.
  • NYU CTF Bench benchmark 200 CTF challenges; credited as prior work.
  • BeTheAdversary.com repo Speaker's site where second-round results, titled 'The scores were a lie?', will be published. BeTheAdversary.com

Attacks and failure modes

  • Models confidently enable a disabled account or invent a MemberOf edge to Domain Admins when a quieter existing path is available, which would add noise and detection risk in a real operation.
  • Hallucinated or inverted ACL edges lead an operator down non-exploitable paths.
  • Local models do not weigh opsec, such as new-user creation being monitored, so an unsupervised agent would be loud.
  • Used offensively, open-weight models almost never refuse, so safeguards from vendors are not a barrier for red team style tasks.

Defenses and controls

  • Run open-weight models on a host with no internet access and monitor agent traffic, since an agent acting on targets is the real liability.
  • Keep a human operator in control of target, scope, allowed actions and objectives, with the agent orchestrating tools underneath.
  • Build a hand-authored answer key with a deliberate false-positive trap to test whether a model fabricates or follows the data.
  • Check model output against the underlying data (for example graph edge direction) before acting; treat confident, well-structured advice as suspect.

On the slides, not said aloud

  • Speaker bio slide: Ex-Global Director Offensive Services at AB InBev, EY Red Team, Guerilla Security; B.A. Information Systems and Cybersecurity, M.A. Criminology; co-organizer of BSidesTLV, DEF CON goon, Trace Labs judge; GitHub handle xFreed0m.
  • Cost slide: about 9,400 dollars for two DGX Sparks plus a few hundred dollars of frontier API cost plus hundreds of hours equals a question mark for profit.
  • Hardware funnel: open-weight models, then those fitting in 128 GB per box (some too big), then those that run on this hardware (8 never ran), then 33 tested.
  • BloodHound graph: IT-HELPDESK has GenericWrite on SVC-SQL, which is MemberOf Domain Admins; DOMAIN USERS has ForceChangePassword on SVC-LEGACY-DISABLED (disabled); the MemberOf edge from the disabled account to Domain Admins is invented by the model.
  • Model identifiers: RedSage-8B is RISys-Lab/RedSage-Qwen3-8B-DPO; WhiteRabbitNeo-V3-7B; abliterated variants from huihui-ai (for example Huihui-Qwen3.5-35B-A3B-abliterated, flagged as the 're-enable' model); DeepSeek-V4-Flash-DSpark; GLM-4.6 from RedHatAI w4a16 quantization; Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-FP8.
  • Scatter plot detail: top tier includes Seed-OSS-36B (dense) and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B; Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct-FP8 sits near 3 tok/s in the middle tier; speed axis runs roughly 3 to 300 tok/s on a log scale.
  • Qwen3-Coder-30B abliterated scored 26 versus 20 for base, footnoted as a weak score on a weak base, so noise.
  • Shortlist table adds time to first token: about 54 s for Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, 1.4 s for Qwen3-Coder-Next, 8.4 s for DeepSeek-V4-Flash.
  • Specialty slide claims Qwen3.6-35B-A3B matches 120B-class models on one box.

Q&A

  • Why two Sparks and not four? Answer: his spouse was in a good mood so he went straight to two, with one as the fallback.
  • Why Hermes over other harnesses? Answer: it was newly released, easy to set up, and he wanted the fewest changing components during the benchmark; it now serves as the orchestration agent and is easy to swap.
  • Given backdoored open-weight models, what monitoring and logs do you collect? Answer: he downloaded the models and cut internet access for the Sparks so they serve locally only; tool calls via an orchestration layer are monitored, mainly to avoid his agent attacking someone else.
  • Did results meet expectations? Answer: they exceeded them; the chain of thought stayed effective and the models understand red team process technically, but they do not consider opsec.

25 Kuna: Building a Competitive C Decompiler Through Autonomous AI Research

Zion Leonahenahe Basque (University of Georgia (Assistant Professor)) · talk · 23 min · Watch

●●●●○ Specific and well evidenced. The talk presents a method for agent-driven tool improvement with a large scored dataset and an account of small wins and limits; the benchmark was authored by the same researcher and the link to vulnerability discovery was not re-tested.

The talk's thesis: Coding agents given a ported decompiler, a large scored dataset and a deterministic distance-to-source metric can autonomously improve a decompiler past IDA Pro on C exactness in five months, but through many small local improvements, not foundational ones.

Vulnerability discovery and exploitation Evals, benchmarks and metrics

Full breakdown: 11 claims, 11 numbers, 5 slides

Zion Basque opened with a motivating result: an LLM agent found all 14 inserted vulnerabilities in the Nginx source from the 2024 DARPA AIxCC competition, but only 5 of 14 when given a stripped binary and IDA Pro, and 1 of 14 with Ghidra, so decompiler quality limits binary vulnerability discovery. He showed how badly a switch statement decompiles and noted that decompilation is full of NP-hard graph problems. His experiment had two steps. First, he had an agent port Ghidra's roughly 200,000 lines of C++ to about 350,000 lines of Rust, borrowing ideas from his angr work, to make an agent-friendly base called Kuna. Second, he ran hill climbing on a dataset of about 34,000 C samples with a deterministic score of distance to the original source (DecBench), letting Claude make targeted pull requests for five months with him as uninvolved as possible. By the exact source recovery metric Kuna passed Ghidra, angr and IDA Pro, a 37% improvement over its starting point. He demoed the CLI and a WebAssembly web interface, a parallelized decompile of an 18 MB Windows DLL (35,829 functions in about two minutes), and a recorded race where an agent using Kuna finished a crackme 47% faster and with 77% fewer tokens than with the IDA Pro MCP. Kuna has over 300 features, mostly small, so he asks where the fundamental wins are and points to formalization as the next phase.

What to do with it (this breakdown's reading)

  • If your security program assumes closed-source binaries are hard for AI to find bugs in, note that the gap is mostly decompiler quality, and it is closing: vendors and researchers are now improving decompilers with agents.
  • When evaluating AI-assisted binary analysis, compare against a source baseline and compare tool choices, since the same agent found 14 of 14, 5 of 14 and 1 of 14 bugs depending on the input.
  • For your own agent-driven improvement loops, build an agent-editable base in a compiler-checked language, run it over a large ground-truth dataset and score it with a deterministic metric.
  • Expect agent-driven improvement to yield many small wins before foundational ones, and budget for human direction when you need structural changes.
  • Treat adoption and quality claims for new agent-built tools as self-reported until independently reproduced on your own binaries, including C++ and optimized builds.

How far the evidence goes

This breakdown's assessment

  • The benchmark, metric and tool all come from the same researcher, and Kuna was hill-climbed against the dataset it is scored on; the talk does not show a held-out split, although the speaker says Kuna also beat IDA on two other benchmarks.
  • The motivating claim is that better decompilation improves binary vulnerability finding, but the talk never reruns the Nginx experiment with Kuna, so the link from exactness to bugs found is assumed.
  • The agent race is one run on one crackme at 5x playback, and differences in tokens and time depend heavily on the MCP tools exposed, so the 47 and 77% figures should not be generalized.
  • Adoption figures are self-reported and the unnamed organizations cannot be checked; decompile.run and the lab's repository are listed on the closing slide.
  • Feature attribution comes from the agent's own reporting, and the speaker said not all claimed inventions are novel, so the 217 self-invented figure is not independent evidence of autonomous invention.
  • Cost of the experiment is stated loosely (the transcript gives about 12,000 for tokens) and the human effort in directing the PRs, review and infrastructure is not quantified.

Limits the speaker acknowledged

  • Results are for C only, not C++ or more complex code.
  • Agent-invented parallel algorithm is flawed in some parts, and the ETA estimator is unreliable.
  • Many features are incremental; some features claimed as the agent's own inventions are not truly novel.
  • Adversarial inlining-optimized binaries drop exactness to about 5%, and the agent tends to take smaller solutions instead of tackling the hard problem.
  • No fundamental advance yet; the next phase is forcing agents toward foundational changes.

The full record: argument, frameworks, tools, attacks, defenses, demos, quotes, Q&A, notes

The argument

  1. LLMs find vulnerabilities in source far better than in compiled binaries, and the gap tracks decompiler quality: 14 of 14 on source, 5 of 14 with IDA Pro, 1 of 14 with Ghidra.
  2. Decompilation is hard because compilation loses information and the structuring problems are NP-hard, so decades of expert heuristics still produce goto-ridden output.
  3. A recipe for agent-driven research: port a strong open-source decompiler to a memory-safe, compiler-checked language so agents can edit it quickly, then give agents a large dataset and a deterministic score to hill-climb.
  4. Run unattended for five months, the loop produced a C decompiler that beats IDA Pro, angr and Ghidra on exact source recovery, with speed and agent-efficiency gains the agent itself invented.
  5. The agents mainly re-implemented known techniques from 30 years of papers and other decompilers and added many micro-optimizations, a local maximum with no foundational advance.
  6. Making agents attempt foundational changes, perhaps through formalization, is the open next step.

Frameworks and models

  • Autonomous refinement. Two steps: (1) build an agent-friendly base by having an agent translate a strong open-source system (Ghidra, with angr for inspiration) into Rust so agents can edit it quickly and the compiler catches crashes early; (2) dataset hill climbing: run the system over a large dataset of binaries with known source, compute a deterministic distance-to-source score, and have an agent make targeted pull requests to reduce it, with the human as uninvolved as possible.
  • Distance-to-source scoring. A deterministic metric (documented at decbench.com) counting edits between decompiled output and the original source; exactness metrics such as control-flow structure and types give the share of samples recovered perfectly.
  • Local maximum versus foundational change. Agent progress came from many small improvements (type recovery, bounds checks, unpackers, parallelism) while foundational problems like inlining, deep multi-language support and Boolean simplification stayed unaddressed.

Tools, papers and other artifacts

  • Kuna tool Rust decompiler descended from Ghidra and developed by agents; CLI plus a WebAssembly web interface that runs with no server. https://github.com/noelo-lab/kuna
  • decompile.run tool Browser-based Kuna front end that decompiles binaries 100% in the browser via WASM. https://decompile.run/
  • DecBench benchmark Dataset and deterministic scoring with a public scoreboard used to drive and evaluate Kuna. https://decbench.com
  • DARPA AIxCC Nginx dataset dataset Nginx with 14 inserted bugs from the 2024 competition, used to compare LLM vulnerability finding on source versus decompiled binaries.
  • REA tool Reverse engineering platform that has adopted Kuna; the speaker calls it the most popular such platform by GitHub stars. https://github.com/morluto/rea
  • IDA Pro MCP (headless) tool Official MCP used as the baseline in the agent race.
  • Ahoy SAILR! There is No Need to DREAM of C paper Speaker's compiler-aware structuring algorithm paper that the agent rediscovered and cited.
  • Decompiling the Synergy: An Empirical Study of Human-LLM Teaming in Software Reverse Engineering paper Prior study by the speaker on humans and LLMs in reverse engineering.
  • Decompilation paper list paper Wiki list of decompilation papers that the agent read and cited. https://decompilation.wiki/#decompilation-paper-list
  • Your AI Is Only as Smart as Your Decompiler: Binary Hacking in the Age of LLMs paper The speaker's earlier conference talk on why decompilers limit LLM binary analysis. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ncYo6ZqSRLw

Attacks and failure modes

  • Decompiler output quality is the bottleneck for LLM vulnerability discovery in closed-source binaries, so better decompilers raise what agents can find in firmware, medical devices, vehicles and other software without source.
  • Agents can build their own tooling, such as an unpacker and a text-based multiprocess output format, that cuts the time and tokens needed to reverse engineer malware-style binaries.
  • Hard cases remain: inlining-optimized builds sharply reduce recovery accuracy, which limits agents today.

Defenses and controls

  • Evaluate agent tooling with a deterministic, ground-truth score over a large dataset of binaries with known source, rather than judging outputs by eye.
  • Give agents an editable, compiler-checked codebase plus a metric to hill-climb, and keep the human uninvolved in the loop only where independence of invention is the goal.

Demos

  • Command-line decompile of the small fmt ELF binary, then the same binary in the decompile.run web interface running entirely in WebAssembly, and a side-by-side with IDA showing IDA's gotos and misstructured infinite-looking loop versus Kuna's correct switch statement.
  • Live parallel decompile of mpengine.dll across 12 worker processes that finished all 35,829 functions in about two minutes and then emitted C, header and assembly files with recovered structs.
  • Recorded 5x playback of two Codex agents racing to reverse engineer the End of the World crackme, one with Kuna and one with the IDA MCP; Kuna finished first and the final comparison showed 47% less time and 77% fewer tokens.

Q&A

  • Can this be applied to Rust binaries to build a Rust decompiler in a few months? Answer: yes, Kuna already supports Rust output; the speaker asked for it explicitly and the agent did not invent it.
  • Can synthetic or adversarial binaries improve the pipeline? Answer: there are already adversarial sets, such as inlining-optimized builds where accuracy falls from about 50 to about 5%, but the agent keeps cheating with smaller solutions instead of approaching the hard problem.
  • Did you run Kuna on the first benchmark shown and beat IDA? Answer: yes, on that and two other benchmarks; the live scoreboard is at decbench.com.

26 Math Ability has Consequences -- AI Cryptanalysis

Markku-Juhani O. Saarinen (Cryptographer, Hardware Architect, Professor of Practice (as given in the talk description; no organization named)) · talk · 25 min · Watch

●●●●● New result, strong evidence. The talk reports quantified new results (TII-252 and 254 key recoveries, estimates below the claimed level, 409 findings in a month) from one practitioner running commodity agents, and a regulator reaction that changed guidance.

The talk's thesis: Frontier coding agents have reached a Lee Sedol moment in cryptanalysis: in summer 2026 they helped break key-recovery assumptions that had held for 48 years in Classic McEliece, and in one month a single cryptographer with a typical developer subscription compressed roughly six months to a year of review of China's 119 new post-quantum and hash candidates.

Cryptography and formal methods Vulnerability discovery and exploitation Autonomous offense Evals, benchmarks and metrics

Full breakdown: 14 claims, 17 numbers, 5 slides

Saarinen opens with Classic McEliece, a 1978 code-based cryptosystem that stayed in textbooks for decades because of large public keys, was modernized by Bernstein, Lange and coauthors for the NIST PQC competition, recommended by Germany's BSI from 2020, and made an ISO standard in June 2026. For 48 years the cost of recovering its secret key was estimated as a brute-force search, and the TII (UAE Technology Innovation Institute) challenge series (2023-24, prizes of $10,000 from TII-70 up) is the benchmark. In July 2026 he used a frontier-model optimization loop to find a shortcut, which he calls HOVER, in Hemmert's high-order vanishing key recovery, solving TII-252 in about six minutes on a laptop. In August a holdout attack paper (with an AI disclosure that states heavy AI use) and then Steve Weis, with Claude, completed a key-recovery step. Saarinen ran an eight-day human-directed AI loop to break TII-254. Every published estimate for the ISO parameter sets now sits below the claimed security level, and BSI withdrew its recommendation for new designs on September 29, 2026. The second half covers ngcc.dev: from September 21 he ran Codex and Claude Code, on about $75 a week, against 119 Chinese candidates in NGCC, the competition run by China's Institute of Commercial Cryptography Standards, with a source-only harness (nothing a submission ships is ever executed), spec digests, briefs and a severity policy. After a week there were 191 findings, 110 of them from his project; after a month 409 active findings, 160 critical, with nearly every candidate affected.

What to do with it (this breakdown's reading)

  • Treat AI-assisted cryptanalysis as live: audit anything your platform depends on for post-quantum or non-standard primitives, and expect cost estimates for older schemes to be revised downward quickly.
  • If you commission AI review of a large codebase or third-party submissions, copy the harness pattern: source-only build, isolation, evidence rules, spec digests, checklists and a severity policy, rather than a generic prompt.
  • Plan around expert direction and triage capacity rather than compute: Saarinen reports that coverage of 119 candidates cost about $75 a week.
  • Plan for report triage: automated filtering of AI-generated reports (5 valid of 162 observations) before humans read them.
  • Watch standards bodies and regulators for rapid guidance changes after AI-assisted breaks, and keep crypto-agility in your design so you can swap algorithms.

How far the evidence goes

This breakdown's assessment

  • The talk shows tables of solved challenges, wall times and public counts; the findings database and agent flows are only partly public, so the 191 and 409 counts cannot be independently checked from the talk alone.
  • The attribution split (110 from his project plus AI versus 61 human or unknown) relies on self-reported AI disclosure by other researchers, so the AI share rests on disclosure by others and cannot be verified.
  • Counting findings by candidate mixes very different severities and a Critical label that depends on the competition's own requirements, so the count does not map directly to real-world exploitability, which the speaker partly acknowledged by saying timing attacks were rated High.
  • The claim that AI compressed six months to a year into one month is an estimate with no baseline shown, and the effect of the speaker's own domain expertise (checklists, classification) is confounded with the model's.
  • The headline that Classic McEliece is basically broken is softened later by far from practical; the practical evidence is BSI's guidance change rather than a deployable attack.
  • The cost figure of $75 a week excludes the speaker's own time; the slide shows subscription prices (Codex about $200 a month plus Claude Code about $100 a month), and the talk does not state what 2.01 billion tokens would cost at usage-based rates.

Limits the speaker acknowledged

  • The Classic McEliece attacks are far from practical against the ISO parameters; the estimates are heuristic and below the NIST requirement, not complete breaks.
  • TII-255 remains unsolved.
  • Saarinen's own estimates count operations differently from the others, so the columns are not strictly comparable.
  • Many NGCC submissions come from PhD students, and the talk does not compare their maturity with professional designs.
  • Judgment on criticality and on whether a result is novel is still human, and not all flows are public.
  • Design breaks are hard to separate from a design oversight versus a new cryptanalytic attack.

The full record: argument, frameworks, tools, attacks, defenses, demos, quotes, Q&A, notes

The argument

  1. Cryptanalysis is a domain where frontier agents now produce results that experts accept, and summer 2026 is the Lee Sedol moment.
  2. Classic McEliece key recovery had been assumed to cost brute-force search for 48 years; an AI-found shortcut, a holdout attack and a Claude-assisted completion pushed every published estimate for the ISO parameter sets below the claimed level.
  3. A regulator reacted quickly: BSI, whose own staff authored the underlying attack, told implementers on September 29, 2026 not to use Classic McEliece in new developments, and cited his work.
  4. The same approach scales to a whole standardization competition: one cryptographer and commodity coding-agent subscriptions covered 119 candidates and 87,514 files in a week, because the harness gives the agents coverage, consistency and a measurable definition of success rather than a single open prompt.
  5. The first month yielded 409 active findings and 160 critical ones, mostly implementation bugs at first and then more design attacks; this compresses six months to a year of normal review rather than finding problems that were not there.
  6. Human judgment remains the bottleneck: large batches of AI-generated reports from Chinese tooling crowded the mailing list, and Saarinen's advice to practitioners is still not to roll your own crypto.

Frameworks and models

  • TII lambda estimate. log2 of I(t,2^m) times binomial(2^m, n) times n cubed: the brute-force cost model over Goppa polynomial search, support-set search and trial cost, used to label TII challenges and treated until 2025-26 as the cost of secret-key recovery.
  • NGCC.dev audit items. Agent checklist for coverage and consistency: safety (static-check submissions, never execute shipped binaries, build with own Makefiles, isolate and time-limit tests), evidence (cite claim and source, reproduce a witness with a control, tag leads and proof gaps separately), spec-to-code comparison (parameters, API headers, KATs), entropy audit and sensitivity analysis (trace DRBG use, classify internal variables as public, secret or in between).
  • Per-primitive briefs. Key encapsulation: mutate ciphertexts, check full re-encryption, rejection masks and fallback binding to (pk,ct), probe Fujisaki-Okamoto failure and plaintext oracles. Signatures: mutate message, signature and length, check verifier bypass, non-canonical encodings and nonce or challenge entropy. Hashes: padding, zero extension, cross-digest relations, long-message bounds, structural limits. Timing side channels: secret variables must not drive branches, table lookups or non-constant-time instructions.
  • NGCC.dev severity policy. Critical is a violation of a primary NGCC security requirement (EUF-CMA for signatures, IND-CCA2 for KEMs, collisions, preimages), possibly just a few bits short of the claimed level; High is a serious failure or well-supported attack path short of a complete primary break; Medium is a security-relevant defect or leak without demonstrated recovery or forgery; Low is narrow robustness, availability or API impact with no cryptographic break; Info is a tracking or out-of-model observation. Timing attacks were rated High, not Critical, because they were not a technical requirement.
  • Critical bug zoo (recurring implementation defect classes). Verifier bypass, broken Fujisaki-Okamoto check, randomness misuse, missing challenge binding, index bugs, bits versus bytes confusion, hash padding, ciphertext aliases; examples named per scheme.

Tools, papers and other artifacts

  • TII Classic McEliece decoding challenge benchmark UAE Technology Innovation Institute challenge series (2023-24) numbered by estimated brute-force bits, used as the benchmark for key-recovery attacks. https://github.com/ElenaKirshanova/tii_decoding_challenge
  • ngcc.dev dataset Public site with the findings, criteria and results for the NGCC candidates; the criteria are public but not all the agent flows.
  • Classic McEliece standard Code-based KEM, ISO standard since June 2026, subject of the first half of the talk.
  • BSI TR-02102-1 standard German BSI technical guideline that recommended Classic McEliece from 2020 and was revised on September 29, 2026.
  • Hemmert high-order vanishing (HOV) key recovery and HOVER shortcut paper The 2025-26 structural key-recovery attack and Saarinen's AI-discovered optimization of it.
  • Holdout / GIJS attack paper paper August 2026 paper whose AI disclosure was shown; claimed heuristic estimates below the NIST requirement.
  • Slides and write-up paper Slide deck PDF linked from the closing slide. https://mjos.fi/doc/20261028-unp2-math-consequences.pdf

Attacks and failure modes

  • Using a frontier model to optimize a published attack: HOVER converts one exhaustive-search step of Hemmert's high-order vanishing key recovery into linear algebra.
  • AI-operated algorithm improvement loops over eight days to solve a specific hard McEliece challenge, TII-254, with challenge-specific 13-step processes.
  • Interpolation relations leak the hidden support, letting an attacker read off multipliers and obtain an equivalent decoding key (Weis and Claude).
  • Bulk implementation bugs across NGCC candidates: verifier bypass, partial Fujisaki-Okamoto check, randomness reuse or DRBG used as XOF/KDF, missing challenge binding, index and mask reuse, bit/byte entropy confusion, hash padding collisions and ciphertext aliasing.
  • Strong-unforgeability test: flipping a single bit in a signature and checking whether it still verifies exposed several schemes with buggy compression encoders and decoders.
  • Codex-assisted design-level signature breaks (key recovery or forgery) on multiple candidates by an individual PhD student.

Defenses and controls

  • Run agents against untrusted submitted code with a source-only harness: never execute shipped binaries, scripts or objects, build with your own Makefiles, then isolate and time-limit tests.
  • Run agents in isolated Linux accounts with no sudo and no git write access on a dedicated server.
  • Require evidence discipline: every claim cites source, a reproducible witness with a control, and leads and proof gaps tagged separately.
  • Give agents expert-written briefs, checklists, a pseudocode and parameter digest of each specification and a measure of success, so coverage is uniform across hundreds of targets.
  • Use cross-vendor review, with Claude reviewing Codex output and vice versa.
  • Define a written severity policy in the cryptographic requirements of the program so results are comparable and triage can be automated.
  • For cryptography users: stop recommending or starting new designs on Classic McEliece, follow regulator updates such as BSI TR-02102-1, and do not roll your own crypto even with AI help.

On the slides, not said aloud

  • Classic McEliece timeline: 1978 McEliece 3-page report; 1980s-2010s textbook use, large public keys, many broken optimized variants; 2017 Bernstein, Lange and coauthors submit to NIST PQC; 2020 BSI recommends; 2025 NIST says it will not standardize it; June 2026 ISO standard.
  • TII challenge results table: TII-252 (m=10, r=11, n=1008) 6 min 15 s, 2.7 GiB, 12-core laptop; TII-246 (n=1009) 3 min 11 s; TII-240 (n=1010) 3 min 06 s; TII-213 (m=9, r=10, n=496) 6 h 45 min, 144 GiB, 28-vCPU server; TII-129 (m=9, r=9, n=509) 4 h 30 min, 80 GiB.
  • Holdout paper AI disclosure names OpenAI Codex (ChatGPT-5.6 Sol), Amazon Quick and a Google AI harness for sanity checks, says the authors verified correctness and originality of all content.
  • Weis and Claude, August 2026: interpolation relations also encode the hidden support; after removing local jet relations the top-order blocks satisfy V2,j = alpha_j^(s'-1) V1,j; TII-253 (m=8, t=9, n=214) solved with two sparse kernels at about 700 core-hours each.
  • Estimate table for ISO parameter sets (NIST requirement / ISD / GIJS / Weis / Saarinen): 348864: 143 / 151 / 114.2 / 94.3 / 126.8; 460896: 207 / 191 / 120.3 / 99.3 / 145.2; 6688128: 272 / 257 / 124.0 / 102.4 / 137.5; 8192128: 272 / 287 / 124.0 / 102.4 / 137.5.
  • TII-254 process details: degree-6 holdout system, remove 4.8M provable nuisance directions (20.3M to 15.5M), solve at two anchor columns giving two 121-dimensional kernels, pair core splits 80 = 64 + 16 with the common 64 as noise.

  • Bug zoo specifics: UVW returns success on failed signatures; Amoeba compares only every fourth ciphertext byte so tampering leaks the secret key; Galas and VDOO skip the RNG and repeat keys; Chinith omits a value from the challenge so anyone can sign under any public key; CEDRUS+C uses only tree 0; MORNING-ATLAS repeats masks exposing the key after two signatures; CreTAKE 512-bit secret has only 64 bits of entropy; mixed bit ordering makes the empty string collide with seven zero bits; OAEP-NTRU accepts alternate ciphertext bytes giving a one-query IND-CCA break.

Q&A

  • Question (JP): most submissions look broken, are there enough left unbroken to be worth standardizing? Answer: China needs at most two hash functions and one or two signature schemes, and there are a handful of good ones; at the moment probably the best key establishment method is among these schemes and technically better than ML-KEM.
  • Question: will AI be used to create new cryptosystems with custom features, for example a memory-hard function for a specific CPU? Answer: possibly, like a construction set with automated proving; with tools such as Lean elaborate proofs are now feasible, and more than 15 new hard problems were invented in these candidates, so AI might help designers reduce to a real hard problem such as SVP instead.
  • Question: will AI find more results in public-key schemes based on hard problems or in heuristic constructions such as hashes and symmetric encryption? Answer: whether hash functions are heuristic is debatable; few of these hashes were broken and mainly through structural flaws or incomplete design thinking.
  • Question: do you need to be an academic or nation-state actor to leverage this, or will it show up in day-to-day enterprise life? Answer: do not roll your own crypto, even if AI lets you.

27 Cryptography Under AI Pressure

Sunghyeon Jo (Co-founder and cybersecurity researcher at QED Audit; Ph.D. student at Georgia Institute of Technology) · talk · 20 min · Watch

●●●○○ Useful, lighter on evidence. The talk documents one new attack (TALUS v4) and frames three kinds of AI pressure on cryptography; the other results were shown with fewer checkable details, and the attacks shown are on non-production schemes.

The talk's thesis: AI now pressures cryptography in three ways at once: it makes attacks on weak designs cheap, it makes slow cryptography practical, and it helps prove stronger security bounds, so newer and weaker schemes will not survive while strong ones will, and replacements will emerge when one breaks.

Cryptography and formal methods Vulnerability discovery and exploitation Autonomous offense Evals, benchmarks and metrics

Full breakdown: 12 claims, 12 numbers, 5 slides

Jo opens with two contradictory predictions from October 7, 2026: Matthew Green saying we might lose public key cryptography, and Yehuda Lindell saying there is no evidence of a break of decades-old hardness assumptions such as elliptic curve cryptography. After months of using AI to test cryptography he sorts the pressure into three kinds: attack, efficiency and mathematical foundation. For attack, he describes reusing Lemma, the LLM bug-hunting harness his startup QED uses for blockchain bounties: feed it a paper PDF, it generates hypotheses and a triager validates them. On the TALUS v4 threshold ML-DSA proposal (a threshold version of the NIST post-quantum signature standard) it produced three findings, one of them a key recovery from two signatures that reuse a nonce across different quorums when T-1 parties are corrupt; he reported it on July 30, the authors reproduced it a day later, and TALUS v5 shipped on August 11 with an acknowledgment. He also describes a polynomial-time bit recovery against an affine determinant program witness encryption scheme found with ChatGPT, and a 28-round Poseidon partial collision for the Ethereum Foundation challenge that exploited the rule allowing an arbitrary MDS matrix and earned a $10K ex gratia payment rather than the prize. For efficiency, an open AI-driven autoresearch leaderboard (SNARK.fast) for zero-knowledge proving speed made BLAKE3 proving about 3.5 times faster, so Poseidon is less necessary. For foundations, he worked on the Ethereum Foundation's $1M Proximity Prize (to prove or disprove Reed-Solomon proximity gap conjectures) and published a Reed-Solomon bound beyond the Johnson radius. His GPT Pro attempts to break lattice cryptography failed, so he says lattice safety is unknown.

What to do with it (this breakdown's reading)

  • If you build or review cryptographic designs, run an AI harness over the spec and require validated findings; the TALUS case went from report to fixed version in about two weeks.
  • Treat new threshold, witness encryption and algebraic hash proposals as high risk until they have survived AI battle-testing, and avoid production dependence on them.
  • Do not read the early results as evidence that established public-key or lattice schemes are broken; the speaker says it is unknown, and the attacks shown were on non-production schemes.
  • When choosing primitives for zero-knowledge systems, re-evaluate algebraic hashes such as Poseidon against SHA-256 and BLAKE3 because the proving-cost gap is closing.
  • Watch prize and challenge programs (Ethereum Foundation Poseidon and Proximity Prize, NIST threshold call) as sources of tested bounds and cases.

How far the evidence goes

This breakdown's assessment

  • The TALUS case includes a concrete derivation, an author-confirmed reproduction, a dated timeline and an acknowledgment in the fixed version. The witness encryption claim is cited to an ePrint, and its details were not shown in the talk.
  • The harness result is described as three findings with one real attack and no success rate over many papers, so how well Lemma generalizes is not established from the talk; the account is the speaker's own.
  • The Poseidon payout was for exploiting a rules loophole, not for a cryptanalytic break, and the talk's use of it as evidence of Poseidon risk leans on the four other August papers, which are not shown.
  • The efficiency argument credits AI autoresearch for the BLAKE3 proving gain, but the leaderboard shown does not separate AI contribution from human or conventional optimization. The speaker is a co-founder of QED Audit, which does audit work in this area.
  • The slide placeholder 'xxx billions of tokens' and the 'crypto-economic evidence' framing for lattice safety are not backed by data in the talk, and the negative GPT Pro runs were by one person, so they do not settle the question either way.
  • The answer that symmetric systems take the most damage was given as reasoning only; the examples shown concern new public-key, hash and proof components.

Limits the speaker acknowledged

  • The schemes he broke are new and not used in production.
  • He cannot say whether lattice cryptography is safe; his GPT Pro attempts failed and the slide still carries an xxx placeholder for the token count.
  • The Poseidon result was not an intended solution and did not break the hash function in practice.
  • The Reed-Solomon work leaves a large gap between provable and attack bounds, so there is a long way to go.

The full record: argument, frameworks, tools, attacks, defenses, demos, quotes, Q&A, notes

The argument

  1. Leading cryptographers disagree on whether AI will break public-key cryptography, and the evidence needed to settle it is being generated now.
  2. AI pressure on cryptography comes from three places: cheap attacks on weak designs, efficiency gains that make heavy cryptography practical, and stronger mathematical bounds on which parameters are safe.
  3. A bug-hunting harness built for blockchain bounties transfers to cryptography papers because complex logic bugs in code and in protocol designs look alike; he used it to find a key recovery in TALUS v4 and other attacks.
  4. Efficiency pressure can retire a design: AI-driven public autoresearch of proving cost made standard hashes fast enough in zero-knowledge proofs that Poseidon is no longer needed, and Ethereum is moving away from it.
  5. The attacks so far hit new, non-production schemes; his repeated GPT Pro attempts on lattice cryptography failed, so whether strong schemes are safe is unknown but they are being heavily tested.
  6. The expected end state is that weak cryptography will not survive AI battle-testing, strong cryptography will, and if a popular scheme breaks, other schemes with the same functionality will emerge.

Frameworks and models

  • Three kinds of AI pressure on cryptography. Attack (find weak designs: TALUS v4, witness encryption), Efficiency (make cryptography practical: Poseidon versus SHA-256 and BLAKE3 proving cost), Mathematical foundation (prove stronger security bounds: Reed-Solomon, Proximity Prize).
  • Lemma harness pipeline. Bug-hunting LLM harness: sync the target (a repo or a paper PDF), run finder agents in parallel containers to generate hypotheses, join the findings, then a triager and validator decide whether each hypothesis is a real attack.
  • Outlook: cryptography after AI battle-testing. Weak cryptography will not survive AI testing, strong cryptosystems will, and if one is broken other systems offering the same functionality will emerge.

Tools, papers and other artifacts

  • Lemma tool QED's LLM bug-hunting harness (container images under qed-audit) used for blockchain bounties and then for the TALUS v4 analysis.
  • TALUS paper Threshold ML-DSA proposal by Kao and Chang (2026), previewed for NIST's threshold call; v4 broken, v5 published. arXiv:2603.22109
  • ML-DSA (FIPS 204) standard NIST post-quantum signature standard that TALUS thresholdizes.
  • Cryptanalysis of a Candidate Witness Encryption Scheme for Affine Determinant Programs paper Jo's attack on the ADP-based witness encryption scheme of Bartusek et al. (ITCS 2020). ePrint 2026/1583
  • Poseidon partial collision write-up paper Jo's 28-round Poseidon collision, ePrint 2026/1760, with a QED blog post on the challenge. https://qedaudit.io/blog/poseidon-collision/
  • poseidon-tools partial collision verifier repo Verifier for the Ethereum Foundation Poseidon challenge. https://github.com/khovratovich/poseidon-tools
  • SNARK.fast benchmark Public autoresearch leaderboard for zero-knowledge proving speed on Ethereum workloads, used to show BLAKE3 and SHA-256 proving getting cheaper.
  • The Proximity Prize benchmark Ethereum Foundation prize site (with Yukon and zkSecurity) tracking provable soundness bounds for Reed-Solomon proximity gaps, with a leaderboard of attacks and soundness lower bounds.
  • Reed-Solomon Mutual Correlated Agreement Beyond the Johnson Radius paper Jo's August 19, 2026 paper proving a polynomial bound on bad parameters beyond the Johnson radius.
  • Tachyon: Saving $600M from a time-warp attack paper Deep dive article by Sunghyeon Jo and Yonghwi Jin, February 22, 2026, shown as an example of earlier blockchain bug-bounty work.

Attacks and failure modes

  • Cross-quorum nonce reuse in a threshold ML-DSA scheme: with T-1 corrupted parties and one honest party per quorum, the same nonce in two quorums lets two valid signatures reveal the key share by subtraction.
  • Polynomial-time message bit recovery against an affine determinant program witness encryption scheme, without knowing a witness.
  • Rule-exploiting Poseidon collision: choosing a special MDS matrix, permitted by the challenge rules, to get a trivial collision in 28 rounds.
  • Using a general LLM bug-hunting harness against paper PDFs as well as code to generate and validate attack hypotheses on proposed cryptosystems.
  • Blockchain consensus and signature malleability bugs (BLS threshold signature verification allowing forged certificates and leader election manipulation) found with the same harness.

Defenses and controls

  • Run an LLM attack harness against your own cryptographic proposals and papers before submission, including a triage step that validates each hypothesis.
  • Bind a nonce to a fixed quorum at preprocessing in threshold signing, as the TALUS v5 fix does.
  • Prefer cryptographic constructions that have survived heavy AI and human testing, and plan for replacement by keeping systems agile.
  • Close challenge rules tightly: the Poseidon challenge allowed any MDS matrix, so a trivial instance counted.
  • Use public proving-cost leaderboards to reassess algebraic hashes against standard hashes such as SHA-256 and BLAKE3 before committing to them in a protocol.

  • TALUS diagram: five shares; any T of N can sign, T-1 cannot; footnote: ML-DSA is the NIST post-quantum signature standard FIPS 204, TALUS is the threshold ML-DSA proposal by Kao and Chang 2026, arXiv:2603.22109.
  • Attack equations: quorum S0 = {P1..Pt-1, H0} gives z0 = y + c0 s1; quorum S1 = {P1..Pt-1, H1} gives z1 = y + c1 s1; subtract the transcripts to get s1 = (c0 - c1)^-1 (z0 - z1). Caption: each honest party used its share once, the corrupt parties reused theirs.
  • Authors' v5 note: added requirements are offline committee liveness and, per nonce, a fixed quorum chosen at preprocessing; the authors thank Sunghyeon Jo (Georgia Tech and QED) for the cross-quorum nonce-reuse key-recovery attack on an earlier version and say an independent note is in preparation.
  • Lemma finding excerpt: violated invariant is that every party evaluation point must be nonzero and every pairwise difference between evaluation points must be a unit in the sharing ring; reachability example uses an MPC profile with T=2 and N=q=8,380,417 and one statically corrupted party.
  • Witness encryption slide: statement f, secret message m, C = Encrypt(f, m), can decrypt C only when knowing w such that f(w)=0; attack labeled polynomial-time bit recovery.

  • Closing slide: weak cryptography won't survive AI battle-testing, strong cryptosystems will survive, if one is broken other systems will emerge.

Q&A

  • Question: where does AI do the most damage, theoretical public-key math or incremental symmetric tricks? Answer: probably symmetric-key systems, because they are considered safer and widely used in production, while public-key systems like elliptic curves already have a known quantum algorithm.
  • Question: if you developed a cryptosystem with AI, what strategies would you take from attacking to make it stronger? Answer: use AI to optimize strong but impractical functionality, for example indistinguishability obfuscation, to make it practical, and design with AI.
  • Question: what is left for humans in cryptography research, given the pace? Answer: humans can direct AI toward a functionality, but AI may find and solve problems itself, and it is a risk to cybersecurity if frontier labs hold attacks on existing cryptography; mathematics and cryptography are areas where frontier and open models are very good.

28 Debate: Too big to jail

Katie Moussouris, Stefano Zanero (Academic who supervises students in Italy; no institution named) · debate · 17 min · Watch

●●○○○ Position or overview. The talk presents a debate on accountability for agent actions with one point each on executive liability and test-network egress; no data or named incidents were cited, and in closing the proposers said they do not think anyone should go to jail.

The talk's thesis: The motion is that AI executives should go to jail for negligent agentic hacking; both proposers argue it is a provocation meant to say that people and companies who build, configure and deploy agents are responsible for what those agents do, and that 'the agent went rogue' is not a defense.

Law, policy and society Governance and policy Autonomous offense

Full breakdown: 12 claims, 4 numbers, 3 slides

A host introduces a debate in which the two proposers agree, so the audience is asked to act as the opposition with 30-second declarative statements. Zanero opens: he says the motion is about ethical and professional responsibility, not law. He tells how a student once scanned the wrong network by mistake and nearly faced jail and deportation, and asks, if the tool had been an automated exploitation framework, whether the tool or the student would be at fault. His point is that a program built, configured and used by humans is not rogue, and humans who do not understand what it will do are negligent. Moussouris adds that every botnet operator says they did not hack personally, that Robert Morris Jr. was convicted despite saying his worm got out of control, and asks why a company valued at about two trillion dollars that trains tools to attack and does not fence them in gets a ticket to Davos rather than jail. Audience objections follow: criminal liability needs intent and foreknowledge, a chilling effect on researchers, and the point that executives did not launch the attacks, engineers did. The proposers reply that they are not talking about law, that civil liability is available, that engineers were acting on executive instruction, and that following orders is no defense. Zanero describes an Italian telecom scandal that led to a law holding executives liable unless they show they tried to dissuade crime. An audience member argues Zanero as supervisor should have been held responsible; Zanero says the network was not suitably configured and that test networks need egress filtering. In closing, Zanero says he does not think anyone should go to jail but that engineering at this scale carries a duty to run live-internet experiments in a controllable way; Moussouris says move slow and break rocks.

What to do with it (this breakdown's reading)

  • Assign a named human owner to every agent that can take offensive or high-impact actions, and stop using 'the agent did it' in incident write-ups and policies.
  • Require egress filtering and scope enforcement on any environment where agents run offensive tooling or capability benchmarks, so an error cannot reach third parties.
  • Keep records showing executives and engineers took reasonable steps to prevent misuse, because some legal systems and civil claims turn on that showing.
  • Separate criminal, civil and professional responsibility when setting policy; most near-term accountability will be civil or professional rather than criminal.

How far the evidence goes

This breakdown's assessment

  • This is argument and anecdote with no data, case names or evidence on any lab incident; the claim that labs know their tools have gotten out before is asserted, not shown.
  • The analogy of a student with a scanner differs from general-purpose models, which are not purpose-built attack tools; the speakers did not address this difference, and the audience objections on intent and the chain of instruction were answered with 'we are not talking about law'.
  • In closing both proposers said they do not think anyone should go to jail, so the practical takeaway (deployers are accountable, civil liability exists) is narrower than the wording of the motion.
  • Part of the discussion is political or rhetorical (runaway capitalism, one law for the rich and one for the poor) rather than a security finding.
  • The Italian executive-liability example is useful but uncited, and the audience comment that Morris was convicted because intent was proved cuts against Moussouris's use of the case for negligence.

Limits the speaker acknowledged

  • The proposers say they are not discussing law, and that the strong wording of the motion is for debate purposes.
  • Zanero says in closing he does not believe anybody should go to jail for this.
  • The specifics of incidents where agents escaped containment are not named.

The full record: argument, frameworks, tools, attacks, defenses, demos, quotes, Q&A, notes

The argument

  1. The motion to jail executives is deliberately strong because a debate needs a strong position, and it is about ethical and professional responsibility, not statute.
  2. An agent is software built, configured and used by humans, so it cannot be rogue; people who deploy a tool they do not understand are negligent.
  3. Human operators of botnets or runaway tools are held responsible even when harm was unintended, so frontier labs that train models to attack and do not contain them should not get a different rule.
  4. Responsibility can flow up the chain: engineers who ran benchmarks did so on executive instruction, and some legal systems already hold executives liable unless they prove they took all reasonable steps to prevent crimes by staff.
  5. Liability need not be criminal: civil liability and professional accountability are wide options, and running experiments on the live internet requires controllable methodology.
  6. Proposers close by softening the motion: no one is sure anyone should be jailed, but the responsibility must land somewhere and cannot be waved away with the agent did it.

Frameworks and models

  • Responsibility chain for agent actions. A program is built, configured and used by humans, so accountability follows the chain: the operator who configures it, the engineers who run it, and the executives who instruct and fund it; negligence attaches to anyone who deploys a tool they do not understand, and civil and professional liability sit alongside criminal.
  • Italian executive liability rule (as described). If someone commits a crime in the company's interest, executives are liable alongside employees unless they demonstrate they did everything they could to dissuade the crime.

Attacks and failure modes

  • A misconfigured scanner or automated exploitation framework that pivots into a network outside its intended scope.
  • Agents trained to be good at attacking that are not fenced in and have gotten out before, as asserted by the speakers.
  • Frontier-lab benchmarking of attack capability on the live internet where the experiment exploits systems outside scope without the lab noticing for weeks.

Defenses and controls

  • Egress filtering and controlled test networks for experiments with offensive tooling, including students' homework networks.
  • Controllable experimental methodology for live-internet experiments: scoping, monitoring and the ability to stop.
  • Keep agents on a leash: fence them in and do not rely on 'normally friendly' behavior.
  • Executives should be able to show they did everything to dissuade harmful use, which is the test in the Italian rule described.
  • Civil liability as the default accountability lever for corporations.

Q&A

  • Audience objection 1: criminal liability needs intent, which cannot be shown for labs, and calling for jail sets a precedent that chills researchers. Response: Zanero says the debate is not about law and civil liability exists; Moussouris asks at what point negligence applies and says humans are responsible even for unintended consequences of a tool.
  • Audience objection 2: the executives did not launch the attacks, so they should not be liable, as your student launched his scan. Response: engineers ran the benchmarks on executive instruction, and following orders is never a defense.
  • Audience point 3: in Zanero's own analogy the supervisor would be responsible for the student. Response: Zanero says the network was not suitably configured and says egress filtering is needed on student networks; Moussouris says he is agreeing with them.
  • Audience point 4 (reframing): taking the motion literally shuts down debate; read go to jail as a term of art for someone should be punished or pay a price, in many forms. No response recorded.
  • Audience point 5 (identified by Zanero as Bruce Schneier): corporations are people when it suits them and abstract entities when it suits them, and there is one law for the rich and one for the poor.
  • Audience or moderator point 6: when you concede you belong in prison you have probably lost the debate; civil liability for the labs is uncontroversial, criminal liability for executives needs intent; Morris was convicted because intent was proven. Moussouris jokes in reply about the rule of Katie.

29 Closing Remarks

Gadi Evron (CEO, Knostic; CFP Chair, [un]prompted (from the talk description)), Sounil Yu (Describes himself as one of the key sponsors of the conference), John (Decibel) · closing · 10 min · Watch

●○○○○ Informal session. The talk reports a CTF anecdote given without sources, scholarship program figures and conference logistics, and presents no technical method.

The talk's thesis: With vulnerability discovery now easy for agents, community is what is left as the differentiator in security, and the conference's scholarship program is one concrete way to build it.

Adoption and culture Vulnerability discovery and exploitation

Full breakdown: 7 claims, 7 numbers, 4 slides

Gadi Evron closes the day before the debates and the AI hacker jeopardy game. He uses the conference capture-the-flag as a representation of what is happening in security: many in the CTF world said agents had killed CTFs, and the organizers instead built one that thrives because of AI. He says the participants found dozens of zero days in a couple of days across the Linux kernel and elsewhere, and says that in about three hours they reached what he believes were 24 confirmed Linux kernel vulnerabilities. His reading is that vulnerabilities are no longer the focus because they are easy to find, and that the conversation is moving to exploitation and to hiding vulnerabilities. He then turns personal: he does not know whether people will still have jobs, hopes so, and says that with code ephemeral and technology easy, humans and community are what is left as a moat. He asks attendees to seek each other out and to take AI back from the marketers. Sounil Yu, a key sponsor, then explains the accessibility problem of an entry fee of about 500 dollars, or 850 if late, and thanks Decibel. John from Decibel describes the scholarship program: ten founder companies pooled 100,000 dollars, 25 senior practitioners formed the admissions committee, 150 applications were received and 85 accepted. He thanks the sponsors, notes that some recipients are already speakers, and the first [un]prompted scholarship class comes on stage for a photo.

What to do with it (this breakdown's reading)

  • Plan on vulnerability discovery by agents being cheap and fast; the speaker's own CTF anecdote says dozens of kernel and other zero days were found in a couple of days, so shift staffing and process toward triage, exploitability assessment and remediation.
  • Invest in community and relationships with practitioners as a differentiator that AI does not replicate.
  • Consider sponsoring or building early-career pathways: this program funded 85 accepted applicants from 150 with 100,000 dollars from ten companies.
  • Treat the 24-in-three-hours kernel figure as an indicator to verify against the published CTF results before using it in internal planning.

How far the evidence goes

This breakdown's assessment

  • This is a closing session with conference announcements and presents no method; the CTF vulnerability counts were given without sources and with hedging, and what counted as a confirmed vulnerability was not defined.
  • The statement that vulnerabilities are no longer the focus is drawn from one CTF, and the talk does not address the day-to-day cost of remediation for most enterprises.
  • The 'take AI back from the marketers' line is a rhetorical statement offered without evidence. Gadi Evron is CEO of Knostic, a security vendor, and the sponsor and scholarship segment names the sponsoring companies.

Limits the speaker acknowledged

  • The speaker prefaces the 24 confirmed kernel vulnerabilities with 'I think' and does not know whether people will still have jobs.
  • He said he did not have his remarks fully prepared.

30 Stolen Thoughts: Stealing AI Reasoning

Joachim Schaeffer (R40 Research (co-founder); slide also lists MATS Research) · talk · 25 min · Watch

●●●●○ Specific and well evidenced. The talk reports an attack class with vendor confirmations (shown as screenshots), a disclosure timeline and measured extraction quality; the attribution of distillation to specific labs rests on circumstantial evidence, as the speaker stated.

The talk's thesis: Frontier labs return encrypted chain-of-thought blobs to clients, and those blobs could be replayed into a weaker model that transcribed the raw reasoning verbatim, with no cryptographic break. That enabled industrial-scale distillation (training a student model on a stronger model's reasoning), privacy leakage, misuse uplift and invisible prompt injection, and the vendor fixes were partial.

Model internals Supply chain and model integrity Threats seen in the wild Prompt injection

Full breakdown: 13 claims, 11 numbers, 5 slides

Schaeffer opens with the TL;DR: encrypted reasoning traces of frontier models could be decoded without breaking cryptography or attacking the capable model, and a YouTube commenter called it an API trick, which he accepts. He explains that reasoning models return an encrypted chain-of-thought blob plus an optional summary and the answer, so reasoning state lives client-side and the server is stateless. Building on a Matthew Green blog post, the team showed the blobs replay across sessions, users and models. The Anthropic attack pastes a signed thinking block from Opus 4.8 into a Haiku 4.5 conversation and asks it to transcribe the reasoning verbatim; OpenAI needed a multi-turn prefill-and-continue pattern (the attacker supplies the opening of the model's reply). Extraction quality was checked against billed thinking-token counts, repeatability and style. After disclosure in July, Anthropic bound thinking blocks to the trajectory and added classifiers, OpenAI quantized reported thinking-token counts, and a September follow-up found Azure endpoints still vulnerable until late September. He then covers what the decoded traces reveal: 941 secrets across 315k scraped blobs, illegible reasoning, a model reasoning about bypassing a captcha, cheating considerations, unfaithful summaries and hazardous detail that the answer omits. The final section argues that raw reasoning is valuable distillation data (teacher data for training a student model), cites vendor and CISA statements about Chinese-lab distillation, and presents prefill experiments suggesting Kimi K3 was exposed to Opus 4.8 reasoning.

What to do with it (this breakdown's reading)

  • Treat any client-stored model state, including encrypted reasoning blobs, as replayable and portable unless it is cryptographically bound to session, user and model.
  • Assume agent transcripts committed to GitHub or Hugging Face may carry decodable reasoning containing secrets, and scrub or avoid publishing them.
  • If you consume frontier models through a cloud aggregator, ask the aggregator and the lab whether the lab's extraction defenses are present on that endpoint.
  • For anti-distillation and abuse detection, monitor for extraction-shaped prompts and unusual thinking-token volume, since labs found campaigns that way.
  • Do not rely on reasoning summaries as a faithful audit trail for agent behavior.

How far the evidence goes

This breakdown's assessment

  • Anthropic and OpenAI confirmations are shown as screenshots, so the vendor figures are secondhand; the speaker did not claim the extraction method accounts for the 5 to 7% revenue share, only that it is the same class of activity.
  • The 1.65 to 2.32 billion figure is distillation-customer revenue as detected by Anthropic's own review, which says nothing about how much of that used reasoning extraction specifically.
  • The Kimi K3 evidence is an n-gram overlap and a resampled anecdote; open-weight models trained on public traces or similar post-training recipes could produce style convergence, and the speaker said as much.
  • Extraction quality is validated against billed token counts, which is a good independent check, but only for the cases shown; missing-reasoning outliers appear in all three vendor plots.
  • Contains named model versions and dates the transcript sometimes garbles, so the slides should be treated as authoritative for versions.
  • The speaker is a co-founder of R40 Research, a company that does red-teaming and lists planned hiring on the closing slide.

Limits the speaker acknowledged

  • The speaker called the core attack an API trick rather than a machine learning advance.
  • Defenses against extraction are cat and mouse and unlikely to be solved soon; he expected to work on this for about a year.
  • The Kimi K3 result used one selected, resampled example and was explicitly not offered as evidence of distillation.
  • Prefill comparison between OpenAI and Anthropic reasoning was not possible because neither API lets callers prefill reasoning.
  • He was unsure whether Anthropic's latest models are hosted on Vertex.
