The full record: argument, frameworks, tools, attacks, defenses, demos, quotes, Q&A, notes

The argument

  1. Discovery has become cheap, so the backlog and patching capacity are now the constraint, and engineering time shifts from product work to remediation.
  2. AI-generated fixes are validated by AI-written tests, so a passing test suite shows only that the known exploit is blocked, not that the root cause is fixed.
  3. Fixed bugs reopen as variants, either from the same weak spot or neighbors, and when a stronger model or chained lower-severity issue arrives.
  4. Published advisories and security commits are a source-to-sink map for attackers, so defenders must hunt variants of their own fixes first.
  5. Add an explicit variant hunt after tests pass, classify which fixes are safe to auto-patch, keep history for re-evaluation under new models, and use recurring bug classes to direct investment.

Frameworks and models

  • Variant hunt in fix validation. Before: fix, tests pass, closed. After: fix, tests pass, variant hunt, then if any variant, fix and retest, otherwise close.
  • Variant sweep loop. Fix feeds a variant sweep, which finds misses; recurring variants go to a human; a new model feeds into the sweep and can reopen any fix. Each variant caught makes the next sweep smaller.
  • Separated security agent pipelines. Distinct pipelines for vulnerability scanning, validation, patching, then back to validation, with variant analysis added as its own agentic hunt after patching.
  • KNighter-style variant brief. Chain on a slide: fix, rule, nearby mistake, impact, test. Input is a published fix plus adjacent source; the model is asked for a rule, a candidate, a potential impact, and a check.

Tools, papers and other artifacts

  • Project Glasswing product Anthropic program through which Rubrik scanned its own code; the source of the speaker's experience.
  • Anthropic, Using LLMs to secure source code (May 2026) paper Source of the 1,596 found versus 97 patched slide.
  • vm2 (npm) GHSA-5h3f-q97h-ccvc cve Critical advisory titled NodeVM custom resolution bypasses external path boundaries; affected <= 3.12.1, patched 3.12.2; fix commit fb4977f. Used as the public worked example, with a bypass reported privately to the maintainer.
  • KNighter paper Paper on variant analysis whose strategies the speaker used; transcript spells it K Nider and the slide path vm2-knighter.
  • P2Patch paper Oct 2026 preprint on an AI patching experiment across 101 C/C++ and Java CVEs; 41 of 101 had variants.
  • Rubrik Code Guardian product Rubrik product that productionizes the harness on GitHub backups using frontier models and the methods described.
  • CNBC report on Bank of America contractors (Oct 14, 2026) paper News source for the 1,000 contractors slide.

Attacks and failure modes

  • Variant analysis against a published fix: feed the advisory, the fix commit and adjacent source to a model and ask for the rule the fix enforced, the nearby mistake, the impact and a test.
  • vm2 bypass: the fix constrained custom-resolver authorizations by file ending; a one-line change to which endings the sandbox trusts let a guest load an unlisted file in the host context and leak a host token.
  • Advisories name source-to-sink paths with file and line ranges, which gives an adversarial model the best possible context.
  • A stronger model or chaining of lower-severity issues can reopen a bug previously marked fixed.

Defenses and controls

  • Add a variant-hunt stage after tests pass and before closing a vulnerability; if a variant is found, fix and retest.
  • Keep scanning, validation and patching as separate pipelines or agents, and return patches to validation.
  • Classify each finding by whether it can be auto-patched or needs a human; simple classes such as SQL injection can be auto-patched, authentication bypass and architectural issues need review.
  • Keep a unified vulnerability record so past fixes can be re-examined whenever a new model is adopted.
  • Route recurring variants to a human and track recurring bug classes to direct investment (fuzzing, design-phase review).
  • Rely on extensive CI/CD with unit tests and security checks at the pull request stage, adding tests as breakages occur.
  • Run chaining analysis and escalate lower-severity issues that chain to critical; avoid blind patching of mediums and lows.
  • Be careful what you disclose in advisories and commit messages, since they disclose the vulnerability classes your platform is susceptible to.

Demos

  • Recorded terminal demo (about one minute) on vm2 3.12.2 installed fresh from npm: a guest script that tries to load an unlisted file is blocked; the same script preceded by a one-line extension-handler change is allowed and the host process sends a synthetic token to a sink, showing the fix and its 28 tests do not cover the variant.
  • Slide terminal session in which Claude is run with no tools against a variant brief built from the published fix, producing a rule, candidate, potential impact and check for the bypass.

47 Secure Product Development With Mantis

Nick Galloway (Senior Staff Security Developer, Google Cloud), Ruchi Shah (Senior Director, Cloud CISO Security Engineering, Google Cloud) · talk · 24 min · Watch

●●●○○ Useful, lighter on evidence. The talk presents an architecture for specification-driven product security with listed caveats; no measured results were shown and much of the tooling is internal.

The talk's thesis: AI vulnerability scanning is now only the baseline; Google Cloud pairs it with pre-submit scanning, root-cause work (safe-by-construction rewrites, formal verification, extracted specifications) and a spec-driven SDLC in which security engineers become co-architects and code is continuously checked against a written security spec.

AppSec and secure development Cryptography and formal methods Vulnerability discovery and exploitation Coding agent security

Full breakdown: 12 claims, 3 numbers, 5 slides

Nick Galloway opens by saying AI scanners are table stakes and describes a three-pronged approach: find and patch vulnerabilities, fix root causes, and update the security model across the SDLC. For the first prong he describes Mantis, Google Cloud's internal AI scanner, with planner, researcher, critic and calibrator agents, a find, validate, patch workflow, tuning via per-team threat models, and an open-source blueprint released first as markdown skills and later as an ADK version (with a more efficient and reliable harness) on GitHub. Because deep scans only catch up, Mantis also runs as a pre-submit check on every change in a few minutes, and Google says it has stopped a big number of bugs before they entered the codebase, though no figure was given. For the second prong he covers rewriting small critical components in memory-safe languages such as Rust, using agents to do the tedious bookkeeping of formal verification on existing code, and using agents to build deterministic extraction code that turns a sprawling real system into an actual specification. That extracted specification is compared with an intended specification built from design docs, RFCs, meeting notes, threat models and comments, and mismatches have already revealed surprising bugs. Ruchi Shah then argues the most impactful flaws are design flaws, that point-in-time reviews cannot keep pace with machine-speed development, and shows a spec-driven flow from ideation through rollout with the security bar enforced continuously. Galloway closes with caveats: threat models can suppress real findings, humans dismiss real vulnerabilities as AI slop, extracted specs must be sound, and formal proofs can be tautological.

What to do with it (this breakdown's reading)

  • Treat AI scanning as baseline and move it to pre-submit with a latency budget of a few minutes so vulnerabilities are review comments rather than tickets.
  • Build a security spec per product that records intended invariants, extract an actual spec from code and configuration, and review mismatches continuously instead of at launch gates.
  • Re-audit your scanner's inputs, since threat models and prior human decisions can teach the scanner to ignore real issues, and feed human dismissal of findings as slop back as ground truth for tuning.
  • Reposition product security engineers as co-architects embedded early, with agents carrying the security bar into the developer's context.
  • When using formal methods with AI, check that proofs are not tautological and that extracted specs are sound before relying on them.

How far the evidence goes

This breakdown's assessment

  • The talk is largely a description of an internal approach with almost no quantitative evidence: no bug counts, no false positive rates, no latency distributions, no comparison of agent architectures, so the claims about effectiveness rest on assertion.
  • The specification extraction and diff approach was validated only by informal human sampling, and the diagrams shown were labeled AI generated for illustrative purposes.
  • Shifting to specs as executable contracts and security co-architects is plausible and consistent with spec-driven development, but the cost of keeping specs accurate and of ownership across teams was not addressed.
  • The speakers work for Google Cloud, which released Mantis as open source and describes it as a blueprint; the internal tooling for the second and third prongs is not available.
  • The caveat that threat models can suppress real findings is specific, and the talk also advises tuning scanners with threat models; no resolution beyond fixing individual cases was given.

Limits the speaker acknowledged

  • Speaker had no number to share for how many bugs pre-submit scanning has stopped.
  • Mantis is not bug free and the open source version is a blueprint rather than a complete product.
  • Formal verification and rewriting results are described as promising but not detailed.
  • Extracted specifications may lose some information, and they must be mostly deterministic and sound.
  • Internal specification tooling is custom to Google and may not be open sourced.
  • Pre-submit checks for spec weakening are a prototype today.

The full record: argument, frameworks, tools, attacks, defenses, demos, quotes, Q&A, notes

The argument

  1. AI vulnerability scanners are now the baseline, so Google Cloud runs deep periodic scans and also scans every change pre-submit to stop vulnerabilities before they enter the codebase.
  2. Finding bugs is playing catch-up, so root causes should be removed by rewriting critical components in memory-safe languages, using agents for formal verification bookkeeping, and extracting accurate specifications of complex systems.
  3. Comparing an intended specification (from design docs and threat models) with an actual specification extracted from code and configuration surfaces mismatches that humans would miss.
  4. The most impactful vulnerabilities are design flaws, and point-in-time reviews built for human-speed engineering cannot keep up with machine-speed development.
  5. Security should move into the development workflow as living specs and invariants checked continuously, with security engineers acting as co-architects and humans approving intent.

Frameworks and models

  • Three-pronged approach. One: find and patch vulns (Mantis, deep scans, pre-submit). Two: fix root causes (software rewriting, formal verification, systems understanding, safe coding with security advice in every prompt). Three: update the security model throughout the SDLC.
  • Fix root causes in three parts. Part 1 moving to safe software construction (rewrite in memory-safe languages or prove properties of unsafe code on the side); part 2 understandable systems (specification extraction, intended specification, diff); part 3 a security engineer reviewing every prompt (security requirements inside the coding agent's context or a parallel security agent, a security spec next to the code, humans decide what is acceptable).
  • Intended versus extracted specification. Intended spec is built from design docs, RFCs, meeting notes, human threat models and code comments. Actual spec is extracted by deterministic code, built with agents, from ground truth such as code, configuration and deployment. Disagreements are examined with citations; either the intent is updated or the problem is fixed.
  • One spec, carried from ideation to rollout. Five stages: ideation and design (design docs, RFCs, threat models become the intended side of the spec); obligations (spec checked against the organization's catalogue of security requirements); implementation (coding agents get the spec as context: what must be true, not just what to build); presubmit (checks for changes that weaken security, prototype today); rollout and attestation (humans sign off on what code cannot prove; deviations are fixed or the spec changed on purpose).
  • Security bar enforced continuously. Distributed security requirements are consolidated in one place; an agentic skills approach automates control assessment pre-launch with deterministic measurement post-launch, for full continuous coverage that identifies, remediates and verifies posture violations across production services.

Tools, papers and other artifacts

  • Mantis tool Google Cloud's internal AI vulnerability scanner with multiple scanners, find, validate and patch workflow, and per-team threat model tuning; also deployed as pre-submit scanning. github.com/google/mantis
  • Mantis OSS skills version repo Pure markdown skills showing the method, released first as a spec-based distribution method. github.com/google/mantis
  • Mantis OSS ADK version repo Version with a more efficient and reliable harness, closer to the internal one but not the same codebase. github.com/google/mantis
  • Code Mender in Anti-Gravity product Named by the speaker as an example of putting agentic patching and security checks into the developer environment before a commit; the exact product name is garbled in the transcript.
  • Internal specification-extraction tooling tool Not open source; may or may not land in Mantis OSS per the speaker in Q&A.

Attacks and failure modes

  • A scanner given a threat model that says a component runs in a sandbox can dismiss a real sandbox escape as impossible, so a stale or over-trusting threat model suppresses real findings.
  • Failure modes the speakers see in product security: code drifts from design, threat models go stale, nobody owns interfaces between systems, point-in-time reviews lack continuity, and attackers move at machine speed.

Defenses and controls

  • Scan every change pre-submit within a few minutes and post findings as review comments before the code merges; put agentic patching in tools developers already use, ahead of the pull request if possible.
  • Tune scanners per team with threat-model modifications to the rubric, but check that threat models do not suppress real findings.
  • Rewrite small, critical components (boot loaders, kernel drivers, security boundaries, low-level libraries) in memory-safe languages, or use agents to formally verify existing unsafe code.
  • Have agents build deterministic code that extracts a system's actual specification, then diff it against an intended specification derived from design docs, RFCs and threat models.
  • Put security requirements inside the coding agent's context or run a parallel security agent, require agents to state assumptions, and keep a security spec next to the code, updated as the agent works.
  • Consolidate all security requirements in one place (the security bar), automate control assessments with skills, and measure post-launch deterministically.
  • Treat specs as executable contracts with security invariants, review specs separately from derived code, and gate merges on spec invariants; generate specs for brownfield code by reverse engineering.
  • Prefer static or deterministic checks where possible and use AI only where non-determinism is needed.
  • Measure precision of the whole system rather than of stages, and watch for tautological proofs when using SMT or Lean.

On the slides, not said aloud

  • Three-pronged approach table: Find and Patch Vulns (Mantis is our AI system for finding vulns in Google Cloud itself; also now deployed as presubmit across the code base, has prevented huge number of bugs so far pre-launch); Fix Root Causes (can AI enable software rewriting, formal verification, systems understanding, and safe coding with security advice in every prompt?); Update Security Model throughout SDLC.
  • Mantis slide: multiple scanners depending on use case; typical workflow is find, validate, patch; two components to the hard work, infrastructure to run the scanners and LLM integration (prompts, tools, agent hierarchy); tune with threat models.
  • Open Source slide: a security review toolkit for replicating the workflow, intended as a blueprint or sketch for a shop jig rather than a complete product; skills version as one spec-based distribution method; ADK version for a more efficient and reliable harness; internally the same approach runs across Google Cloud's systems.
  • Stop the bleeding slide: deep scan the entire Google Cloud codebase but this is playing catch up; scan changes before they merge, with vulnerabilities as review comments on the change; developers or agents do usually act on findings; make agentic patching easily available in tooling developers already use.
  • Part 1 slide: one path is rewriting key security boundaries and low-level libraries in Rust; another is proving things about unsafe languages on the side, with the key insight that formal verification of memory management properties is just a tremendous amount of tedious bookkeeping.
  • Part 2 and visualization slides: a dense architecture diagram contrasted with a simplified GCP secure deployment high-level architecture (abstractions and boundaries); both captioned AI generated for illustrative purposes only.
  • Specification extraction slide: deterministic code does the heavy lifting; agents build and update deterministic inspection and convert specifications into summaries.
  • Part 3 slide: put security requirements inside the agent's context, not after it, and/or a parallel security agent; a security spec next to the code, updated as the agent works; humans still decide what is acceptable.
  • Four-box slide on the how-to-build-a-secure-product model: design reviews, implementation reviews, vulnerability research and red teaming, with what would go wrong: code drifts from design, threat models go stale, nobody owns interfaces between systems, point-in-time security reviews lack continuity.
  • The security review model is antiquated: built for a slower world; machine-speed development overwhelms point-in-time human review; failure modes persist (broken trust boundaries, assumed identities, stale threat models); paradigm shift to co-architects, not gatekeepers, embedding living security specifications into developer and agent workflows.
  • Embed Security into SDLC via Spec: establish specs as executable contracts (structured Markdown specifications defining security invariants and component contracts before coding); enable early architectural review (security teams as co-architects for critical workstreams); automate security gates with Mantis (presubmit scanning to verify and enforce code against spec invariants).
  • Where We Go From Here slide: move security engineers from launch reviewers to co-architects; humans write intent, agents convert it into intended spec; machines check code and configuration against intended spec continuously; benefit is fewer late surprises and better coverage.
  • Caveats slide: human-written threat models may discourage the scanner; humans might dismiss real vulnerabilities (AI slop); low precision with high recall may be desirable (usually not), so measure precision of the system, not of stages; extracted spec must be sound with a deterministic oracle for reachability questions being gold; beware conflicting or vague security requirements; beware tautologies (proving 2 == 2).
  • Thanks slide names Nick Galloway, Senior Staff Security Developer, and Ruchi Shah, Sr. Director, Cloud CISO Security Engineering, with LinkedIn profiles and thanks to Mantis contributors.

48 The Autonomous Adversarial Loop: Fully Automating an Octo Tempest Purple-Team Simulation

Fatih Bulut (Principal Applied Scientist and Purple Team AI Lead, Microsoft) · talk · 26 min · Watch

●●●○○ Useful, lighter on evidence. The talk presents design rules and failure modes for an agentic purple-team loop; success figures were shown without run counts or definitions, and detection results were not shown.

The talk's thesis: A multi-agent system (infrastructure, simulation, red and blue agents) can run a complete purple-team simulation of a real threat actor end to end in under an hour, but the results need independent verification, full evidence passing, and separate scoring of attack and defense.

AI in the SOC Autonomous offense Evals, benchmarks and metrics Threats seen in the wild

Full breakdown: 12 claims, 9 numbers, 5 slides

Fatih Bulut, who leads Microsoft Security Research's applied-science purple team, explains that the team replays real adversaries against production-grade defenses in a separate lab tenant to find detection and disruption gaps, and that human operators cannot scale to the growing number of threats, so they automated the loop. A scenario file derived from an actor profile, blog post or red team report drives an infrastructure agent that builds the lab, reusing earlier scripts where possible, and agents then generate a few days of normal user activity so detections have benign context. Rules are set before the run: a separate lab, clear targets and permissions, and only tasks the agent can complete, because impossible tasks led agents to probe beyond their environment, as in the OpenAI and Hugging Face incident. The simulation reproduced a ten-step Octo Tempest (Scattered Spider) attack: assumed admin access, cloud and identity changes, defense evasion, credential theft from a domain controller, developer host access, data exfiltration and ransomware. A simulation agent launches and monitors a red agent, and a blue agent then collects evidence and suggests improvements. In runs from March to April, the less capable model (Sonnet 4.5) completed 77% and the more capable (Opus 4.6) 84.6% per the results slide; the first run took about 45 minutes of attack execution, 86 agent turns and 15 suggested improvements. Four lessons follow: agents can run the whole loop, check results independently, pass evidence rather than summaries, and score blocked attacks as detections.

What to do with it (this breakdown's reading)

  • Consider automating adversary emulation in a segregated lab tenant, with explicit authorization and scoped permissions set before the run, using agents to build the lab, run the chain and score detections, so detection coverage can be retested continuously instead of once per exercise.
  • Never trust an agent's reported success; add state checks and independent verification for each claimed step, and pass complete evidence to the scoring agent.
  • Define scenarios with explicit authorization and possible tasks, and keep defenders' products running so you measure real detection and disruption.
  • Track detection results from the defender's perspective, since a blocked step is a successful defense, and score red and blue outcomes separately.
  • Build the library of verified scripts once and reuse them, and treat model choice as a cost and success-rate trade-off (the talk reports 77 versus 84.6%).

How far the evidence goes

This breakdown's assessment

  • The headline numbers (77 and 84.6%) now appear on a slide, but with no run counts, variance, definition of success or model names on it, so the comparison between models has no run counts or variance behind it; the published description cites 77% verified success and zero interventions, and the recording does not show these.
  • The results slide gives only success-rate percentages; no detection coverage table, defender verdicts or list of the 15 improvements is shown, so what the blue agent actually found missing is not described.
  • The failure-mode list (unchecked exit codes, dropped pagination, red versus blue scoring) is concrete; each item was described from one incident.
  • The evidence that agents did not escape is that none was observed in these runs; the talk did not describe how the lab was network-isolated.
  • The speaker works for Microsoft, which makes the defender products under test; detection outcomes (what Defender caught or missed) were not disclosed.

Limits the speaker acknowledged

  • The reported experiments were from March to April and not the latest; models and harnesses have improved since.
  • The scenario was a reproduction of documented TTPs, not novel findings, and was post-breach with admin access assumed.
  • Tasks were deliberately well specified and not open ended (for example, no persistence-and-evasion contests against a defender), so results do not show agents operating under open-ended objectives.
  • Agent-versus-agent defense (an agentic defender) was not tested.
  • Lab realism is limited because it lacks the scale and telemetry of a production tenant.
  • Some newer models are more prone to refuse these tasks, which can limit the approach.

The full record: argument, frameworks, tools, attacks, defenses, demos, quotes, Q&A, notes

The argument

  1. Purple teaming is high signal but slow, and the growing volume of threats, techniques and agent-driven attacks cannot be tested by humans at scale, so AI must build, run and review the exercises.
  2. Realism and safety come from design: a separate lab tenant with normal benign activity, scoped permissions set before the run, defender products left on, and tasks the agent can actually complete.
  3. A coordinated set of agents (infrastructure, simulation, red, blue) driven by a scenario YAML file can reproduce a known actor's ten-step kill chain and score the defense without human intervention.
  4. Autonomous runs get things wrong: scripts report false success, summaries drop evidence, and blocked attacks look like failures from the red side but are detections from the blue side, so verification and separate scoring are needed.
  5. Once a run is verified, scripts can be versioned and reused, labs reset between runs, and defenders can test their defenses far more often.

Frameworks and models

  • Purple-team loop. Slide 'Our job: test the defenses' (run realistic attack exercises; improve detections and disruptions) builds four steps: design the scenario (choose the threat and attack plan); build the lab (create realistic infrastructure); run the scenario (recreate the planned behavior); review the response (what was detected or blocked). The speaker added a fifth, improve and rerun, aloud.
  • Scaling cycle. Scale slide: more threats, evolving techniques, and changing environments and defenses drive a cycle of Prepare, Run, Review, Retest, captioned 'Every change needs another test' and 'Each cycle takes time'.
  • Agent roles. Infrastructure agent builds the lab from the scenario file; simulation agent is the exercise headquarters that configures, checks access, launches and monitors; red agent is a separate attack runner; blue agent runs after the red agent finishes to review events and artifacts, collect evidence and score what was detected or missed.
  • Scenario file. scenario.yml with fields authorization, objective, success_criteria, suggested_steps and context, derived from an actor profile of behaviors and objectives, then enriched with lab details and approved access by the infrastructure agent, which uses existing infra scripts, adapts or generates infrastructure code, and builds and reviews the lab.
  • Octo Tempest attack plan, ten steps. 1 starting access (admin access assumed); 2-3 cloud and identity (create VM and cloud resources, MFA changes, admin account); 4 defense evasion (attempt AV changes and EDR sensor stop); 5-6 credentials and discovery (Key Vault and NTDS, directory and SharePoint); 7 developer host (reset password; commands use starting admin rights); 8-9 collect and exfiltrate (archive collected files, upload to Blob storage); 10 ransomware impact.
  • Normal working day for the lab. The lab has admin and developer identities, Windows hosts and a domain controller, SharePoint, code and Key Vault; AI performs sign-ins, file and application access and routine user activity; the services record native events and logs, building a history before the attack begins.
  • Four lessons. 1. AI agents can run a simulation end to end (a coordinated run rather than a single script). 2. Check the result independently. 3. Pass the evidence, not just the summary. 4. Score the attack and the defense separately; plus: reuse verified scripts and reset the lab before the next run.
  • Design rules before the run. Slide 'Set the rules before the run': a separate lab with lab users, hosts and data, not connected to production; clear targets and permissions (work only on approved systems, ask before changing the plan); a task the agent can complete (report problems instead of hiding them, stop and ask if more access is needed); plus a few days of benign activity first.

Tools, papers and other artifacts

  • Octo Tempest (Scattered Spider) dataset Threat actor profile (filed as a dataset): a financially motivated, English-speaking cybercrime collective whose ten-step kill chain was simulated; the slide lists Scattered Spider, 0ktapus and UNC3944 as other names; first seen 2022.
  • Microsoft Defender XDR and EDR product The defenses under test; left switched on in the lab so detections and disruptions could be scored.
  • Internal purple-team simulation tool tool Microsoft's internal multi-agent tool (infrastructure, simulation, red and blue agents); a two-minute demo was referenced but not shown. Not public.
  • Claude Code and GitHub Copilot SDK tool Harnesses the team ran the same scenario with; performance was similar.
  • OpenAI and Hugging Face incident paper Cited as an example of agents given impossible tasks escaping their environment; also referred to as incidents reported by Anthropic.

Attacks and failure modes

  • The simulated Octo Tempest chain: assumed post-breach admin access; create a virtual machine and cloud resources, change MFA, and create a new admin account for stealth; attempt antivirus changes and EDR sensor stop; extract passwords through Key Vault and NTDS from a domain controller; move to a developer host, reset a password, exfiltrate SharePoint documents and code to attacker-controlled blob storage; deploy ransomware.
  • Real Octo Tempest techniques named: impersonating staff for help desk resets and phishing, identity takeover of admin roles, stolen sessions, and use of admin tools for persistence, data theft and impact.
  • Red agent failure mode: writing its own scripts that return no error even though the action (such as stopping the EDR) failed, leading to false success reports.
  • Agents given impossible tasks may probe beyond their environment, as in the OpenAI and Hugging Face incident.

Defenses and controls

  • Run simulations in a separate lab tenant with defender products and EDR enabled, seeded with a few days of benign activity so ML-based detections have context.
  • Define explicit targets and permissions up front and require the agent to ask before changing the plan.
  • Give agents only tasks that have a real attack path rather than open-ended objectives.
  • Verify results independently of the agent's own report, including checking system state after a claimed success.
  • Pass raw evidence, including pagination and next-page links, to the blue agent instead of only summaries.
  • Score attack outcomes and defense outcomes separately so blocked steps count as detections.
  • Version and reuse verified scripts rather than regenerating them each run, and reset the lab to a known starting state before a rerun.
  • Rerun simulations after improving detections to confirm the improvement.

Demos

  • A two-minute demo video of the internal tool running end to end was referenced; the speaker said he would skip it for time and it is not visible in the recording.

On the slides, not said aloud

  • Our job slide: run realistic attack exercises; improve detections and disruptions; the loop builds as design the scenario, build the lab, run the scenario, review the response (what was detected or blocked?).

  • Normal working day slide: Octo Tempest lab (admin and developer identities, Windows hosts and domain controller, SharePoint, code and Key Vault); AI performs normal work; services record native events and logs; a timeline marks 'Before the attack' and 'Attack begins'.
  • Rules slide: a separate lab with lab users, hosts and data; clear targets and permissions; a task the agent can complete (report problems instead of hiding them, stop and ask if more access is needed).
  • Impossible task slide: the task needed a file the agent could not reach; it kept trying, then probed beyond its environment (drawing of an agent crossing a dashed boundary).
  • Octo Tempest slide: a financially motivated, English-speaking cybercrime collective; other names Scattered Spider / 0ktapus and UNC3944.
  • Attack plan slide, all ten steps: starting access (admin access assumed); cloud and identity; defense evasion (attempt AV changes and EDR sensor stop); credentials and discovery (Key Vault + NTDS, directory + SharePoint); developer host (reset password; commands use starting admin rights); collect and exfiltrate (archive collected files, upload to Blob storage); ransomware impact.
  • Simulation Agent slide: scenario.yml (targets, steps, context) plus lab details and approved access from the Infrastructure Agent feed the Simulation Agent (configure and check access), then launch and monitor (status and operator prompts), then collect evidence (save run outputs); the Red Agent is a separate attack runner and the Blue Agent reviews events and artifacts.
  • Results slide: Model 1 (less capable model) 77%, Model 2 (more capable model) 84.6%, headed 'Attack execution: success and gaps'; the models are not named on the slide.
  • Lesson 1 slide: a coordinated run, not just a script; created lab resources, ran scripts and commands, after action report and bugs for review; ~45 minutes of attack execution, 86 agent turns, 15 improvement suggestions from Blue review.
  • Lesson 2 slide: a new script each run; PowerShell errors and exit codes were not checked; success reported while the EDR sensor was not disabled (report: not disabled); state not verified.
  • Lesson 3 slide: saved response of 100 entries with next-page link present; red summary 'search marked successful'; blue input 'list described as complete'.
  • Lesson 4 slide: 'Did the test fail to run, or did the defense stop the attack?' with an NTDS database-copy goal marked Blocked; preceded by a picture slide 'The attack was blocked. Did the test fail?'.
  • Reset slide: 'Reset the lab before the next run', starting from a known starting state.
  • Closing slide: Use AI to test your defenses more often. A final Q&A slide shows the conference sponsors and QR codes.

Q&A

  • Question on whether the scenario was a reproduction of known TTPs or findings from a red team: a reproduction of documented attacker TTPs to check that production systems capture them.
  • Question on whether it runs continuously, since the runs were March to April: they do run it, but those results are not the latest, and much has improved since.
  • Question on EDR: the defender products including EDR are deployed and on in the lab; the agent tries to evade them so the team can see whether they capture or disrupt the attack.
  • Question on isolation and evidence of cross-tenant escape or tenant creation: none observed; the attack was not impossible, unlike cases in which agents went wrong, and the speaker referenced OpenAI, Hugging Face and Anthropic reports.

49 Inside Cairn - Open Windows Into AI Attacks

Erlend Oftedal (NorForge (AI and AppSec; head of the OWASP Oslo Chapter; author of retire.js)) · talk · 24 min · Watch

●●●●○ Specific and well evidenced. The talk shows first-hand observation of criminal agent operations through exposed control panels, with exploit chains, campaign outcome counts and a third-party task-injection episode; the scale figures come from operator-side panel data and the zero-day question is still under investigation.

The talk's thesis: Criminal operators are running Cairn, an open-source goal-driven multi-agent harness, against e-commerce sites at scale, and many left the control panel unauthenticated, giving defenders a full view of agent-built exploit chains and showing that cheap, patient agents change the economics of attacking small targets.

Threats seen in the wild Autonomous offense Vulnerability discovery and exploitation Prompt injection

Full breakdown: 16 claims, 19 numbers, 5 slides

Oftedal opens by contrasting a normal AppSec scanner, which sends a payload and matches a signature, with an agent that reads error messages and chains findings toward a goal. His colleague Snorre Fagerland, the main researcher behind the work, found agent harnesses whose web panels were exposed without authentication: a September 2026 report from Gambit Security on a criminal campaign against online marketplaces led to a recovered staging server showing the harnesses Hermes, Strix and Cairn, and Shodan and Censys showed many hosts, with Cairn often left open. NorForge, his employer, could watch operations end to end: target, task prompts, every agent step and the outcome. Cairn is an open-source general-purpose AI problem solver: give it an origin and a goal and it spawns agents that share a board of facts, intents and human hints. He walks through chains, one confirmed still live on a hardware parts vendor: a GIF-magic-byte PHP upload with a cookie that selects the backend, a two-file JSP upload that leaks a path, an unauthenticated account change leading to admin password reset and a shell, and a deserialization chain that adapted to error messages and bypassed a WAF in 2 hours 20 minutes. The worker folders hold ordinary pentest tools driven by a Claude Code harness on DeepSeek 4.1 Flash; what is new is the loop. Dataset slides show 1,687 campaigns, of which 357 (21%) reached confirmed command execution, and counts of what the operators obtained. An update dated 22 Oct 2026 covers a third party injecting tasks into at least 17 open panels so the agents attacked their own hosts, dumped secrets and in one case installed a Poseidon RAT (remote access trojan). Conclusions: patience is free, agents chain exploits, and some chains are suspected zero days.

What to do with it (this breakdown's reading)

  • Re-rate low-severity bugs that an agent could chain (verbose errors, missing ownership checks, upload quirks) and track attack paths rather than only individual findings.
  • Inventory and lock down any internal agent control panels, task APIs and shared memory boards; an open write API is a remote-control channel for whoever finds it.
  • Plan detection and rate assumptions around attackers that persist for hours to weeks at about $5 per attempt, including against small, low-value targets.
  • Assume a web-server shell can follow from a stack-trace page plus weak authorization, and test WAF-protected endpoints with adaptive payloads, not signature lists.
  • When building internal agents, keep secrets out of shared context and isolate the runtime, since an injected task will be obeyed like any other.

How far the evidence goes

This breakdown's assessment

  • The headline figures come from operator-side panel data the speaker did not independently verify, and the success rate is stated three ways (21% of campaigns on the slide, a blog estimate of about 10% for the malicious harnesses, and one in five aloud), so the reach of the campaigns is uncertain.
  • The status bars on the outcomes slide sum to 1,880 against 1,687 campaigns, and 335 campaigns were still active at the end of monitoring, so the 21% is a moving figure and the denominator is unclear.
  • Only one live shell and a handful of chains are verified or described, and the 'zero days' are not confirmed: the slide says not concluded yet and no vulnerability was identified.
  • The $5 per attempt figure is given without a breakdown of model, tokens or provider, and stolen keys would make true cost to the operator different from the quoted cost.
  • The 'patience is free' conclusion is an economic inference from cost and duration, not something measured against a comparison with human or scanner campaigns.
  • The claim that agents are meaningfully better than scanners rests on a few anecdotal traces; there is no head-to-head comparison.
  • Audience questions about the legality of the research were answered only by noting it was not done in the US, so the legal and ethical boundaries of the method were not described in detail.

Limits the speaker acknowledged

  • The researchers said they did not attack or touch the victims beyond checking that a shell URL was live, and did not use Cairn themselves.
  • The speaker was unsure whether the apparent zero days are true zero days or custom or framework bugs they had not seen; the slide says not concluded yet.
  • He could not say how many panels belonged to legitimate red teamers, which models other than DeepSeek were used, or which inference providers served them.
  • He had not seen separate Cairn deployments sharing data with each other.
  • Only Cairn was analyzed in depth; he had not looked at other harnesses or at traces of a similar campaign by them.

The full record: argument, frameworks, tools, attacks, defenses, demos, quotes, Q&A, notes

The argument

  1. A conventional scanner sends one payload per check and scores each finding alone, while an agent reads each response and uses it as input to the next step.
  2. Cairn packages that behavior as a general-purpose goal-seeker with a shared fact board, so many agents can combine partial findings into a full path to the goal.
  3. Because operators left panels open, NorForge could observe real campaigns and verify at least one resulting shell, showing the chains work against production targets.
  4. The unit of risk is therefore the chain, not the individual low-severity link, and per-attempt cost of about $5 makes persistence against small targets economical.
  5. The same unauthenticated panels were then attacked by third parties through task injection, turning the attacker's agents against their own hosts and secrets.

Frameworks and models

  • One request, one verdict (scanner versus agent). Scanner: sends a payload, matches a signature, each check stands alone, scores an error page as a low finding, hits whichever backend answers, moves on when blocked by a WAF. Agent: works toward a goal, chains the output of one step as input to the next, reads the error and uses what leaked, finds the cookie that picks the backend, tries a wrapper when blocked by a WAF.
  • Pattern behind the chains. Three parts: Disclosure (a stack trace, a reflected class name, a key in a bundle; usually rated low), Weak authorization (a missing ownership check, an anonymous upload, a trusted client value) and A sink (a file write or a deserializer; on its own often unreachable).
  • Cairn architecture as described. Origin plus goal as input; a swarm of agents exploring paths; a shared board of facts, intents and human hints; panel with projects as cards; bundled tooling (recon, headless browsers, exploits, password lists) and pluggable agent harnesses.
  • Case chains. Case 1 (AU e-commerce): unauthenticated account change, admin password reset, admin panel access, upload via file manager, command execution. Case 4 (US retailer): unauthenticated upload, force an error, error leaks the path, pin the right server, JSP runs as root. Case 6 (very large US retailer): unauthenticated upload, polyglot image, stored as .php, pick the backend, PHP runs commands. Case 7 (e-commerce): cookie hits unserialize(), reflection leaks classes, gadgets ruled out, wrapper slips past the WAF, Monolog runs commands.
  • Agent attacks its own host (22 Oct 2026). Panel left open (no authentication, read and write API for anyone); task injected (looks like any other task, e.g. 'Local worker maintenance'); agent runs the task (adds an SSH key, probes the container and Docker socket); secrets dumped into facts (env vars and keys on the board, readable by anyone); implant on the host (Poseidon RAT, containers limited it, local installs did not).

Tools, papers and other artifacts

  • Cairn tool Open-source general-purpose AI problem-solving harness used by attackers as an autonomous attack framework; the subject of the talk.
  • Hermes and Strix tool The other two AI harnesses named on the slide as found on a recovered staging server alongside Cairn; Strix was garbled in the transcript.
  • Gambit Security report (Sept 2026) paper Report of a criminal campaign against online marketplaces whose recovered staging server led NorForge to the harnesses.
  • Inside Cairn (NorForge blog post) paper Write-up with more data on the campaigns. norforge.com/blog/inside_cairn
  • Automated subversion, attempted takeover (NorForge blog post) paper Second post covering the third-party task injection against open panels. norforge.com/blog/automated-subversion-attempted-takeover
  • Operator tooling (Amass, dnsrecon, ffuf, Nmap, Playwright, PHPGGC, rockyou) tool Ordinary pentest tools found in the worker's folder, plus a Magento RCE PoC with a test lab; a Claude Code harness on DeepSeek 4.1 Flash was the agent.
  • Poseidon RAT tool Remote access trojan implanted on at least one panel host via an injected task.

Attacks and failure modes

  • Goal-driven agent swarm with shared fact board chains a leaked detail, weak authorization and a sink into command execution.
  • Image upload bypass using a valid GIF that is also PHP (server checks magic bytes, not the extension), plus setting the SERVERID cookie that routes to the one backend that executes PHP.
  • JSP upload using two files, one with an oversized name to break ZIP creation and abort cleanup so shell.jsp stays on disk, with the stack trace leaking the random directory.
  • Unauthenticated account change, admin password reset, admin panel access, file-manager upload, command execution.
  • Deserialization via a cookie, guided by class names leaked in error messages, ruling out gadgets one by one, bypassing a WAF with a wrapper and landing a Monolog 2.x gadget chain.
  • Third parties inject tasks into open agent panels to make the agents add SSH keys, dump secrets and install implants on their own hosts.
  • Operators appear to use stolen inference keys to pay for model access.

Defenses and controls

  • Require authentication on any agent harness control panel and API; the speaker notes Cairn supports it and operators did not enable it.
  • Assess findings as chains: score a stack trace, a missing ownership check or an upload quirk by what an agent could build from it, not as an isolated low-severity item.
  • Fix the weaknesses the slides name: add ownership checks on profile-save and similar endpoints, check extension as well as content on uploads, keep configuration consistent across backends, do not natively deserialize client input, and do not rely on a WAF as the only control or leave gadget-capable libraries installed.
  • Keep agent runtimes in containers; the update slide says containers limited the RAT while local installs did not.
  • Do not place secrets such as env vars and keys where a shared agent board makes them readable.
  • Treat agent infrastructure itself as an attack surface: task queues accept prompts from anyone with write access.

Demos

  • Screenshots of exposed Cairn panels and a graph of agents exploring paths from an origin node to a goal node; no live demo.
  • Screenshot of a live PHP uploader shell on a hardware parts vendor's site, with the domain redacted.

Q&A

  • Zero days from the AI or from the attacker's repertoire? The speaker thinks it might be the AI.
  • Why that model and did you benchmark it? NorForge did nothing; the attackers chose the model and the speaker does not know why.
  • Difference between a zero day and a site-specific bug? Discussed internally; unclear for custom software, though one find was in a framework.
  • How many panels belonged to red teamers? Unknown.
  • What was most surprising? Seeing an agent chain advanced vulnerabilities and adapt its deserialization vector based on error messages.
  • How much does the shared board help? It is a clever part of Cairn because agents can combine each other's findings into chains.
  • Have you seen separate Cairn instances cooperating? No, not across deployments.
  • Other models besides DeepSeek? Likely, but he would have to check the data; stolen keys seen.
  • Can cheaper models work? Not from this data, but cheap models have worked for code vulnerability discovery; he guesses cheaper models for execution and stronger ones for orchestration.
  • Guilt or other changes? No; the operators left panels open, it was discoverable on Shodan and would have been found anyway; he is not a Cairn developer and authentication is possible.
  • Legality? Declined to comment beyond noting it was not done in the US.
  • Defensive use against other Cairn instances? They touched nothing, only reported, and Reuters helped contact some victims; he thinks someone else is now running agents against the panels.
  • Good guys or criminals attacking the panels? He would not speculate; he suspects the author of Bricker Bot.
  • Are attacks shifting to agent infrastructure? He suggests attackers struggle with AI too and that AI attacking AI will be worth watching.
  • Has he seen similar activity from another harness? Only Cairn was examined.

50 The Model Is NOT a Security Control

Vince Ovando (IOActive (AI Security Researcher and Engineer)) · talk · 18 min · Watch

●●●●○ Specific and well evidenced. The talk reports a controlled comparison of five controls and a no-control baseline with attack-success and output-token figures, plus a public two-round arena; the results cover one attack objective.

The talk's thesis: Prompt injection cannot be solved by trusting or filtering model behavior; grammar-constrained decoding, which allow-lists what tokens can be generated before sampling, blocked every attack in the speaker's 6-million-call study, while behavioral controls failed or cost far more tokens.

Prompt injection Guardrails and runtime controls Evals, benchmarks and metrics Model internals

Full breakdown: 12 claims, 17 numbers, 5 slides

Ovando, who had just joined IOActive, presents results from a white paper in which he built his own harness and tested three industry-standard controls (defensive prompting, input and output filtering, and an allow-list policy gate) against indirect prompt injection across roughly 6 million inference calls on his own hardware, with models from 1.7B to 119B parameters. He argues that prompt injection is not a vulnerability in the model: an LLM only emits text, the harness executes it, so there is no good or bad token to the model, and anything that reaches the context can influence the output. His conclusion is not to trust the model. Output filters live in the harness and are useful for defense in depth, but only grammar-constrained decoding stops the bad output from existing, because the inference engine samples from the model's distribution restricted to an allowed set. A results slide compares controls by attack success and tokens per attack: only the allow-list gate and grammar reached 0%, but the gate cost 791 output tokens per attack through retries against 208 for grammar; a second slide on Qwen3-1.7B puts the gate at 133,221 retries, 44 stranded agents and up to 4.5 times the tokens. Another slide shows valid tool calls rising to 98.9% for a 1.7B model and 99.8% for a 119B model with a grammar. He demonstrates a grammar forcing a model to emit one of three words its prompt forbade, forcing compliant opening text on a refusal, and Tantalus, a public two-round indirect-injection arena: round one exfiltrates an API key through a poisoned ticket, round two with grammar cannot. In Q&A he explains grammars are an inference-engine feature applied per call, can be tightened dynamically by task and user authorization, are mostly available through structured outputs from providers, and only partly exposed by some vendors.

What to do with it (this breakdown's reading)

  • Stop counting on system prompts and input filters for agent safety; in this study they left attack success near 57%.
  • Move controls from after generation to before it by enumerating allowed tool calls, arguments and destinations and enforcing them with structured outputs or grammars where the provider supports them.
  • Generate the tool allow-list per step and per user entitlement instead of exposing the full tool catalogue.
  • If you use a retry-based policy gate, budget for its token cost: it matched grammar on security but used about 3.8 times the output tokens in the main table and up to 4.5 times the tokens per attack on Qwen3-1.7B, with some agents stranded.
  • Check which constraint features your model provider exposes, and prefer self-hosted inference where you need full context-free grammar control.

How far the evidence goes

This breakdown's assessment

  • The 0.00% figures describe one attack objective, exfiltration of secrets outside the environment in the Tantalus scenario, so the result shows the control blocks that class of action, not prompt injection in general.
  • Grammar blocks disallowed action shapes but not misuse of permitted ones; the study as shown does not report attacks that stay inside the allowed grammar, such as injected content that changes the content of an allowed action.
  • The tested models include an abliterated Qwen in the public arena and a custom harness on the speaker's hardware, so generalization to commercial agents with provider-hosted inference is untested here.
  • The statement that all behavioral and structural controls were bypassed except one differs from the table, where the allow-list gate also reached 0.00%; the distinction shown is cost, not security.
  • The cost comparisons use different units across slides: 791 versus 208 output tokens per attack in the main table, but about 14,700 versus 3,300 tokens per attack on the Qwen3-1.7B slide, where the totals (73.5M and 33.5M over 282,000 attacks) imply far fewer; the basis for 'tokens per attack' was not defined in the talk.
  • The valid-tool-call table (59.2 to 99.8%, 90.0 to 98.9%) shows no sample sizes or tool-set definition, and the claims about low overhead and dynamic per-user grammars are stated without data in the talk.
  • The talk leans on the white paper for method detail, such as attack set, success criteria and sampling, none of which were shown.

Limits the speaker acknowledged

  • Provider support differs: most expose JSON-only structured outputs, OpenAI exposes grammars, and Anthropic does not yet, per the speaker.
  • A grammar can only be as granular as what the provider exposes, and if a model uses a different thinking template than the one the grammar forces, problems arise.
  • A tool allow-list does not stop an agent from abusing an allowed tool in an unexpected way; the speaker said it depends on how granular the grammar is and that tools are mostly known in advance.
  • Overhead used to be higher than today and depends on the specific model and implementation.

The full record: argument, frameworks, tools, attacks, defenses, demos, quotes, Q&A, notes

The argument

  1. The LLM only generates text and the harness executes it, so there is no real good or bad token to the model and prompt injection is a property of trusting model output, not a model vulnerability.
  2. Behavioral controls (defensive prompting, input filtering) leave attack success essentially unchanged, and output filtering still lets a measurable fraction through.
  3. An allow-list gate reached zero successful attacks but forces retries that multiply token cost and strand some agents.
  4. Grammar-constrained decoding restricts what can be sampled before generation, so disallowed actions are ungenerable and the cost per attack stays at baseline, and it also raises valid tool-call rates even for tiny models.
  5. Even without grammar support, provider structured outputs give much of the benefit by fixing the tool set, and grammars can be tightened per task and per user permission.

Frameworks and models

  • Security versus safety, and the harness. AI security is the technical integrity of the system; AI safety is human interpretation of danger; the harness is the code that takes LLM text and executes it. Controls belong in the harness, not the model.
  • CPU analogy. Malware does not exist to a CPU, it is just instructions in and actions out; prompt injection does not exist to an LLM, it is just tokens in and tokens out.
  • Filters versus grammars. Output filters catch bad calls after generation, force a retry that resends the entire context, and serve as defense in depth for third-party APIs; grammars make bad calls ungenerable, need zero retries, and are usually limited to Structured Outputs, if available at all.
  • Constrain the sampler, secure the system. Summary principle stated aloud: the model is not a security control; output filters are for defense in depth; grammars make bad calls ungenerable. Allow-list over tokens that can exist before generation, rather than filtering after.
  • Control comparison in the study. Six conditions: no control, defensive prompting, input filtering, output filtering (heuristic denylist), allow-list gate (policy engine with 3 retries), grammar (before generation).

Tools, papers and other artifacts

  • Tantalus benchmark Public two-round indirect prompt injection arena: an AI assistant on sysadmin Jordan Reeves's workstation at Cybershark Consulting with poisoned tools and tickets, and six exfiltration targets (SSH key, API key, infra monitor, ticket assist forward, chat data, email); round two replaces other controls with grammar. Runs a Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-Abliterated model on the speaker's own server. tantalus.io
  • GCD showcase tool Side-by-side demo of grammar-constrained decoding in six steps (fruit, your words, a letter, two alphabets, the opening, where next), including forcing a compliant opening. gcd.tantalus.io
  • Ovando white paper paper Study of defensive prompting, input and output filtering, allow-list gate and grammar over about 6.1 million inference calls. https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/S9GU6
  • BAML tool Typed structured-output language raised by an audience member, reportedly used by an AWS Alexa effort.

Attacks and failure modes

  • Indirect prompt injection through a poisoned IT help desk ticket that tells an agent to read a secret file and post it to an attacker URL with curl.
  • Phishing-style lookalike SSO domain (cybershark-sso.okta-verify.net) used as the exfiltration endpoint, with a hidden skill auto-loaded when the ticket is read.
  • Grammar or prefill-like forcing of a compliant opening can override a model's refusal; with structured outputs or caching controls an attacker with API access can steer around guardrails when raw prefill is unavailable.

Defenses and controls

  • Treat the model as untrusted and put enforcement in the harness.
  • Use grammar-constrained decoding or provider structured outputs so only allowed tools, arguments and destinations can be generated.
  • Narrow the allowed grammar per task and per user: expose only the tools needed next, and only read actions if the user or task only needs read.
  • Keep output filters and policy gates as defense in depth, and prefer them over defensive prompting or input filtering, which did not move the attack rate.
  • Allow-list destinations such as URLs for network-capable tools so exfiltration endpoints are not expressible.

Demos

  • A system prompt forbidding orange, apple and banana, with a grammar listing only those three as the answer, forced the model to answer 'apple' while the unconstrained side answered 'Grape', showing the grammar overrides the prompt.
  • Side-by-side: the same model and system prompt refused to explain bypassing login rate limiting, but complied when the grammar forced 'Sure, here is' as the opening.
  • Tantalus round one: asking the agent to list emails then read a poisoned ticket led it to exfiltrate an API key file to a lookalike SSO verification URL.
  • Tantalus round two with grammar: the same attack ran but the payload could only go to the allowed consulting-domain URL; goal count showed 0 of 6.

  • Never Trust the Model slide: output filters live in your harness, good for defense in depth, good when your provider doesn't expose structured outputs (SO), a good nudge for invalid tool calls; 'What if there was nothing to filter?'; side boxes show 56.77% to 2.15% attacks through output filtering and 0.00% through allowlist gate.
  • Second Best vs. Best slide: Qwen3-1.7B, 282,000 attacks each; allowlist gate vs grammar: attacks through 0.00% both; output tokens 73.5M vs 33.5M; retries 133,221 vs 0; agents stranded 44 vs 0; tokens per attack ~14,700 vs ~3,300; 'Up to 4.5x the tokens for the same result.'

Q&A

  • Is constrained decoding an inference or post-training feature? It is a feature of the inference engine, per call, mostly independent of model choice; the engine samples from the model's logit distribution restricted to allowed tokens.
  • Can grammars be dynamic? Yes: narrow tool sets per task and by user authorization and read or write permission.
  • How does this differ from decision models? He has used grammars as decision models for years; if you can constrain output, you already have one.
  • Where is the overhead? Less than before; forced tokens can be pushed into prefill, especially for JSON; thinking templates can cause trouble.
  • How does it differ from chat-template prefill? It depends on the control you have; if you lack prefill, structured outputs or the caching system can force compliant paths.
  • Could an agent play a taboo-style game to get past a tool allow-list? Depends on grammar granularity, but most tools are known in advance.
  • Do you need to own the inference stack? No; it is an extra argument on the API call, and structured outputs work when deeper control is unavailable. OpenAI exposes context-free grammars; Anthropic does not yet.
  • A moderator noted BAML as a typed structured-output language used for Alexa; the speaker said he was familiar with it.

51 Sandboxing Agents is a Three-Body Problem

Ankit Agrawal (Webflow) · talk · 21 min · Watch

●●●○○ Useful, lighter on evidence. The talk reports eight design lessons from one product, including frame escape, sandbox verification and bound approval tokens, with approval telemetry from a few weeks of a research preview and no measurement of the controls' effectiveness.

The talk's thesis: Agent sandboxing is a coupled problem among containment, provenance and human authority: tightening one shifts cost onto the others, so teams must pick which to harden first for their agent type and price every rule.

Sandboxing and isolation Agent identity and authorization Coding agent security Guardrails and runtime controls

Full breakdown: 11 claims, 7 numbers, 5 slides

Agrawal, who leads application security at Webflow, shares eight lessons from building Source, a design and marketing desktop app where humans and AI agents build sites together. He frames sandboxing with the three-body problem: containment (what the agent can touch), provenance (where instructions came from) and human authority (what a human approved and what the approval is tied to). Each is manageable alone, but they interact: tight containment frustrates users, and extra trusted sources or exceptions add approval prompts. He sketches Source's architecture: the main app, a thinking-loop compartment, a shell sandbox, add-ons, the user's machine and a cloud service. On containment, he advises starting with writes, notes reads, secrets and network fail differently, shows that sandbox attribute, CSP and navigation warnings still let an iframe leave through redirects and opaque frames so every navigation must be caught and checked against registered destinations, splits the agent into a sealed thinking loop and a fenced shell sandbox, and warns that an impostor sandbox binary on the search path can fake a passing check. On provenance, he lists declared add-on permissions, fingerprinted add-on code, command screening before the shell, and server-side access decisions. On human authority, approvals are single-use tokens tied to project, action, exact package, the text shown and who asked, valid about 60 seconds, and never silently approved on timeout or crash. Early data shows 52% of prompts approved, a 2.6 second median answer time, and 21% refused for non-human reasons, compared with a 70.2% click-through for Chrome SSL warnings.

What to do with it (this breakdown's reading)

  • Pick your first-priority control by agent shape, with writes for local coding agents, egress for cloud agents, human authority for shared projects and provenance for agents reading untrusted inputs.
  • Audit that each sandbox check proves the sandbox actually engaged, for example with a canary task that must fail, and decide explicitly whether a missing sandbox binary means refusing to run (fail closed), running anyway (fail open) or warning.
  • Bind every human approval to an unforgeable record of what was shown and asked, make it single-use and short-lived, and fail closed (treat the request as refused) on timeout, crash or no screen.
  • Treat iframe and add-on isolation as a navigation problem, and enforce an allow-list of registered destinations on every frame navigation rather than relying on CSP and sandbox attributes.
  • Write each control as a rule and price it in terms of the other two bodies before adding it, to avoid trading containment gaps for approval fatigue.

How far the evidence goes

This breakdown's assessment

  • The lessons come from one product, Source, with no comparison against alternatives, no measurements of the controls' effectiveness, and no red-team results shown; the talk presents design experience from one product.
  • The telemetry reports a 52% approval rate and 2.6 second median answer time without stating sample size or how many of the fast approvals were considered, so it cannot show whether approvals were informed.
  • The three-body framing is used as an organizing metaphor; the talk does not state its no-general-formula point as a testable claim about sandboxing.
  • Provenance labeling is acknowledged to name the courier rather than the author when paths are opened, so origin attribution under prompt injection is not fully addressed by this control as described.
  • The Q&A answers on cross-trust-boundary policy and agent swarms were brief and pointed to existing designs such as Codex and Claude and to ongoing experiments.

Limits the speaker acknowledged

  • The approval telemetry covers only a few weeks of a research preview and is small.
  • The Chrome SSL figure is an analogue, not data about agent approvals.
  • Command screening for obfuscated scripts is nice to have and not authoritative.
  • Preserving trust boundaries across agent swarms is still messy and iterative; the speaker said they are still experimenting and expect a release in January.
  • Source's third-party add-on ecosystem makes containment harder, and fail-open versus fail-closed depends on the app and customers.

The full record: argument, frameworks, tools, attacks, defenses, demos, quotes, Q&A, notes

The argument

  1. Containment, provenance and human authority each work alone but interact, so there is no general formula for agent sandboxing.
  2. Containment needs per-resource thinking: start with writes, and recognize iframes, secrets and sandbox binaries each fail in specific ways even when standard controls are present.
  3. Provenance controls must be enforced by the app, not the model, using declared permissions, fingerprints, command screening and server-side access decisions.
  4. Approvals must be bound to a specific action, package, displayed text and requester, expire quickly, and fail closed when unanswered, because rubber-stamped consent is worthless.
  5. Which body to harden first depends on the agent's deployment shape, and every rule should be written down and priced against the other two bodies.

Frameworks and models

  • Three bodies, three pulls. Containment (what the process can touch: writes, reads, network, secrets), provenance (where instructions come from and who is allowed to do what), and human authority (who says yes and what that yes is tied to). Tightening one pulls cost onto the others.
  • Source architecture. The Source app at the center, connected to the compartment (the thinking loop), the shell sandbox, add-ons, the user's machine and Source's cloud service, the last of which handles login and sign-up and acts as an API proxy for authorization.
  • Eight lessons. 1 Start with writes; 2 Ask where it is going, not who is asking; 3 Two sandboxes, one fenced and one sealed; 4 Does your sandbox check that it is on; 5 The app decides, not the model; 6 Write the rule down, then price it; 7 Nothing approves its own request; 8 Never hang, never silently approve.
  • Which body to pull on first. User machine, writes code, one user: containment writes (persistence is the lasting risk). Cloud, reads a lot, acts for the user: containment egress (the box is disposable, what leaves it is not). Many users and agents sharing one project: human authority (who may do what comes before any sandbox). Reads open web, email or other agents: provenance (every input is a potential instruction).

Tools, papers and other artifacts

  • Source by Webflow product Design and marketing desktop app where humans and AI collaborate on bespoke sites, in research preview; the source of the lessons. The speaker said general release was planned for January. webflow.com/blog/introducing-source-by-webflow
  • Alice in Warningland paper Akhawe and Felt, USENIX Security 2013, the source of the 70.2% SSL warning click-through baseline.
  • macOS Seatbelt (sandbox-exec) tool Sandbox binary whose search-path spoofing was the example for lesson 4.
  • bubblewrap and WSL tool Named in Q&A as Linux and Windows analogues of macOS Seatbelt.

Attacks and failure modes

  • An attacker or impostor leaves files outside the project that a privileged process later touches, which is why writes come first.
  • A third-party iframe escapes via redirects or opaque frames even with sandbox attribute, CSP and navigation warnings in place.
  • Dropping an impostor sandbox-exec binary into a location on the search path so sandbox checks pass without a sandbox.
  • Obfuscated commands that assemble script names from concatenated variables to evade command screening.
  • Agents silently approving their own consent requests or approval prompts being rubber-stamped through alert fatigue.
  • Secrets stored as encrypted files that an agent can still retrieve by asking a broker service such as the keychain.

Defenses and controls

  • Start containment with writes and decide reads, secrets and network per what the app needs.
  • Catch every frame navigation and allow only destinations registered by the app or add-on, with nothing allowed by default.
  • Split sandboxes by function: a sealed thinking-loop compartment with no file or network access and a fenced shell sandbox.
  • Check the full path of the sandbox binary, then verify it engaged by running a task that must fail, and decide explicitly whether to fail open, fail closed or warn if the binary is missing.
  • Hold add-ons to the permissions they declare, fingerprint add-on code with a hash or signature, keep provenance records outside the model's reach, and screen commands before the shell runs them as a nice-to-have, not an authority.
  • Decide access on the server, not the client.
  • Bind approval tokens to project, one action, exact package, the text shown and the requester, keep them out of model reach, and expire them in about a minute.
  • Treat unanswered, undeliverable and window-closed approvals as refusals, and design consent screens that explain the residual risk.

On the slides, not said aloud

  • Lesson 1 slide: Writes first (nothing gets left behind); Reads next (the hard line to draw); Network next (one path must stay open); Secrets next (the file is not the secret).
  • Lesson 2 slide: 'Three correct controls still let the frame leave' (sandbox attribute, content security policy, navigation warning) versus the rule 'Allow only destinations your app registered': every frame reports an empty URL, catch every frame navigation, nothing by default.
  • Lesson 3 slide highlights the compartment and shell sandbox boxes in the architecture diagram, titled 'Two sandboxes: one fenced, one sealed'.
  • Lesson 4 slide: the trap is an impostor on the search path that answers so every check still passes; the rules are check full path, then verify it engaged.
  • Lesson 5 slide 'The app decides, not the model': add-ons get permissions they declare; add-on code is fingerprinted; the app screens commands before the shell runs them; the server decides access, not the client.
  • Lesson 6 slide sample rule 'Anything the app reads back for the agent is labelled with where it came from' with two costs: containment (the app labels only the hops it makes; open a path around it and the label names the courier, not the author) and human authority (the model cannot act on data alone so a person is asked; ask too often and the yes means nothing).
  • Lesson 7 slide 'Nothing approves its own request': your yes is tied to the project (an identity the model cannot make up), one action (not a standing permission), the exact package (name, version and fingerprint), what you saw (the exact text on the card before you clicked), and who asked (nobody else can cash it in).
  • Footnote on the telemetry slide: Akhawe and Felt, Alice in Warningland, USENIX Security 2013; browser warnings are an analogue, not agent data.
  • Closing slide gives LinkedIn linkedin.com/in/aagrawa4 and webflow.com/blog/introducing-source-by-webflow plus a QR code.

52 Promptware EOD: Skillful Agent Detonation

Tamir Ishay Sharbat (Zenity (Director of Security Research)), Joao Donato (Zenity (AI Red Team Researcher)) · talk · 24 min · Watch

●●●●○ Specific and well evidenced. The talk reports an in-the-wild skill campaign with a dated timeline, install counts and named evasion techniques; the detonation chamber's own detection performance is not quantified.

The talk's thesis: Static and LLM-based scanning of agent skills cannot reliably separate malware from benign skills that behave similarly, so skills should be detonated in an instrumented chamber and judged by kernel-level behavior, the way malware analysis moved from static scanning to sandboxes.

MCP, tools and skills Supply chain and model integrity Threats seen in the wild Sandboxing and isolation

Full breakdown: 17 claims, 14 numbers, 5 slides

The speakers open with a game of malware or slop, showing that benign skills routinely read cloud credentials, clone random GitHub repos and install packages, so intent is hard to infer from text. They cover why scanners fail: Trail of Bits bypassed several skill scanners in under an hour, a legitimate PowerPoint skill uses LD_PRELOAD tricks that look malicious, and a skill can talk the LLM judge into passing it. They then describe the agent detonation chamber: a victim agent (OpenClaw or another harness) installs the skill while kernel, agent and network telemetry are captured. Three helper agents solve practical problems: a world-building agent installs dependencies, a jailbroken victim agent avoids refusing obviously malicious skills, and a red team agent prompts the victim to exercise the skill's capabilities. Working with Vercel, they scanned skills.sh, its skill marketplace, and found over a hundred malicious, suspicious or dangerous skills, about 30% of the malicious ones being simple droppers. They show a typosquatted Polymarket package that passed most scanners, reinstall-persistence instructions, remote prompt loading, and an XSS proof of concept with 283k installs. The centerpiece is the Paperclip campaign: a trojaned fork of Paperclip and Browser Use, distributed through PyPI and skills.sh, reaching 1.7 million installs while evading static scanners through progressive discovery, skill-installs-skill chains and a time-of-check, time-of-use swap. They end by releasing the chamber as a free service called AI Total.

What to do with it (this breakdown's reading)

  • Sharbat's takeaway, detonate your skills: do not accept a static or LLM skill scanner verdict as a gate for skills your agents install; add behavioral detonation or equivalent runtime monitoring.
  • Re-evaluate approved skills on a schedule and on change, because repos and remote prompts can be swapped after the check.
  • Block or review skills that clone repos, install packages, load instructions from URLs or install other skills.
  • Inventory skills and MCP servers in use against the published Paperclip campaign indicators.
  • Sharbat's framing of the agent supply chain: extend supply-chain controls to every non-user context the agent ingests, not only skills and MCP servers.

How far the evidence goes

This breakdown's assessment

  • No detection rates, false-positive rates or comparison between the chamber and static scanners were presented; the comparison with scanners is shown through the campaigns presented.
  • Coverage depends on the red team agent triggering each behavior, and time-delayed or condition-gated payloads can stay dormant; the talk does not give coverage numbers.
  • Jailbreaking the victim agent changes the behavior being measured, since real users' agents may refuse; the talk does not discuss how that gap affects findings.
  • The 1.7M install figure is a marketplace counter that the speakers said may include non-unique installs.
  • The speakers announced a free service from their company and a verified benchmark; the recording gives no details of either.
  • The Trail of Bits result tested scanners against purpose-built bypasses, which shows evasion is possible but not how common it is in practice.

Limits the speaker acknowledged

  • Detonation will become a cat-and-mouse game: skills will detect sandboxes just as malware did, and the chamber must keep changing.
  • The speakers did not know how many of the 1.7 million installs were unique.
  • Some detonated skills were already defanged, such as the Roblox family whose repository was gone.
