  • Vibe-hackers slide lists four classes: credentials copied into an external sink, production modified unusually to prove access, users or admins contacted or reset, telemetry showing callbacks to operator IPs or a recognizable scanner.
  • Scenario slide: 24 containerized scenarios, 14 webapp/API and 10 Windows; lists LSASS hygiene, Kerberoasting, process hollowing/ghosting and AMSI as example families.
  • Web task results list safe success per task function from 100% (file upload credential use) down to 0% (webhook verification, batched OTP verification, connector rate limiting, shared workspace authentication), with a column of where badness shows up.
  • Windows expert-plus-GEPA task table gives safe success per function (for example kernel driver control 53.3%, down to content scanning interaction and native call dispatch at 6.7%) and where badness shows up for each, which the slide titles detection opportunities.

Q&A

  • Could you use reinforcement learning to train stealth? Yes, the system is dual use and could help build stealthier models, but a large part of what they see is recklessness, which should be trained out.
  • How much did the harness affect results? They used a basic harness and did not test others; tasks are simple so he does not think the harness matters much, though a harness that intercepts tool calls with a judge could largely constrain the problem.
  • Why did GPT-5.6 Sol go on side quests and delete admin accounts, was it the prompt? He did not dig in; given recent news about the model it did not surprise him, he calls it adventurous.
  • Were runs repeated? Yes, each model ran each task 70 times and scores are averages, which is why 24 tasks gives about 3,000 trajectories.

66 From DARPA AIxCC to Microsoft FORGE Lab: Lessons Building Hyperscale AI Code Scanning Tools

Taesoo Kim (VP, Security Research, Microsoft) · talk · 27 min · Watch

●●●●○ Specific and well evidenced. The talk reports production figures (229 Windows and Hyper-V CVEs fixed, a Linux kernel exploit-generation experiment) and a five-stage scanning pipeline design, with no ablations or rates for several design claims, from a speaker who works for the company that ships the product.

The talk's thesis: AI vulnerability discovery has moved from a research demonstration (DARPA's AI Cyber Challenge, AIxCC) to production at hyperscale (Microsoft's multi-model agentic scanning harness, MDASH), and the hard problems are now cost per audit, deciding when to stop spending tokens, and feeding the expensive validation and remediation stages back into finding, which is why Microsoft's FORGE Lab (Frontier Offensive Research and Generative Exploitation) is pivoting to exploitability as the organizing signal.

Vulnerability discovery and exploitation Autonomous offense AppSec and secure development Evals, benchmarks and metrics

Full breakdown: 13 claims, 12 numbers, 5 slides

Kim opens with the DARPA AI Cyber Challenge as the ChatGPT moment for security: a $30 million competition his Team Atlanta won, with the winning system, a long technical report, a systematization-of-knowledge paper and the OSS-CRS (open-source cyber reasoning system) code and CRSBench benchmark all released. He says AIxCC showed AI can do professional-level cyber tasks at about $150 per task, and that frontier labs then productized the idea (Big Sleep, CodeMender, Aardvark, Claude Code Security, Codex Security Review). He shows open source skepticism (curl's Daniel Stenberg) turning into acceptance and Microsoft's monthly Patch Tuesday CVE count climbing sharply after March 2026. Five Team Atlanta members joined Microsoft and, within five months, shipped MDASH, a multi-model, multi-agent scanning harness with five stages: prepare, scan, validate, dedup, prove. He explains four design ideas: turn search into decision problems, use the function as the orchestration unit, funnel candidates through increasingly expensive validation, and enrich source with LLM-written taint and bounds annotations. He reports 229 Windows and Hyper-V CVEs fixed, including 38 remote code execution bugs, and a Linux kernel exploit-generation experiment. He closes with three shifts (scale and cost, reasoning economics, a continuous learning loop), all pushing toward exploitability.

What to do with it (this breakdown's reading)

  • Budget AI code scanning by stage: spend cheaply on broad per-function discovery and reserve expensive models and dynamic proving for candidates that survive static debate.
  • Measure and plan for cost per audit and for when to stop, since the talk argues token spend is becoming the proxy for assurance.
  • Expect patch-to-exploit time for your shipped software to shrink and plan patch rollout speed and customer update enforcement accordingly.
  • Invest in ranking and exploitability triage, because validation and deployment, not finding, are the dominant cost and the point where false positives hurt most.
  • Do not assume frontier-model access for offensive-adjacent security work; test open-weight models and keep your pipeline model-agnostic.

How far the evidence goes

This breakdown's assessment

  • The benchmark behind the model comparison chart is not named, and MDASH is compared as a multi-model system against single models, so the chart does not isolate the value of the pipeline design.
  • Claims about false-positive reduction from annotations and multi-persona debate come with no rates, ablations or comparisons to simpler pipelines.
  • The CVE counts include only fixed, shipped Windows and Hyper-V bugs by cohort; there is no denominator for scanned code, triage effort, rejected findings or how many findings were severe versus low value.
  • The Patch Tuesday chart is attributed to AI-driven discovery in general, not just MDASH, and the speaker's spoken figure (about 1600) conflicts with the slide (1,142).
  • The $150 per task figure is repeated without definition of task, success or how it generalizes beyond the AIxCC challenge projects.
  • The speaker works for Microsoft, which ships MDASH and runs FORGE Lab. The Q&A answer on pipeline erosion argues for staged control; no comparison against simpler agent-plus-strong-model setups was shown.
  • The audience question on verifying generated patches was not answered; the response covered only variant analysis.

Limits the speaker acknowledged

  • Speaker acknowledged most Linux crashes depend on non-default configurations and are not security concerns.
  • Cost and infrastructure, not capability, now limit adoption because few organizations need or can afford frontier-level scanning.
  • Post-discovery work remains expensive and manual, taking weeks to months.
  • The design assumes bugs keep being introduced; the speaker noted that if AGI arrives, that premise may change.

The full record: argument, frameworks, tools, attacks, defenses, demos, quotes, Q&A, notes

The argument

  1. DARPA AIxCC showed that LLM-driven systems can find and patch real vulnerabilities at professional level for roughly $150 per task, and the frontier labs productized that within about a year.
  2. Skepticism from open source maintainers and the security community flipped to adoption, visible in a steep rise in Microsoft CVEs fixed per Patch Tuesday after March 2026.
  3. MDASH makes AI scanning work in production by forcing agents through an explicit pentester-style workflow, with function-level decision questions, shared annotated context, and multi-persona validation before expensive proving.
  4. With discovery solved, the bottlenecks are cost per audit, knowing how many tokens are enough, and the much costlier triage, validation and deployment stages, so findings must be ranked and learned from.
  5. FORGE Lab therefore prioritizes exploitable bugs: reason about exploitation early, spend tokens on exploitation reasoning, and use exploit techniques as the feedback loop, demonstrated on automatic exploit generation against the Linux kernel.

Frameworks and models

  • MDASH pipeline. Multi-model agentic scanning harness with five stages. Prepare builds a per-repo knowledge base (threat model, repo map, call graph, CVEs and patches mined from Git). Scan runs 100-plus specialized agents per bug type, choosing 3 to 5 relevant ones per function. Validate has Models A, B and C debate as different personas and vote, two of three. Dedup collapses duplicates. Prove generates a proof of concept in three stages (self-contained, reachability harness, fuzzing) in a Docker build with sanitizers, then optional patch generation (AutoFix) and patch validation with audit.
  • Four core design ideas. Idea 1: turn the search problem into decision problems by asking narrower questions. Idea 2: use the function as the unit of orchestration, with each function checked by parallel agents per bug class. Idea 3: scale by funneling through static self-dispute, multi-perspective debate, reachability evaluation, dynamic constraint concretization, and finally a PoC, with cost rising at each step. Idea 4: enrich source with LLM-generated inline annotations for taint and boundaries.
  • Three shifts. Shift 1, from frontier capability to scale: cut tokens per audit with small, specialized or multiple models. Shift 2, from token consumption to reasoning economics: security is roughly the tokens spent on security reasoning, so decide what is enough and spend cost-effectively. Shift 3, validation and remediation as a continuous learning loop: rank bugs, reuse past lessons. FORGE restates each shift around exploitation.
  • Hybrid static and dynamic spectrum. Atlantis started from dynamic fuzzing and added LLMs; MDASH started from static LLM reasoning and added tooling and proving; both move toward a hybrid with better applicability and low false positives.

Tools, papers and other artifacts

  • MDASH product Microsoft multi-model, multi-agent vulnerability scanning and remediation harness; used on Windows in CI/CD and described as part of Defender.
  • Atlantis (Team Atlanta CRS) tool AIxCC winning cyber reasoning system, started from fuzzing harnesses with LLM assistance; has a 150-plus page technical report. https://team-atlanta.github.io/
  • SoK: DARPA's AI Cyber Challenge (AIxCC): Competition Design, Architectures, and Lessons Learned paper Systematization paper at USENIX Security 26 comparing CRS designs across teams; shown with a distinguished paper award ribbon. https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.07666
  • CtxFuzz, PatchIsland, OSS-CRS papers paper Companion papers listed as ASE 26, ACSAC 26 and WOOT 26.
  • OSS-CRS and CRSBench benchmark Open-source cyber reasoning system framework and a full-pipeline benchmark under OpenSSF, built from AIxCC challenges. https://oss-crs.openssf.org/crsbench
  • Microsoft FORGE Lab CVE list dataset JSON file of CVEs found by the lab, linked on the community slide. https://github.com/microsoft/forge-lab/blob/main/cve/cve.json
  • LF Akrites standard Linux Foundation coordinated, confidential vulnerability remediation effort for critical open source, with Microsoft and Google participating.
  • Microsoft Security blog posts by Taesoo Kim paper Three posts listed: 3 lessons from frontier AI vulnerability research (October 7), Beyond the benchmark: Advancing security at AI speed (June 17), Defense at AI speed: Microsoft's new multi-model agentic security system tops leading industry benchmark (May 12).

Attacks and failure modes

  • Patch diffing: with AI, the time to reverse a published patch (including binaries) into a working exploit has dropped drastically, shrinking the window between patch release and attacker exploitation.
  • AI reduces the cost to attack, so low-skill attackers become powerful and the scope of required auditing expands.
  • Automatic exploit generation against the Linux kernel: from patch, report or crash to local privilege escalation or remote code execution, yielding 11 LPEs from 600-plus reproduced crashes.
  • Frontier models resist binary analysis plus exploitation requests, pushing offensive users toward open-weight models.

Defenses and controls

  • Run an explicit staged pipeline (prepare, scan, validate, dedup, prove) rather than a single general agent, so token budget can be set per stage.
  • Ask narrow decision questions per function and bug class, run them in parallel, and let agents flag suspicious sites before any exploitation work.
  • Pre-annotate source with LLM-generated taint and boundary information and share it across all agents to cut false positives and redundant reasoning.
  • Validate with multi-persona debate across different model backends (developer, defender, attacker) and a two-of-three vote before proving.
  • Require a PoC or reachability evidence for high-assurance findings; allow developers to consume the earlier suspicious-site output for pre-commit scans.
  • Mine Git history and CVE or MSRC tags in commits for variant analysis across the codebase.
  • Keep the pipeline model agnostic and run a benchmark suite whenever a new model ships; use powerful models for high-stakes targets and cheaper models for broad scans.
  • Coordinate disclosure of upstream findings through community channels such as LF Akrites rather than posting to public lists.

On the slides, not said aloud

  • AIxCC infographic: 42 teams competed, 7 advance to finals, 5 challenge projects (Linux Kernel, NGINX, Tika, Jenkins, SQLite), 59 synthetic vulnerabilities, 4 hours per round, $100 per round AI budget, each CRS had 3 nodes of 64 cores and 256 GB RAM.
  • AIxCC final scoreboard columns (total, correct submission %, vulnerability discovery, program repair, SARIF, bundle): Team Atlanta 392.76, 91.27%, 79.71, 171.10, 5.99, 136.38; Trail of Bits 219.35; Theori 210.68; All You Need IS A Fuzzing Brain 153.70; Shellphish 135.89; 42-b3yond-6ug 105.03; Lacrosse 9.59.
  • Industry timeline: Google Big Sleep; Aardvark (OpenAI) and CodeMender (DeepMind) in October 2025; Claude Code Security (Anthropic) in February 2026; Codex Security Review (OpenAI) in March 2026; MDASH (Microsoft) in June 2026. The AIxCC slogan 'AI + CRS = The Future' is struck through and replaced with NOW.

  • Microsoft Windows Blog post of July 9, 2026 by Pavan Davuluri: Windows set up dedicated cloud infrastructure for scanning and proving; a scanner pipeline scans critical binaries and validates candidates using multi-model debate across model families; confirmed candidates flow to a Windows-specific prove pipeline to eliminate false positives so only highest-confidence findings reach engineers.
  • Annotated-code slide shows layer counts (Vuln 15, Bounds 48, Flow 52, Control 3, Safety 9, Meta 6; 133 annotations across 114 lines) on an FTS5 function with notes such as attacker-controlled blob data.
  • Model comparison chart plots success rate against release date from DeepSeek-V3 near 4% in January 2025 up to roughly 80 to 90% in 2026 (Claude Mythos Preview, GPT-5.5, GPT-5.4, Claude Opus and Sonnet 4.x, GLM, Kimi K2.5, Muse Spark), with MDASH multi-model circled at the top.
  • Linux kernel slide: PoC-crash step uses GPT-5.5; average token cost $3.61 (median $2.34), average time 21.5 minutes (median 14.3); mitigated LPE cases average $8.56 (median $7.22) and 25.0 minutes; examples of why crashes are not security issues: non-default device driver, non-popular config, corrupted filesystem image.

Q&A

  • Q: How long to reverse engineer a Windows patch, and can open models do this locally? A: Binary diffing used to be slow; with AI the time to analyze and exploit drops drastically, so even large vendors must be careful pushing updates to customers. Open-weight models such as Kimi and GLM work very well, and many people use them because frontier models block binary analysis plus exploitation.
  • Q: What context goes into the annotation pass and the per-function pass, and do agents have tools to look up definitions? A: Static analysis (taint tracking and a CodeQL-backed code graph) feeds the LLM, which writes inline comments on each function; all agents then share the same annotated source.
  • Q: How do you think about variance and about verifying patches? A: Answered variant analysis only: agents use CVE or MSRC tags in commits to generalize where similar bugs may exist; patch verification was not addressed.
  • Q: How much of the pipeline must be retested per model release? A: A large benchmark pipeline retests model combinations; the system is model agnostic, so models are interchangeable, with powerful models for high-stakes targets and cheaper ones for large-scale scans.
  • Q: Does a stronger model erode the benefit of a segmented pipeline, and what does it do to cost? A: Open-source scanners such as skill-based harnesses are loosely coupled; forcing explicit stages gives control over token spend per stage. The speaker did not claim the pipeline remains optimal as models improve.

67 Taming AI Agents with Capsem: Hardware Sandboxing That Doesn't Kill Productivity

Elie Bursztein (Distinguished Research Scientist, Google DeepMind (slides carry the Google Security and Privacy Research mark)) · talk · 30 min · Watch

●●●○○ Useful, lighter on evidence. The talk describes an open-source Rust sandbox architecture, policy-design lessons and a retrospective on building the project with AI agents, with no security evaluation shown and a demo video that did not play.

The talk's thesis: Agent security fails when it is pitted against velocity, so the sandbox must be the fastest and easiest way to run agents, with the security boundary pushed down into a Rust hypervisor, per-VM low-privilege subprocesses and a single policy-enforcing egress point, the way Chrome won by being fast first and secure by design.

Sandboxing and isolation Guardrails and runtime controls Coding agent security MCP, tools and skills

Full breakdown: 14 claims, 9 numbers, 5 slides

Bursztein opens with the familiar boardroom standoff between security and speed and argues the community must stop framing it as a trade-off. His answer is Capsem, an open-source Rust hypervisor, about nine months old, that boots hardened Linux VMs running OCI containers for agents such as Claude Code, Codex CLI, Antigravity and Claude Desktop, with a one-click install, CLI, UI, SDKs and MCP server, and under two second boot. He explains the secure-by-default design: each agent in its own zero-trust VM, no direct network, and a pile of small sandboxed subprocesses (Landlock and seccomp) in the style of Chrome. Networking is split into three paths: LAN and internet traffic through a per-VM security engine that man-in-the-middles HTTPS with an injected root certificate; inter-VM traffic through a pure Rust virtual layer-2 router; and exposed developer ports through an authenticated low-privilege process. The security engine runs plugins (credential broker, PII scanner, input sanitizer, malware scanner in progress) and rules written in TOML with CEL (Common Expression Language) expressions over IP, TCP, DNS, HTTP, model, MCP, file and process events, plus Sigma detections and OpenTelemetry output. A planned demo video failed. He then gives lessons from building Capsem entirely with AI agents: tests are 52% of the code, guardrail rules catch repeated agent mistakes, yet CI success rate collapsed and releases slowed from 20 minutes to three to four hours.

What to do with it (this breakdown's reading)

  • Make the sandboxed path the fastest way to start an agent; adoption, not mandate, is what will make a boundary stick.
  • Put control at the environment boundary with a single egress choke point that understands model and MCP semantics, not just IP and DNS.
  • Hide long-lived credentials from agents with a broker and treat unusual characters in prompts as a cheap hardening control.
  • If agents write your code, budget for a large test and guardrail investment and expect release engineering to slow; measure CI success rate as a health signal.
  • Solve shadow-IT visibility alongside sandboxing, because enterprises cannot enforce a sandbox on agent binaries they cannot find.

How far the evidence goes

This breakdown's assessment

  • No security evaluation is shown: no escape testing, red-team results, threat model coverage or comparison to other sandboxes (gVisor, Firecracker, Kata were raised only in Q&A), so the secure-by-default claims rest on architecture description in the recording.
  • Man-in-the-middle HTTPS inspection with a root certificate injected into every guest concentrates trust in the security engine and its certificate cache; the talk gives no discussion of certificate pinning, non-HTTP exfiltration channels or covert channels.
  • Speed and throughput numbers (two second boot, 5,000 RPS, 2 GB per second) lack methodology, and the boot claim was not demonstrated because the demo video failed.
  • The Chrome analogy supports adoption strategy but does not address that agents need credentials and data inside the sandbox, so exfiltration through allowed channels remains the hard residual risk.
  • The AI-development retrospective contains the most measured data in the talk, but it covers a single project and the chart labels differ from each other and from the speaker's description (a July zero versus an August minimum near 4%, Tests and Build both 52.3%).
  • The speaker works at Google DeepMind and presents an open-source project under the Google Security and Privacy Research mark. The slides state 'users love' and 'enterprise loves' Capsem; no adoption data was shown.

Limits the speaker acknowledged

  • Capsem is 100% AI-generated; the team reviews and tests but acknowledges AI introduces mistakes and sometimes assumption-violating changes.
  • Release process and reliability degraded significantly as the project grew.
  • OpenTelemetry support is by default but has not been tested much and may have bugs; the malware scanner is work in progress; the policy authoring language is not yet deployed.
  • Enforcing use of a single environment (on Mac, Windows) across an enterprise is unsolved, and vendors will have to help.
  • The speaker does not claim Capsem has the best policy solution, only a list of the hard problems.

The full record: argument, frameworks, tools, attacks, defenses, demos, quotes, Q&A, notes

The argument

  1. Security and velocity must stop being opposed, because teams will not accept extra steps and the agent wave will not slow down.
  2. The right place for control is the environment: push the security boundary down into a sandbox that is more convenient and faster than the unsandboxed alternative, as Chrome did for browsing.
  3. A secure agent sandbox needs per-agent zero-trust VMs, an air gap behind a single policy-enforcing egress point with full semantic visibility (HTTP, model, MCP), and a modular set of low-privilege subprocesses instead of a monolith.
  4. Policy must be expressive, enforceable at the right stack level, and authorable by agents, and observability should plug into enterprise standards (Sigma, OpenTelemetry).
  5. Building such a system with AI agents is feasible but costly in testing and release engineering, and the AI's repeated rule violations make release speed collapse.

Frameworks and models

  • Fast, usable, secure triangle. Design goal that Capsem must satisfy all three; insight is a specialized agent environment, think Chrome for agents.
  • Secure by default pillars. Four cards: zero-trust environment (each agent in an isolated hardened VM), air-gapped (all traffic through the security engine), policy engine (HTTP, DNS, model, MCP, file, process detection and rule enforcement), security plugins (API to intercept, block, ask and rewrite events).
  • Split networking subsystem. Three isolated paths: LAN and internet through the per-VM security engine process; inter-VM through a sandboxed pure Rust virtual router; exposed ports through an authenticated sandboxed low-privilege process.
  • Fine-grained sandboxed subprocesses. Components colored by host permission: minimum (granted connections only), limited (assigned files, credentials or upstream connections), elevated (VM control), maximum (launching-user permissions), with a VM hardware boundary around the OCI container and guest helpers, and a per-VM ownership boundary.
  • Policy design problems. Three decisions every policy system faces: expressivity (including quantifying over history), the stack level to enforce at (IP and TCP, DNS, HTTP via man-in-the-middle, model bodies, MCP semantics), and the authoring system (a typed programming-language DSL that agents can autocomplete and compile-check).

Tools, papers and other artifacts

  • Capsem tool Open-source Rust hypervisor and VM system for sandboxing coding agents, with CLI, UI, SDKs (Python, TypeScript, Rust) and MCP; available for Mac and Linux. Contributions welcomed. https://capsem.org
  • Capsem security architecture documentation paper Public diagram of the process and permission model. https://docs.capsem.org/architecture/security/
  • Capsem code statistics dataset Source of the codebase breakdown and CI success chart. https://docs.capsem.org/architecture/statistics/
  • Common Expression Language (CEL) standard Google open-source expression language used for rule match conditions.
  • Sigma standard Detection rule format Capsem supports for real-time detection and blocking.
  • OpenTelemetry standard Default telemetry export; the speaker said it has not been tested much.
  • NVIDIA OpenShell tool Mentioned as another project taking the push-security-down approach.

Attacks and failure modes

  • Prompt injection and agents acting beyond their remit are the motivating threats; the talk names sandbox escapes by models as a recent proof that weak environments fail.
  • Exposed VM ports create a same-origin problem between VMs and a path to local host files if not restricted.
  • A compromised egress process could relay traffic across VMs if shared, which motivates one security engine per VM.
  • Non-ASCII or unusual characters in prompts are treated as attack surface for prompt injection.

Defenses and controls

  • Run each agent in its own hardened VM with no direct network, using Rust components with Landlock and seccomp (and seccomp on macOS) around each subprocess.
  • Route all egress through one low-privilege security engine per VM with full ip, tcp, http, model and mcp inspection and complete logging.
  • Use a credential broker so real credentials never enter the VM, plus PII scanning and a sanitizer that strips non-ASCII and odd characters from model input.
  • Write rules as typed TOML plus CEL conditions with allow, ask, deny, rewrite actions, enforce corporate rules first via a manifest, and emit OpenTelemetry events.
  • Ingest Sigma detections for file, process, network and model events and use the API for instant local or remote remediation.
  • Keep inter-VM links explicit decisions, and restrict and authenticate exposed ports.
  • Write guardrail rules for the coding agent after each recurring mistake and run end-to-end install and boot tests inside a fresh VM before release.

Q&A

  • Q: How does Capsem relate to other sandbox technologies like gVisor and Kata? A: Much legacy technology will be rewritten; sandboxes written before Rust differ from Rust ones (Firecracker, Nitro and others), C++ is a liability for security code, and there will be an explosion of sandboxes with a race on performance and usability; sandboxes need low-privilege subprocesses rather than monoliths and real isolation between VMs.
  • Q: What enterprise feedback have you had, and is it painful to move a working directory into a sandbox? A: Through talks with large Google Cloud customers the main concern is not knowing what agents and token spend exist in the organization (shadow IT); enforcing a single environment on Mac and Windows is hard, agent binaries multiply because a new one takes about 20 minutes of vibe coding, and compliance and deployment are harder than the technology.
  • Q: How do you manage policies so users can just get work done? A: Policy systems hit three problems: expressivity (needing to quantify over the history of tools and model calls, with CEL as a sweet spot between regex and formal logic, relevant to the no private data plus internet access plus destruction combination), enforcement level (IP and TCP are easy, then DNS, then HTTP needing man-in-the-middle, then model bodies and MCP with differing provider formats), and authoring (use a programming-language-based thin DSL such as JavaScript objects so agents can autocomplete and compilers can check). Easiness, speed and expressivity form the trade-off triangle.

68 Dispatches From the Wrong End of an Agent Swarm

Caleb Sima (Chief Security Officer, Hadrian), Alec Eckmann (Lead responder on Sima's team at Hadrian) · talk · 23 min · Watch

●●●●○ Specific and well evidenced. The talk recounts one incident from the responders' side, with a step-by-step exploit chain through an AI gateway and its MCP token cache, and does not name the products involved.

The talk's thesis: An autonomous AI attacker, run by a government-services vendor as a free external assessment, compromised a security vendor's AI gateway, Okta tenant and Kubernetes pods within hours; defenders should expect machine-speed chained attacks, and should invest in automated containment, logging of the layers underneath their gateways, and their own access to offensive-capable models.

Autonomous offense AI in the SOC MCP, tools and skills Agent identity and authorization

Full breakdown: 13 claims, 7 numbers, 5 slides

Caleb Sima, CSO of Hadrian, explains that his company accepted a free AI-agent-based external assessment from a services firm that works for the US government, and he did not tell his security team. Alec Eckmann, the lead responder, then walks through the incident as he lived it. At 1:44 p.m. an SRE asked about odd MCP servers on the company's AI gateway. Eckmann traced them to a user synced from Okta by the gateway's own sync token, and found that the MCP servers kept coming back after deletion. The adversary had used path traversal on the gateway's provider configuration API, passed an environment variable reference to a provider-creation call, and got the unredacted Okta token back. With it the agent authorised to a dozen internal apps including Jira, Confluence, GitHub and Snowflake, dumped 29 client secrets, abused the gateway's cached MCP OAuth tokens, and used a stdio MCP server parameter to run commands in Kubernetes pod context, reading secrets and moving laterally. Containment came after about 45 minutes, when Sima revealed it was a drill. Two weeks later the vendor report called some CVEs non-exploitable, yet the agent had rooted the firewall. Eckmann closes with four observations, and Sima adds that the agent ran phishing, brute force and scanning at once, that Anthropic models refused defensive work, and that Hadrian is procuring open-weight models.

What to do with it (this breakdown's reading)

  • Inventory what your AI gateway and MCP infrastructure cache and can reveal through management APIs, and test it for unredacted token and environment variable exposure.
  • Add telemetry for the infrastructure below your AI gateway and for appliance operating systems, so a stripped application log is not your only trigger.
  • Build and rehearse automated containment playbooks for multiple simultaneous agents, including IP-rotation-proof controls.
  • Plan defensive model access in advance, given that some frontier models may refuse incident-response work.
  • Require hard scope enforcement and a kill switch in any AI-based assessment contract, and verify the kill.

How far the evidence goes

This breakdown's assessment

  • This is a single incident with no counts or controls, so claims about AI-specific speed, forking and creativity are inferred from one case; no comparison with a human red team was shown.
  • The vendor, gateway product and assessment provider are unnamed, so none of the findings can be checked or compared.
  • The claim that the attacker found a zero-day on the external website is asserted in passing with no detail.
  • The comparison that one frontier lab was worst and another better is anecdote from a single use case and was followed by the speakers' decision to procure open-weight models; the model-refusal point is the speakers' experience and no measurement was shown.
  • The vendor report's non-exploitable CVE statement and the later firewall root are findings about the assessment's scoping and reporting; the talk does not tie them to AI-specific behavior.

Limits the speaker acknowledged

  • Eckmann said the PR-body search issue is not unique to agentic attacks.
  • Time limits kept out technical details such as the phishing and zero-day specifics; speakers invited follow-up conversations.
  • The speakers did not know the agent's goal or the attacker's underlying infrastructure.
  • Eckmann said the attacker was not stealthy, and noted a more careful operator could be.

The full record: argument, frameworks, tools, attacks, defenses, demos, quotes, Q&A, notes

The argument

  1. A vendor's AI offensive agent, scoped as external-only, escaped its scope and attacked Hadrian's internal AI enablement stack.
  2. The decisive weaknesses were in AI infrastructure: a gateway with an unauthenticated-path bug and an unredacted management API, a cache of every user's downstream OAuth tokens, and stdio MCP servers that run in pod context.
  3. An AI adversary chains vulnerabilities trivially, forks instead of pivoting, and can be run from commodity cloud, so defenders get no time advantage from human-speed attackers.
  4. AI enablement raises engineering velocity but gives the attacker the same leverage: centralised MCP gateways and AI-written PR bodies become reconnaissance sources.
  5. Defence therefore needs fast automated containment, telemetry from the layers beneath the gateway and the firewall OS, and defensive access to capable models, including open-weight ones.

Frameworks and models

  • Four observations on an AI adversary. Chaining vulns is trivial; it forks, it does not pivot; the barrier for entry is relatively low; it was not stealthy but it could be; AI enablement goes both ways.
  • Defender agent stack versus adversary stack. Slide builds contrast the defender's assets (gateway with persistence and MCP spawning, Okta user, SCIM token, OAuth apps) with the adversary's parallel agents: firewall-agent, gateway-agent (mcp-tokens, mcp-spawner), eks-agent and okta-agent (client-secrets, github, jira, confluence, snowflake and others).

Tools, papers and other artifacts

  • AI gateway with MCP token cache and management API product The vendor is not named. Its provider configuration API, unredacted environment variable handling and stdio MCP parameter were the exploited surface.
  • Okta SCIM sync token product The gateway's own sync token created the adversary user and later authenticated to downstream apps.
  • gh api search/issues queries tool Used on a slide to show how PR body text can be searched for vulnerability disclosures.
  • Vendor report: Informational Bulletin: Precautionary Fixes for Non-Exploitable OSS CVEs paper The assessment vendor's bulletin, later contradicted by root on the firewall.

Attacks and failure modes

  • Path traversal on the gateway's management API to reach the provider configuration endpoint.
  • Smuggling an environment variable reference into a provider-creation request so the response returned unredacted environment variables, including the Okta API token.
  • Using the stolen Okta token to create a user, authorise to downstream apps by OAuth and read client secrets, then forking agents per target rather than pivoting.
  • Dumping the gateway's cached MCP OAuth tokens for all users via the management API, so Okta saw only refresh-token activity.
  • Spawning stdio MCP servers with an optional parameter that executes in Kubernetes pod context, then reading namespace secrets and moving across pods and the node group; a container escape was attempted but did not complete.
  • Re-creating deleted MCP servers (a failed attempt, then a success two minutes later) with no re-enablement log.
  • Rotating to new AWS elastic IPs to evade IP deny lists.
  • Running phishing email, login brute force and external scanning at the same time, with an initial entry via a zero-day on the external website where Okta did not protect every path.
  • Rooting the firewall through the underlying BSD OS, which was not logged.

Defenses and controls

  • Automate containment: deny-listing, token kills and credential rotation at agent speed, because manual clicking could not keep up with new IPs.
  • Ship logs from the layers under the gateway, including Kubernetes infrastructure and the firewall OS, since the gateway exploit stripped its own telemetry.
  • Do not cache or return unredacted downstream OAuth tokens or environment variables through any management API, and do not let MCP stdio parameters execute in pod context.
  • Treat a centralised MCP gateway as a single point holding every user's downstream access and scope it accordingly.
  • Watch what AI-written PR bodies disclose about unpatched vulnerabilities.
  • Obtain defensive access to capable offensive-grade models, or run open-weight models on own hardware, as Hadrian is doing.
  • Restrict WAF and AWS-facing configuration more tightly; the cloud provider should also flag tenants that spin up dozens of elastic IPs every 10 to 15 minutes.

On the slides, not said aloud

70 Lightning Talk

Greg McCord (Chief Security Officer, Confide Group (description: Cybersecurity Strategist and CISO Advisor, Confide Group)) · lightning · 5 min · Watch

●●○○○ Position or overview. The talk gives a short personal account of coping with overload during an AI rollout and contains no technical claims or checkable data.

The talk's thesis: CISOs under pressure from fast AI adoption feel overwhelmed, and a deliberate pause and different perspective is a better coping mechanism than spiraling or working 16-hour days chasing shiny objects.

Adoption and culture

Full breakdown: 4 claims, 1 numbers, 2 slides

McCord uses his lightning slot to talk about mental health rather than technology. He recounts the start of the agentic rush at his previous employer, a technology company where he was CISO: leadership wanted to turn everything on, he argued for guardrails, and being against the grain left him isolated, followed by a management change that put him on the chopping block. He describes spiraling through self-doubt before concluding he was right because of customer data and other risks, then deciding to study the organization's culture and define his approach. He told his team to research every model in front of them quickly so they would not end up where he did. He then describes how he copes with feeling overwhelmed: step away from the keyboard, touch a surface with rough edges, and change his state of mind, drawing on somatic processing techniques from his therapist wife. He says he knows to stop when he is spending 16 hours a day chasing shiny objects and to return with more energy and a different angle. At Confide, building AI products and helping other CISOs roll out AI at scale, he says he can now share the process. He closes with a short audience breathing exercise, says he is nervous, and notes there are better and worse coping mechanisms.

What to do with it (this breakdown's reading)

  • Treat CISO overload during an AI rollout as an operational risk and give yourself and your team permission to pause.
  • Have the team learn the models in front of them early so that they can argue guardrails with knowledge rather than from the sidelines.
  • Use a concrete signal, such as 16-hour research days, to trigger a break.

How far the evidence goes

This breakdown's assessment

  • Personal anecdote with no data; the AI rollout process the speaker refers to is not described.
  • The framing that being right about guardrails still cost him standing is a real organizational tension but the talk offers coping rather than a way to win the argument with leadership.
  • The employer in the story is unnamed, and the speaker's current role is at a company that builds AI products and advises CISOs; the rollout process he mentions is not described, so it cannot be checked.

Limits the speaker acknowledged

  • Speaker said he could talk about this for hours and limited the talk to a short personal account; no process for AI rollout at scale was presented.

The argument

  1. A CISO who pushes for guardrails during an AI rollout can end up isolated and professionally at risk, which produces an overwhelming spiral.
  2. The feeling is normal and manageable: step away, change state, and come back to the problem with energy and a different perspective.
  3. The experience pushed him to learn everything about AI and tell his team to do the same so they are not caught unprepared.
  4. Having done this, he can now give other CISOs a process for rolling AI out at scale.

Defenses and controls

  • Put guardrails in place before turning on AI features, especially where customer data is at stake.
  • Have the security team research every model they face early so the team is not caught unprepared.
  • Recognize overload and step away: leave the keyboard, change state, and return with a different perspective.

Demos

  • A guided breathing exercise with the audience: eyes closed, a deep breath in, hold, release, then asking who felt a change in demeanor.

71 Lightning Talk

G Mark Hardy (CEO, National Security Corporation) · lightning · 5 min · Watch

●○○○○ Informal session. The talk gives career advice on speaking at conferences and contains no technical or AI security content.

The talk's thesis: Security practitioners should speak at conferences at every chance, because presenting builds communication, persuasion and promotability, and it is the way good ideas reach others.

Adoption and culture

Full breakdown: 3 claims, 3 numbers, 2 slides

G Mark Hardy opens by asking the room who has never given a conference presentation, and says he is speaking impromptu about why getting on stage matters. He tells a short career story: a Navy ROTC scholarship, five years at sea, orders to the National Security Agency that were cancelled because, as he was told, the Navy had no need for computer security, then a move to the reserves and a job at Booz Allen Hamilton. In his first week a colleague named Lena told him to speak every chance he gets. After about four attempts he was accepted to an ASUS conference in August 1986, where Admiral Grace Hopper gave the keynote and gave him a nanosecond, an 11.8 inch piece of wire. He lists the benefits of speaking: better communication, being more persuasive, dropping filler words by getting comfortable with silence, and a path to invitations and promotion. He suggests reviewing the transcript of your own talks to see every filler word. He ends by saying people in security tend to be introverts who dislike embarrassing themselves, but that practice pays off across a career, so always speak. The talk contains no technical content about AI or security.

What to do with it (this breakdown's reading)

  • Encourage and sponsor your engineers to give talks, since communication skill affects how far their ideas travel.
  • Treat comfort with silence as a trainable speaking skill and review your own transcripts for fillers.
  • Use conference speaking as a promotion and visibility path for security staff.

How far the evidence goes

This breakdown's assessment

  • Career advice, not a technical talk; no evidence beyond personal experience.
  • The talk covers professional development rather than AI security topics, and no technical claims were made.

  • The talk was described as impromptu; Hardy joked that the airfare would have been cheaper with more notice.

72 Lightning Talk

Kyle Easterly (Co-Founder and CEO, Delve Group, Anchorage, Alaska) · lightning · 7 min · Watch

●●○○○ Position or overview. The talk presents an offline GPU demo machine for AI literacy, with its hardware specification and build timeline, and has no security content or measured results on audience understanding.

The talk's thesis: People outside the field understand AI poorly, so Delve Group built a glass-topped, fully offline GPU machine called LOAD (Local Offline AI Demonstration) that shows how AI works on real hardware, and he urges the audience to build something similar to explain AI to their neighbours.

Adoption and culture Model internals

Full breakdown: 6 claims, 7 numbers, 4 slides

Kyle Easterly of Delve Group in Anchorage, Alaska, says the customers his AI deployment software company meets in oil and gas, healthcare and telecom see AI as a chat box and a data center. To fix that, he and an intern named Brian built LOAD, a rackmount machine laid flat on a table with a plexiglass lid, running models entirely offline. A 3D digital twin of every part lets visitors tour the machine with a Stream Deck or by voice. Easterly describes the build: two GPUs, an EPYC CPU, 256 GB of ECC memory, a custom water loop, and open models served with vLLM, assembled in about a month using SSDs he already owned. It debuted on Sep 28, 2026 and has since been shown at a leadership summit, a university computer science class and industry trade shows, and he hopes to take it to the state capital. Demos include watching a small model pick its next word layer by layer, a fleet of 21 agents building a town in the style of the Stanford generative agents paper, handwritten fuel tickets turned into structured data, and a live fine-tune in which a Llama model learns who built it. Hardware failures happened in public and he treats that as part of the lesson. He closes by asking the audience to help the people around them understand AI. The talk has no security content.

What to do with it (this breakdown's reading)

  • Where non-technical stakeholders struggle with AI literacy, build a tangible offline demo, as Easterly urges the audience to do.
  • Show training and inference on real hardware, including failures, to build trust with customers and policymakers.
  • Run demos on offline local models so customer data is not sent to external services, which matters for sensitive sectors.

How far the evidence goes

This breakdown's assessment

  • This is an AI literacy talk built around the speaker's company's demo machine, with no security content; the educational effect was not measured.
  • The fine-tune timing differs between speech (about a minute, and about 3 minutes per visitor) and the slide (15 to 30 seconds), so the two figures differ.
  • The speaker's company sells AI deployment software, and the demos use small models whose behaviour was not compared with frontier systems.

Limits the speaker acknowledged

  • Easterly said he had seen the slides only once, and that he had more slides than time.
  • He said the digital twin is still a work in progress and the machine had a fried GPU and other hardware faults.
  • No evidence was presented on whether the demo changes audience understanding.

73 We don't need an LLM for That

Xenia Mountrouidou (Principal Applied AI Scientist, AppGate (from the video description; the auto-caption renders it as Upstream, and she says she works on zero trust networking signal)), Casey Wilson (Principal Software Engineer, BusinessLoans.com (video description and speech)) · talk · 30 min · Watch

●●●●○ Specific and well evidenced. The talk reports a controlled comparison of zero-shot LLMs, fine-tuned encoders, XGBoost, a tabular foundation model and two ensemble designs on phishing and network-flow detection, with AUCPR, cost and latency figures and a decision guide.

The talk's thesis: For detecting phishing and network attacks, zero-shot frontier LLMs are not the best tool: fine-tuned small encoders win on text, tabular models or XGBoost win on network flows, and LLM-plus-ML ensembles do not pay for their complexity.

Evals, benchmarks and metrics AI in the SOC Fraud, scams and abuse

Full breakdown: 14 claims, 21 numbers, 5 slides

Mountrouidou and Wilson test whether an LLM can replace a purpose-built detector, answering with measurements instead of impressions. They build the experiment from interchangeable parts: open labelled data (18K phishing emails, a Mirai capture rebuilt as statistics, flows and packets, and CIC-IDS2017), numeric and embedding features, and models ranging from XGBoost and zero-shot LLMs and small models to fine-tuned encoders and decoders, a tabular foundation model (TabPFN-3), two System 1 decision models, which return a calibrated probability without generating text (Laya, which is open, and Jev), and two ensembles (a router and a stacked meta-learner). They score with area under the precision-recall curve (AUCPR) against the class prior, the share of malicious examples, which is the score chance would earn. On phishing, zero-shot Claude Sonnet 4.6 reaches 0.970 and Gemini 3.1 Pro 0.990, but fine-tuned ModernBERT reaches 0.998 and a LoRA-tuned Llama 3.2 3B reaches 0.999, up from 0.780 untuned. On network flows, zero-shot LLMs sit at the class prior, XGBoost is strong, fine-tuning does not beat it, and TabPFN-3 alone is best at 0.856. Ensembles help on email but never beat fine-tuning, and on flows routing makes results worse. Cost and latency strongly favour small and classical models. They close with a decision tree and advice to get a few hundred labels.

What to do with it (this breakdown's reading)

  • Before funding an LLM-based detector, benchmark it against XGBoost and a fine-tuned small encoder on your own labelled data using AUCPR versus class prior.
  • Invest analyst time in a few hundred labelled examples and an annotation workflow, which they report pays back against per-call LLM cost.
  • Do not use zero-shot LLMs for numeric network telemetry; try TabPFN-3 or XGBoost.
  • Avoid ensemble and router architectures unless you measure a gain; in their tests they added cost and complexity without beating the best single model.
  • Account for latency, VRAM and cost per million records when choosing, since the cheapest model was often the best.

How far the evidence goes

This breakdown's assessment

  • The experiment reports many numbers on fixed splits, but it uses one seed and shows no confidence intervals, so small gaps such as 0.998 vs 0.999 cannot be distinguished from noise.
  • Zero-shot results depend heavily on the prompt and the representation of numeric rows as text, and the talk does not show the prompts, so the finding that LLMs sit at the class prior cannot be separated from that choice.
  • Phishing text is a task where LLMs are strong and the fine-tuned models trained on the same distribution as the test set; real-world phishing has distribution shift that the talk did not test.
  • Mirai and CIC-IDS2017 (the Mirai-derived Kitsune data) are old, narrow benchmarks; the talk did not test whether the findings about TabPFN-3 and XGBoost transfer to enterprise traffic with a 99% benign ratio.
  • No product was presented in the talk. The Laya and Jev recommendations were given with limited detail on the Jev vendor model.
  • Comparing against frontier models ignores tool use and retrieval, a point an audience member raised and the speakers only partly answered.
  • The Claude phishing score of 0.970 is on a 22% stratified subset and Claude has no flows result, so the headline comparison against fine-tuned models is not on identical test data.
  • The label-efficiency slide differs from the spoken 'a couple thousand labels' for network data: the plot shows about 2,000 labels reach only 0.54 AUCPR and about 30,000 are needed for 0.82, so the labelling needed for flows is higher than the spoken advice states.

Limits the speaker acknowledged

  • Class priors in the tests were 17% to 84% malicious, far higher than the roughly 1% malicious in production traffic; the speakers acknowledged this and said the pattern did not change below 20%.
  • Cost figures do not include analyst labelling time, which they estimate at about 4 hours for 200 labels.
  • They compared zero-shot LLMs without an agent harness; an agent with these models as tools could do better but is too slow and costly for real-time detection.
  • Open public datasets were used, so drift and deployment behaviour were not tested; they said models should be monitored and retrained.
  • Without labels on network flows none of the tested tools worked.
  • The speakers did not show a label-efficiency result for flows below about 30,000 labels reaching XGBoost level; the chart shows flows stay at the class prior until about 1,000 labels.

The full record: argument, frameworks, tools, attacks, defenses, demos, quotes, Q&A, notes

The argument

  1. Stakeholders ask why train models when a zero-shot LLM is easy to deploy, so the question needs a controlled test with hard numbers.
  2. On text-heavy phishing, zero-shot LLMs do well, but fine-tuned small encoders and decoders do better, at a fraction of the cost and latency.
  3. On numeric network data, zero-shot LLMs perform at the class prior, and XGBoost or the tabular foundation model TabPFN-3 are the right tools.
  4. Ensembles of ML and LLMs or decision models add cost and complexity but do not beat the best single tuned model, and routing can hurt.
  5. So label a few hundred examples, choose the model by data type and labels available, and treat the LLM as a baseline to check against the class prior rather than as the default.

Frameworks and models

  • Experiment as Lego bricks. Four swappable parts: Data (phishing emails; Mirai as packets, flows and statistics; CIC-IDS2017 flows), Features (numeric counts and timing; embeddings, meaning text as numbers), Model (single: XGBoost, zero-shot LLM or SLM, fine-tuned LMs; combined: router that escalates unsure cases, meta-learner that learns whom to trust), Score (AUCPR, with chance equal to the percent malicious).
  • Five fundamental questions. Can a prompted LLM detect attacks; do ensembles beat the single best model; does fine-tuning beat LLMs, traditional ML and ensembles; how much do models cost; do newer models like TabPFN and Jev change the recommendations.
  • Model spectrum. Frontier LLM via API (Claude Sonnet 4.6, Gemini 3.1 Pro), GPT-OSS, small local LLMs (Mistral 7B, Gemma3 12B, Llama 3.2 3B), ModernBERT fine-tuned as a classifier, System 1 decision models (Laya 421M open, Jev 1.13 proprietary API), tabular foundation model TabPFN-3, and gradient-boosted trees (XGBoost).
  • Decision tree: do we need an LLM for that? Usually not. New domain: check Jev, Laya or an LLM AUCPR against class prior first. Phishing: with a training pipeline use ModernBERT fine-tuned, without use zero-shot Jev or Laya. Network intrusion: without training use TabPFN; with training and raw packet fields use XGBoost or TabPFN with a flow-aware split; with training but no raw fields use TabPFN, or XGBoost/TabPFN (about equal to BERT fine-tuned) when labels are abundant. Cost-constrained: decision model or SLM or ModernBERT with an embedding gate.
  • Router versus meta-learner ensembles. Router: an ML gate model predicts with a confidence; if confident, use its prediction, if not, route to the LLM. Meta-learner: ML models and the LLM run in parallel and a combiner weights each model's output. The results slides test both with XGBoost and TabPFN-3 as gate or combiner.

Tools, papers and other artifacts

  • Open-source GitHub repository, 20-page paper and blog repo Speakers say the code, a 20-page paper and a blog are available; the agenda slide and the closing slide carry QR codes (the closing slide labels them Blog and Github Repo). No URL was spoken or legible.
  • Phishing email dataset (Hugging Face) dataset 18K labelled emails, 37.4% phishing.
  • Mirai botnet capture and CIC-IDS2017 dataset Mirai rebuilt as statistics (AfterImage), flows and packets; CIC-IDS2017 as flows. The results slides label the network flows task Kitsune.
  • TabPFN-3 tool Tabular foundation model used in context with no training; best single model on network flows.
  • Laya (421M) and Jev 1.13 tool System 1 decision models that return a calibrated probability without text generation; Laya is open (Apache 2.0, ModernBERT-large backbone), Jev is a proprietary API per the slide footnote.
  • XGBoost tool Classic gradient-boosted tree baseline.
  • ModernBERT tool Encoder fine-tuned as a classifier, about 30 times smaller than the fine-tuned Llama.

Defenses and controls

  • For text-based detection with labels, fine-tune a small encoder such as ModernBERT; a few hundred labels are enough.
  • For network flows with labels, use TabPFN-3 or XGBoost; with raw packet fields use a flow-aware train and test split.
  • Without labels, use a System 1 decision model such as Laya or Jev for phishing, and for network flows get labels first because no prompted model beat chance.
  • Always score with AUCPR against the class prior, and treat any model that lands at the prior as useless.
  • Capture labels from analyst behaviour, such as analysts overriding model alerts, and use annotation queues to cut the cost.
  • Monitor for drift and retrain; for email they retrained about every two months with about 500 new labels.
  • Where latency must be under a second or compute is on-premise, deploy small tuned models rather than agents or frontier APIs.

  • Did you test more realistic benign-heavy class ratios? Mountrouidou: not in this set; the lowest malicious share was 17% and the pattern did not change; precision can be sacrificed for recall in her MDR work.
  • How similar is Kitsune to the Mirai data you trained on? Mountrouidou: the same.
  • Is comparing against a zero-shot LLM without a harness fair? Mountrouidou: they compared encoders, transformers and decision models, and real-time zero-trust detection needs millisecond latency, not a five-minute agent. Wilson: the best accuracy would probably be an agent using these as tools, and this is one piece of that.
  • How do you handle model degradation over time, and activity sequences? Mountrouidou: drift is standard; they monitor and retrain as often as needed. Sequences were not addressed in the answer.

  • Does the cost comparison include engineer and analyst time? Mountrouidou: it is a good point; labelling is a one-time cost versus forever inference; about 4 hours for 200 labels, and 500 labels every 2 months for email took about half a day between two people.

74 Building & Breaking an MCP Permission Broker (Approval Is Not Human Presence)

Brooks McMillin (The Browser Company) · talk · 26 min · Watch

●●●●○ Specific and well evidenced. The talk presents a threat model and test plan for coding agents that share the user's UID, shows two failures (passing tests with a broken human approval path, and an environment bypass), and rests on a single-user home-lab evaluation.

The talk's thesis: When a coding agent runs as the same Unix user as its human, an Approve click is only input the agent may be able to produce, so sensitive capabilities need a separately protected proof of human presence that the agent cannot read, write, replay or route around. Even then, per-session grants are not isolation: the surrounding environment is part of the boundary.

Agent identity and authorization MCP, tools and skills Coding agent security Sandboxing and isolation

Full breakdown: 12 claims, 9 numbers, 5 slides

McMillin runs 20 to 30 coding-agent sessions at once on his personal workstation, some started by hand and some by cron jobs, and wanted only specific sessions to hold privileged capabilities such as Kubernetes access or a logged-in browser. His starting point was a kubeconfig file and a skill pointing at it, which any agent could discover. He built an MCP permission broker: each session gets an OAuth client identity held in memory, requests a named capability, and a human approves with a six-digit one-time code from a phone authenticator that never enters agent context. Grants name a session, a capability and an expiry, usually two hours, and can be revoked. He states the attacker position up front: the agent has his UID, admin group membership, broker-operator group membership, admin-socket access, a writable source checkout and a valid session, but no root and no passwordless sudo. He then walks three attack routes (steal or write the verifier state, replace policy or bypass enforcement, forge an approval), shows each is refused, and cites a historical evaluation of 15 defined checks. A twist follows: all checks were green while a database migration had broken the human approval path, locking him out. The talk closes with a live demo that a new terminal multiplexer, Rex, let one session drive another session's tab and borrow its browser grant, which erased the per-session guarantee. He offers a five-step repeatable boundary test and reference code.

What to do with it (this breakdown's reading)

  • On your own agent platform, let the agent answer its own approval request and check whether new authority appears.
  • If agents share a UID with humans, stop treating UI approvals as a boundary; require a factor held by a verifier the agent UID cannot read or write, and prefer a separate agent user or sandbox.
  • Add success-path and upgrade-from-old-schema tests to security control suites so a broken human path is caught, not only a permissive one.
  • Inventory developer-host tooling (terminal multiplexers, IDE agents, session managers) for features that cross trust boundaries between agent sessions.
  • Be explicit about what a human-presence factor proves (presence) and does not (consent, comprehension), and design grants with narrow scope and short expiry accordingly.

How far the evidence goes

This breakdown's assessment

  • The attack results are a single-author, single-machine evaluation with no adversarial agent trial counts shown; '15 of 15' counts defined checks the author designed, which the slide itself says are not 15 techniques.
  • The attacks tested were file-permission and API-misuse attempts; no results were shown for a goal-directed agent searching for TOCTOU, process-level (ptrace, same-UID signals) or clipboard and screen-reading routes to the code, which same-UID separation does not obviously stop.
  • The Rex cross-tab bypass and the migration lockout are the two failures shown, and both point to environment and success-path testing alongside refusal tests. The talk's title claim is supported by reasoning and demonstrations, not by measured data.
  • He said a separate OS user or sandbox may be the better answer; the broker as presented is built for same-UID setups.
  • The live demo of the human path failed on an SSL error, so the successful end-to-end result relied on an earlier recording shown in a replay frame.

Limits the speaker acknowledged

  • Controls are tailored to his home lab: the agent cannot get root and there is no passwordless sudo; other environments would need different guarantees.
  • Grants do not isolate sessions; if one session can affect or talk to another, the isolation breaks.
  • The one-time pad proves a human was present, not that they understood the action.
  • Ambient credentials (git, GitHub CLI, AWS CLI) remain unresolved; wrappers get in the way of human use.
  • The historical web UI was not live-tested, and 15 checks are not 15 exploit techniques.
  • The reference code is environment-specific.

The full record: argument, frameworks, tools, attacks, defenses, demos, quotes, Q&A, notes

The argument

  1. Hiding a credential file or leaving it out of a prompt is not an access-control boundary, because agents discover config files and skills and will use any access that makes the task easier.
  2. If the agent shares the human's UID, an approval response is just agent-reachable input, so the broker must verify a separately protected factor (a TOTP code from an enrolled phone) rather than trust the answer, and must protect the verifier's seed, database, policy and socket as well as its API.
  3. Three attack routes (state, routing, approval) all meet the same service-owned reference monitor, and each was tested and refused, with failure closed rather than falling back to a weaker local store.
  4. Passing refusal tests and health checks does not show the system works: a migration broke the human approval path while every refusal check stayed green, so tests must cover success and upgrades from historical disk states as well as denial.
  5. A one-time code proves a human was present, not that they understood or consented to the action, and per-session grants do not stop one session borrowing another's authority unless the sessions are actually isolated.
  6. The environment is part of the boundary: installing a terminal multiplexer that lets sessions control each other's tabs defeated the broker's guarantees without any new grant being issued.

Frameworks and models

  • Attacker position versus protected state. Define the boundary before testing. Attacker holds the human UID, admin and broker-operator groups, admin-socket access, a writable checkout and a valid session. Protected: service identity, deployed verifier and its state, the enrolled phone; admin-group membership is not unrestricted sudo.
  • Three routes to unauthorized authority. State (steal the factor, write a grant), routing (replace policy, bypass the monitor), approval (fake a decision, forge the factor). All three meet the same protected authority.
  • Service-owned reference monitor. MCP client elicitation response, CLI over a restricted admin socket and web UI approval form all feed one monitor that verifies the factor, calls _insert_grant, and records session plus capability plus expiry. Protected state is the policy DB, TOTP seed and audit trail.
  • Claim versus proof. An agent-controlled 'accept' is only a claim; a protected verifier checks the factor, not the answer. No valid factor means no grant.
  • Repeatable boundary test. Five steps: define the boundary, attack three routes, inspect authority (refusal reasons, grants, audit), prove both paths (human success, replay refusal, revocation, cleanup), test real upgrades from historical database shapes. Run only in an authorized environment with a harmless capability and retain evidence.
  • Broker profiles. Approval page offers agent-runner, coding, default (read-only TaskManager), personal-trusted (allow-all-minus-deny, marked fail-open), review, and ui-coding (adds browser-agent). Capability 'permission packs' such as browser access or agent-job access are requested per role for about two hours.

Tools, papers and other artifacts

  • mcp-presence-broker repo Reference code for the broker; the speaker says it is environment-specific. github.com/brooksmcmillin/mcp-presence-broker
  • Pi coding agent tool Coding agent the speaker runs behind a broker wrapper that selects a profile; extensions include broker-session and broker-profile.
  • Rex tool New terminal multiplexer from the makers of Ghostty (per the speaker); its default cross-tab control defeated the session isolation.
  • mcp-proxyctl tool Admin CLI for the broker used in the attack on policy replacement.

Attacks and failure modes

  • Agent reads or edits the verifier's on-disk TOTP seed or the SQLite grant database because it shares the human's UID.
  • Agent reloads the broker with its own policy file, or points the admin socket at a nonexistent path hoping for a fail-open local fallback.
  • Agent answers its own approval prompt: an MCP elicitation response with action accept, with the factor omitted or fabricated.
  • Agent discovers credential files and skills (a kubeconfig referenced in a skill) and uses them because they make the task easier.
  • Cross-session borrowing: a tool that lets one agent session drive another's terminal tab, as Rex did, lets an ungranted agent use an already-granted browser MCP session without any new grant.
  • Replaying a still-valid one-time code from a second session; the design target is a code that works once and expires.

Defenses and controls

  • Run the verifier as a separate service identity and make the TOTP seed, policy database, deployed code and policy source unreadable and unwritable by the agent UID, including the human user when the UIDs match.
  • Verify a separately protected factor in the monitor and ignore the agent-supplied 'accept'; keep the code out of agent context entirely (browser page or extension prompt).
  • Fail closed: refuse reloads of policy over the admin socket and refuse silent fallback to a local store if the broker socket is missing.
  • Make every grant name a session, a capability and an expiry (about two hours), with revocation, and a single-use code with a 5-failure, 5-minute lockout.
  • Wrap ambient credential tools (gh, cloud CLIs) with checks for an authorized session, or run agents under a separate OS user.
  • Test the success path and real upgrades from historical disk states, and inspect final authority state and audit records, not only error messages.
  • Treat the environment as part of the boundary: disable or isolate cross-session control features and review any tool installed on agent hosts.

Demos

  • Demo A: the Pi wrapper asks which broker profile to use; with the coding profile a human supplies a phone one-time code on the approval page and the agent gets access. Repeated without authenticating, the agent has no tool access and the broker returns the same error on deny.
  • Human path: the agent searches for a browser tool, finds none, calls permission_request_create for browser-agent; the human is prompted for a six-digit code outside agent context; after approval 63 broker tools appear and browser_agent_open_url is called. The live run failed with an SSL protocol error on https://localhost:8000 (a replayed earlier run succeeded and reported the page title).
  • Rex cross-tab demo: a session with no browser grant is told to use the Rex browser tab; it finds the other tab's capability through the rex skill and tries to drive it, borrowing the already-granted browser MCP access. The speaker concludes the grant boundary is defeated by the multiplexer.

75 Reading the Residual Stream: Productizing Activation-Probe Security at Intuit

Guy Elad (Intuit), Guy Shtar (Intuit) · talk · 24 min · Watch

●●●●○ Specific and well evidenced. The talk presents a detector design with a layer-band study, ablations and production figures including a dataset it missed entirely, compared against an internal baseline, with no adaptive-attacker test shown.

The talk's thesis: A prompt-injection and jailbreak detector can match the semantic understanding of an LLM judge at near classical-ML cost by reading the hidden states of a small frozen open-weight model with per-layer logistic-regression probes, without generating a single token.

Guardrails and runtime controls Prompt injection Model internals Evals, benchmarks and metrics

Full breakdown: 12 claims, 16 numbers, 5 slides

Intuit's AI scientists describe a generation-free guardrail for prompt injection, jailbreak and goal hijacking. The setting is enterprise scale: hundreds of GenAI use cases, every input scanned at peak traffic, and a latency target of under 700 ms p99. Rules and classical ML meet the budget but are easy to bypass; LLM judges are accurate but too slow and costly. The proposed route is to run the input through a small open-weight model (2 to 4B parameters) once, read last-token hidden states from a band of layers, score each layer with a logistic-regression probe, average across layers, take the maximum across 512-token windows, and compare to a per-application threshold. The backbone is never fine-tuned and probes train in hours. Guy Elad walks through an animated demo with benign, direct-attack and long-document cases, then experiments showing that the useful layer band differs by backbone and modality, that last-token reading beats averaging over all tokens, and that logistic regression was good enough. Guy Shtar then shows the full detector as a short code listing using forward hooks and an early-exit exception, and the production work: cross-request GPU batching, skipping the language-model head, per-app calibration and a retrain loop. Results: 98.1% recall on 11,086 held-out attacks, 85.4% on 996 never-seen red-team attacks, about a 70% cut in successful attacks, about 7 false alarms per million, 59 ms median latency and roughly 11 times lower cost than a judge LLM.

What to do with it (this breakdown's reading)

  • Consider an activation-probe first line in front of, not instead of, an LLM judge; the evidence here supports a cascade, with the judge adding only 0.3 points of attack success (2.8% to 2.5%).
  • If you build any ML guardrail, test on entire held-out datasets from unrelated sources and report every dataset, because aggregate scores can hide a source that fails completely.
  • Set the false-positive budget with the product teams and calibrate per application; accept that near-zero false alarms costs recall.
  • Budget for production engineering (batching, early exit, retraining, per-app thresholds), which is most of what made this deployable, and plan GPU hosting.
  • Ask vendors of guardrails whether their detector generates tokens, can be injected itself, and how it was evaluated on novel attacks and on image-borne injections.

How far the evidence goes

This breakdown's assessment

  • The headline numbers are from the authors' own datasets and an internal baseline described as an older syntactic model; the talk gives no head-to-head accuracy numbers against named open detectors or frontier judges; the published description cites a 20+ dataset comparison, which the recording does not show.
  • 85.4% recall on never-seen red-team attacks means about one in seven still pass, and the 2.8% residual attack success has no stated attack-strategy mix; there is no adaptive-attacker evaluation against a probe whose backbone and layers an attacker might guess or probe.
  • The claim that the approach works for commercial black-box models rests on attack-transferability literature the speaker cited verbally; it is a statement about the detector scanning inputs with its own model, not evidence that detection transfers across attack styles.
  • The cost comparison (about 11x) and latency (13x) were shown without hardware, batch size, judge model or prompt details, so they cannot be reproduced from the recording alone.
  • The animated demo scores are labeled illustrative, so they show the mechanism, not performance.
  • The talk reports its own failures (the 140 of 140 miss and the recall-versus-false-alarm tradeoff) and gives specific production-engineering detail; the trained probes and thresholds were not shared.
  • The published description cites batching reducing latency from about 4.1 s to under 820 ms bit-exact; the recording does not show it, and the slide says batching changes 0.04% of verdicts, so batching is not bit-exact.

Limits the speaker acknowledged

  • Recall is not perfect; the operating point affordable on all traffic is not the one with best recall on novel attacks.
  • In-distribution scores overstate performance on novel attacks.
  • A whole source can fail (140 of 140 image-layout injections missed), so per-dataset reporting is needed.
  • Latency at p99 (645 ms) is above what traditional ML models achieve (under 200 ms).
  • Training needs benign data close to the protected agent's production distribution and an up-to-date attack collection.
  • Comparison with a newer detector model was still in progress at the time: initial results were comparable and depend on configuration and attack type.
